News.title: Fire shuts down runway at Heathrow Airport as ‘tinderbox’ grass ignites & firefighters race extinguish blaze
News.content:
A GRASS fire closed a runway at the UK’s biggest airport today.

Heathrow’s southerly runway was closed as the blaze took hold, sparking chaos and flight delays.



Firefighters and emergency services raced to the scene of the inferno adjacent to the tarmac, where planes were waiting to take-ff.

A Heathrow Airport spokesperson told The Sun: “Earlier our teams responded to a grass fire adjacent to the southern runway.



“The fire was extinguished quickly, both runways are operational and flights continue to arrive and depart from the airport.

“We apologise for any disruption caused while emergency services completed their safety checks, but this was essential to ensure the safety of our passengers and colleagues.”

Heathrow Runways posted on social media: “Grass area fire abeam runway 27L has closed the runway, we are now single runway ops on 27R UFN.”

Flyers faced with disruption took to social media, one wrote: “The one time I fly from Heathrow, it’s down to 1 runway and the trains down are disrupted by swans on the tracks. Can’t make it up.”

A second added: “Fun morning at London Heathrow Airport with a grass fire being dealt with beside runway 27L.

“Despite the recent rain, the grass is still like a tinderbox.”



A third said: “Looks largely contained. Water cannons had been brought out on both sides of the grassy verge that was on fire.”

This comes after Gatwick Airport was forced to ground all flights yesterday due to a “technical issue”.

It is understood a plane was stuck on the runway and was seen surrounded by fire trucks.

Many EasyJet flights were forced to divert to other airports in the area.

Last month a grass fire again beside the runway caused chaos for passengers at Heathrow.



London Fire Brigade were called to the scene and battled the blaze which was said to have caused one hectare of grassland.

Many passengers had their flights delayed by hours as the number of planes able to take-off and land was reduced.

News.title: Police probe after anti-Reform UK heckler ‘has hair pulled & is manhandled as she was thrown out of party conference’
News.content:
COPS have urged an anti-Reform UK heckler to come forward after she appeared to have her hair pulled and face grabbed when heckling Nigel Farage.

The woman was thrown out of the Reform UK conference in Birmingham on Friday afternoon after disrupting Nigel Farage‘s keynote speech.



Widely shared video however appears to show she was manhandled by the crowd as she was led out – with footage seeming to show her hair being pulled and her head grabbed.

The woman was one of a number of protesters to be escorted out after heckling the Reform UK leader.



West Midlands Police has asked the heckler to contact them as they are investigating the incident – but added that they have not received a formal complaint.

The party’s annual get-together was held at the National Exhibition Centre and saw the Reform leader’s speech disrupted four times.



Demonstrators and hecklers were thrown out each time, with activist group Climate Resistance claiming responsibility.

Reform home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf condemned any members who pulled the heckler’s hair.



Asked about the incident, the party’s home affairs spokesman told a conference fringe event: “On the question of whether I condemn people punching people, yes, I condemn people punching people.”

The activist group said the protester is considering whether or not to come forward to police.

A statement from West Midlands Police said: “We’re aware of a video circulating from the Reform UK conference showing an incident with a protester.



“We haven’t received a complaint but would ask the woman involved to come forward and contact us so we can carry out enquiries.

“Anyone with any information should contact us on 101 quoting log number 924 of 5 September 2026.”

News.title: I watched chaos of Lindsay Clancy ‘TikTok’ trial with mums & kids fighting outside court – case collapse was no surprise
News.content:
THE words of the local taxi driver rang in my ears after the judge declared the Lindsay Clancy case a mistrial: “Welcome to America, where they turn abject tragedy into entertainment.”

After watching how the extraordinary five-week trial unfolded first-hand, I wasn’t surprised that the jury, made up of nine women and three men, were unable to come to a unanimous verdict.





It was chaos from the start.

The case is a family tragedy of almost unbearable dimensions.

A mother – described as a “caring” and “wonderful” midwife – strangled her three young children, ages five, three, and eight-months-old, using exercise bands while her husband was picking up food.

She then jumped from a second-storey window at the family’s Massachusetts home and survived but was left paralysed from the waist down.

Her defence team doesn’t deny that she killed her children in January 2023.

They argue that she cannot be held criminally responsible because she was in the grip of postpartum psychosis, overmedicated, and failed by the very mental health system she had turned to for help.

Lindsay apparently heard a voice who told her to hurt herself and her kids.





The prosecution, however, says Lindsay made a calculated, intentional decision to kill her children.

And all of it – the sobbing defendant, the autopsy testimony, the grieving father on the stand – was streamed live for avid true crime fans to watch.

The trial, as a result, attracted the obsessive attention of amateur sleuths and armchair detectives who picked apart every detail and turned it into whodunit content.

Wild conspiracy theories swirled on TikTok and Instagram as people blamed her husband Patrick Clancy, claiming he was the real killer who had framed her.

This was despite CCTV footage and phone records placing him outside of the home during the killings.

Content creators also dissected courtroom footage, Lindsay’s body temperature at the time, and her Apple Watch details.

Lindsay’s lawyer Kevin Reddington became an unlikely hero and his “best moments” were clipped up to be shared by hundreds of people who supported her.

The parallel trial began to leak into the real one after Reddington tried to call a former mental health hospital employee as a witness after he found her through a viral TikTok where she criticised the facility.



As the jury spent seven days deliberating, people began to travel to Plymouth Trial Court to voice their opinion on what they thought the verdict should be.

Mum Christine Fernandes, 48, wearing three exercise bands around her neck, brought her 15-year-old daughter Elsie to protest outside the court.

Holding a “First Degree Murder, Stop The Nonsense” sign, she told me: “I watched the trial from the beginning.

“It caught my attention as I could relate to it in some way, shape, or form as I suffered from postpartum and I was on medications.

“It didn’t make sense to me and I needed to get to the bottom of it.”

She then proceeded to go into detail about what she believed had happened – labelling Lindsay as guilty because she had “evil eyes”.

Her teenage daughter chimed in: “It’s just morally wrong.”

Christine added: “She never reported any voices.

“She never did.



“I think in this situation the prosecution has the more difficult job as they have to do all the work to show that she was aware of what she was doing.

“I’m wearing exercise bands to remind people that three innocent little kids lost their lives that can’t defend themselves.

“It’s disgusting how a mother can do that and then attach an excuse to it to benefit her.

“It has turned the trial into a joke.”

Later that day, after the jury were sent home yet again, Christine screamed to the media and supporters that Lindsay’s lawyer Reddington was “scum”.

She became embroiled in an argument with another mum, who was on Lindsay’s side, and who had also brought her child along.

I had two questions.

Why were these children not in school and is this really an appropriate place to bring them?

I was ignored, however, as they loudly battled one another in a circle akin to the boxing ring.



Onlookers gathered and TikTokers made sure to film it, delighted that they had something to stream to their fans.

At one point, the kid, who looked no older than 10-years-old, told Christine: “Shut your yapper. You don’t know anything.”

In a moment that summed up the atmosphere outside the courtroom, Christine stopped her ranting to tell cameras her name (she even spelt it) and age, just in case they needed it.

It was unlike any court case I had witnessed in the UK.

Here, people were desperate for exposure, whether that be to get themselves on telly, or to gain new followers.

Melissa Merrill, who was spending seven-hours a day live-streaming the outside of the courthouse to TokTok, said she had started with a modest 2,000 followers and had now gained 10,000.

The next day, which happened to be the third day of jury deliberations, 13,000 people were watching.

I interviewed Melissa while she was live on TikTok to that audience (she often stopped to check her comments and speak intermittently to them).



She said she was supporting Lindsay, explaining: “This is touching a lot of mums.

“I had postpartum depression and there’s a stigma around it and mental health.

“Everyone wants to be a picture-perfect mum and it’s harder to admit when you need help as a parent.

“This case has opened up the door to that communication.”

When Melissa spent time in the courtroom – where her livestreaming wasn’t allowed – her 20-year-old son Josh would take over.

I asked him why it was interesting for viewers to watch an empty building? He then asked them my question and they instantly responded.

Josh said: “They want justice.

“They want to know what is going on.



“They want opinions and commentary.

“They want to know what is going through people’s minds.

“It’s all opinion-based.”

Melissa was just one of dozens who had travelled across the US to spend their entire days filming non-stop commentary on the developments.

When Lindsay’s lawyer Reddington left the courthouse everyday, they would also become part of the media scrum, clambering to show viewers his face and competing to ask a question.

At one point, the day before the judge declared a mistrial, it became so frenzied that we were almost crushed in the swarm, with nobody able to move, as TikTokers pushed their way to the front to hug Reddington.

One press photographer, who had been bashed to the point he had fallen to the ground, muttered: “This isn’t normal.”

Reddington himself became somewhat of a celebrity with supporters flocking outside the courthouse in the hope of catching a glimpse of him, telling him that he was an icon, and even giving him presents.

One woman said she had been there every day since the trial ended to tell him what an “incredible human being he was” and hopefully get a selfie with him.

She was dressed in a pink top alongside hundreds of other women who wore the slogan “Peace For Lindsay” to show her they were on her side.



As the deliberations wrapped up, I decided to join the masses and try my hand at livestreaming.

With a meagre 200 followers on TikTok, I wasn’t hopeful that I would get any attention, but to my surprise after an hour of streaming outside the courtroom, I had over 600 viewers.

That became 9,000 views by the time I finished 90 minutes later.

I had to be careful, of course, not to answer questions about what my own opinion was, but I discussed the possibility of a mistrial and told viewers what was going on inside.

This was the moment that Reddington had dramatically asked the judge to remove a juror who he believed was not following the law in regards to reasonable doubt.

The jury was split 11-1.

The judge, however, refused.

People argued in the comments and they rightly told me that I was wrong when I mistook Reddington for the district attorney Tim Cruz.



But dare I say, I started to see the point of these livestreams.

I revelled in the interaction, delighted in answering the questions and experienced the thrill of having a new person watching.

On Friday, when the jury handed a note to the judge to say that they were still deadlocked, and the public awaited the formal ruling of a mistrial, the US media joined in on the spectacle.

A CNN anchor began to cry as she discussed how the children were killed and a legal analyst tried to coin the catchphrase: “The deadlock on Plymouth Rock.”

Now prosecutors will decide whether they want to try the case again.

Let’s hope next time around things will be, as my cabbie aptly put it, a little less farcical.

News.title: I heard the Lindsay Clancy 911 call played in court – harrowing detail debunks the conspiracy theories, says protester
News.content:
A COURTROOM observer at Lindsay Clancy’s explosive murder trial says husband Patrick’s harrowing 911 call blows apart disturbing conspiracy theories surrounding the grieving dad.

Kimberly Souza, 58, has repeatedly attended the high-profile trial at Plymouth Superior Court and believes the devastating audio exposes the truth behind rumors that have swirled online.



Souza, a longtime Plymouth-area resident who now lives about 20 minutes away, first went to court on the seventh day of the trial and has since spent five days inside the courtroom.

She was also pictured holding up a sign outside honoring five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan.



The case has spawned a wave of conspiracy theories on TikTok and other social media platforms, with some armchair detectives going as far as baselessly accusing Patrick of killing his children and framing his mentally ill wife.

Online sleuths have picked apart everything from Patrick’s clothing and shoes on the night of the killings to his demeanor, his subsequent divorce from Lindsay and his remarriage earlier this year.

There is no evidence Patrick, who was pictured with his new wife this week, was involved in the killings and he has never been charged in connection with the deaths.

The speculation has become so intense that his attorney, Howard Cooper, has publicly put influencers and celebrities on notice over what he called defamatory claims about the grieving father.

After a mistrial was declared in Clancy’s trial on Friday, her defense attorney Kevin Reddington spoke out about the conspiracies.

“I think Patrick, you heard the 911 call. I think you can judge his credibility by that 911 call.



“I don’t know what is in Patrick’s mind I mean he testified, and the jury was able to evaluate him.”

Others have questioned details surrounding Patrick’s frantic 911 call, including whether Lindsay was able to speak after she slashed her wrists and neck and jumped from a second story window, leaving her paralyzed from the waist down.

But Souza said hearing the harrowing audio inside the courtroom left her in no doubt about Patrick’s reaction that night and believes his anguish should silence some of the rumors that have dogged him online.

“The biggest moment obviously was the 911 call,” Souza told The U.S. Sun.

“I understand that Patrick wanted it blocked from the public and I understand why now. It’s devastating, it’s heart-wrenching.



“People wouldn’t question him after hearing that.”

Patrick’s voice, she said, was particularly difficult to hear.

“The gut-wrenching voice of Patrick just got me the most, not even exactly what was happening, just to hear it in his voice,” she recalled.



“I can’t imagine faking that. It was absolutely real to me.”

Souza said some jurors were reduced to tears as the call was played.

She claimed, “You absolutely hear Lindsay say ‘basement.’ Then you hear his screams. And him talking about the children, ‘She killed the [f***ing] kids.’

“I don’t know how other people would assume you would react other than being in that position.

“Judging how he reacted and everything, I’m surprised he didn’t do anything to Lindsay himself because those were his three children. It was really hard to hear.”



Souza said she has become increasingly frustrated by claims circulating on social media.

“These controversies on TikTok or social media or whatever, that she couldn’t talk, is all false. She could absolutely talk, even for a brief moment, she could talk. I’m sick of all the conspiracy theories.

“I feel so bad for the man. He’s been going through hell, he’s gone through hell for three and a half years now. He doesn’t want to be here [at the trial]. It’s the last place he wants to be.

“I can’t wrap my brain around it. It’s as if they didn’t do any research themselves. And it doesn’t take much.”

Clancy, 36, has admitted to killing her three children at the family’s Duxbury home on January 24, 2023.



Jurors were tasked with deciding whether she was criminally responsible for their deaths.

Her defense argued that she was suffering from severe mental illness and undiagnosed postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors acknowledge she was mentally ill but argue she understood her actions were wrong and that the killings were planned.

The jury’s deliberations entered a seventh day on Friday after dramatic scenes in court Thursday when the foreperson raised concerns about one juror’s approach to reasonable doubt.

Reddington unsuccessfully pushed for the juror to be removed before Judge William Sullivan clarified the law and sent the panel back to deliberate.

Jurors ultimately remained deadlocked, and the judge declared a mistrial, bringing the end to the weeks-long trial.



Souza said she cannot understand how some people continue to make claims about the case without considering the evidence heard in court.

“I just can’t imagine talking like that without all the facts behind you. And not believing that the police did their due diligence, and the toxicology reports, and the GPS and everything else that has come forward.

“And her own lawyer has said several times during the trial that she did it.”

But Souza doesn’t have a great deal of sympathy for Clancy, telling The U.S. Sun, “I never want her out.

“Just because she’s paralyzed does not mean she’s not a criminal. I think she should be [held] criminally responsible. I think she just couldn’t take her life anymore.”



But others who have attended the trial have a very different view.

Tiffany Ahearn, 39, has been making the trip to court from Woburn and, having previously served time for drug and alcohol offenses, fears for Clancy if she is sent to jail.

She said, “Prison doesn’t do well with people who have or allegedly have murdered their children. No matter what. You’ll forever have that label in a prison.

“In a place like that, you are at risk.”

Amanda Aikulola, of the nonprofit Cherished Mom, has also attended court to raise awareness about maternal mental health and postpartum conditions and met with Clancy’s sister.



The organization focuses on postpartum psychosis, the condition Clancy’s defense contends she was suffering from, maternal suicide and other perinatal mood and anxiety disorders.

Aikulola said she had spoken briefly to Clancy’s family and argued that the case should prompt a broader discussion about maternal mental health.

“My thoughts on the case are that this is not an isolated incident. These things are happening and have been happening for a long time.

“What we hope to see is continued interest in these types of situations, the fractured mental health system that’s been exposed throughout the case, and the conversation around maternal mental health. We want to make sure that it doesn’t end with the verdict.

“When someone is asking for help, like Lindsay was, we need resources and we need healthcare providers educated.”



Asked whether she believes Clancy was failed by medical professionals, Aikulola said she did, but stressed that the problem was broader than any one individual.

“Yes. I wouldn’t say one medical professional, but I think it’s a very complicated system.

“I think we could look at the case, learn from it and understand how to reform and change the system and add additional stopgaps.”

Aikulola also addressed the intense online debate surrounding the case.

“I think a lot of things in our society have highly opinionated people without the understanding, education or context to have the opinions that they sometimes have, but that is just the world we live in.”



She said postpartum psychosis can be difficult to comprehend for people who have never experienced a psychiatric crisis themselves.

“When they go off the rails in any type of way, whether you have a stroke, a neurological issue or a psychiatric issue, and your brain isn’t working well, it’s hard to understand that experience unless you’ve lived it.”

Aikulola stressed that the Clancy case represents an extreme outcome but said there are many people who survive postpartum psychosis and recover.

“This is the worst-case scenario. It was like a perfect storm that brought this outcome to this family, but there are a lot of survivors.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“They share their stories, they teach and they educate, and that lived experience is really helpful for understanding what really happened here.”



If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988, or text the Crisis Text Line at 741741.

News.title: Dog plunged teeth into my little boy’s skull during bloodbath attack…I wrestled huge beast while holding baby daughter
News.content:
SAVAGE BITE Dog plunged teeth into my little boy’s skull during bloodbath attack…I wrestled huge beast while holding baby daughter

A HERO dad saved his son’s life after a vicious dog plunged its teeth into the four-year-old’s SKULL.

Jason Gooders, 36, charged at the dog and ripped it off his son, Noah, after he heard his boy screaming in their communal garden.



Horrendous pictures show the huge gash the dog left on Noah’s head after the mauling, which happened on the boy’s fourth birthday.

The animal’s owner, Shae Wright, was charged with being in charge of an out-of-control dog after the attack but he was let off with a community order earlier last month.



Jason, of Sutton, London, told The Sun that the family were leaving their home for a birthday trip to Chessington World of Adventures when the attack happened.

He said: “Noah ran out the back door to run to our car and then I heard barking and screaming.

“I ran out and saw Noah face down in the dirt in the garden and the brown Mastiff was on top of him. It had attacked him from behind and he had fallen forward.

“I could see its teeth in his head as it had pinned him down with its paws on his shoulders. I thought he was dead. It’s every parent’s worst nightmare. That image still haunts me now. You know every time I close my eyes I can just see that picture.



“Wright’s black dog was standing by Noah’s feet, almost guarding the other dog. It was almost like they were working together.

“I just ran straight at the dogs while holding my one-year-old daughter like a rugby ball in my left arm as I didn’t have time to put her down.

“I basically rugby tackled the brown dog off Noah as best I could. At that point my partner Charlotte came out and I grabbed Noah by his shirt collar and just threw him towards Charlotte and said ‘back indoors now’.

“Noah wasn’t walking and Charlotte pretty much dragged him inside and I scrambled back to my feet, making myself as big as possible to shield Charlotte and Noah.

“I wasn’t looking at the dogs and one of them bit me on the top of my leg and bum, ripping a hole in my shorts. Its teeth punctured my skin and muscle.



“It hurt but the adrenaline was pumping through me. I just shouted really loud and they then ran off.”

Noah’s mum and Jason’s partner, Charlotte Fordham told The Sun: “If Jason hadn’t gone out there my son wouldn’t be here now.

“I’m so grateful for that. I don’t know what I would have done if Jason wasn’t here. I don’t think I would have been able to drag the dog off.”



Jason ran back inside his home with his daughter after the attack, locking the door behind him.

He said: “The dogs were jumping up at the door almost like we had just taken away their dinner.

“I then looked around me and there was just blood everywhere. Tissue and flesh had been torn away from Noah’s skull. I could just see blood all over Noah and I told Charlotte I’m not waiting for an ambulance.

“I picked him up, ran out to my car, strapped him in, and drove to the hospital.

“I drove straight into the car park and ran straight into paediatrics; I didn’t even lock the car – I just left the key in the car.



“I basically kicked the door off its hinges at paediatrics because it’s kind of locked and the staff just turned to face me in shock.

“They saw the blood all over Noah and they came straight over.”

Noah was initially treated at St Helier Hospital, in Sutton, but then transferred to St George’s Hospital for surgery.



A plastic surgeon at the hospital revealed to the family that the bite had gone down to Noah’s skull.

Reading out her victim statement in Croydon Magistrates’ Court, Charlotte, 36, said: “I was told that if the bite was centimetres lower Noah could have died.”

The impact of the attack on their boy – who is now five – has been devastating, Charlotte added.

She told the court: “Noah is extremely anxious now. He no longer wants to be alone. He asks about the dogs all the time.

“He believes they are in dog jail but he’s worried they might break through the bars and try to get him.



“I don’t want Shae to get the dogs back or be allowed to own any dogs in the future.”

Charlotte and Jason praised staff at St George’s Hospital for lifting their lad’s spirits during his stay by giving him birthday gifts.

The couple are now calling on others to donate toys to St George’s by contacting the “St George’s Play Team” on Instagram.

Despite the family’s pleas, prosecutors did not apply for a disqualification order to ban Wright from owning dogs in the future.

Police handed the second dog involved in the attack back to Wright after the incident.



Jason is frustrated that he has not been banned from owning animals.

He said: “The prosecution let us down. My son nearly died and it’s almost like they’ve just gone ‘ah he’s still alive, it’s alright’.

“We knew something was going to happen with these dogs. I’m worried there will be another attack as he’s still allowed to have dogs.”

Charlotte said she always had concerns about the dogs – and even took a picture of one of them off the lead before the attack.

Noah’s seven-year-old brother has also been affected by the attack, suffering nightmares about being chased and recently telling his gran he was “so glad Noah didn’t go to heaven”.



Croydon Magistrates Court heard how Wright took the dog, named Smash, to be euthanised after the attack.

Robert Katz, defending, said Wright showed “empathy and compassion” over the situation and took responsibility, pulling the dogs away after it happened.

He added that it was a “freak incident” that could not have been predicted. Wright moved out of the area following the attack.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Croydon Magistrates Court handed Wright an 18-month community order.

He was ordered to carry out 200 hours of unpaid work and pay the Gooders family £1,000 in compensation.

News.title: Natalie, 17, said she was ‘popping to the shop’ & never came home – 20yrs on her dad has issued a final plea for answers
News.content:
FIND MY DAUGHTER Natalie, 17, said she was ‘popping to the shop’ & never came home – 20yrs on her dad has issued a final plea for answers

A DAD has issued one final plea for answers on the disappearance of his daughter 23 years ago before his “time is up”.

Natalie Putt told her family she was popping to the shops in Dudley, West Midlands, in 2003, but she never came home – leaving behind her newborn son.



New pictures of missing Natalie, who vanished aged 17 and would have been 40 this year, have been released by her father, David Putt.

David, who will be 70 next year, has said he’s desperate for answers so he can finally properly mourn his little girl.



The images show Natalie celebrating Christmas with her family and trying on her dad’s jacket.

David said: “It’s been 23 years since Nat went missing which is a very long time and this year would have been her 40th birthday.

“Somebody out there knows something, and I want to ask them to please come forward and contact the police.

“I don’t care how big or small the information may be, the family needs to know what happened to her.



“I will be 70 next year and I want to know what happened to her before my time is up.”

Natalie left her 11-week-old son Rhys at home with family, saying she was just nipping to the shops – but the teenager never returned.

Following extensive searches, a nationwide appeal and missing person enquiries, Natalie’s disappearance remains a tragic mystery.



Numerous tip offs from the public over the last 23 years have led to underwater search teams trawling rivers and lakes around her home.

Private land in Wombourne, South Staffordshire was also searched and a detailed forensic analysis of Natalie’s former home have all taken place.

David added: “Please try and set your mind back to 1 September 2003 and get in touch if you saw anything that could help the officers looking into my daughter’s disappearance.



“On 15 January 2019 the coroner pronounced Natalie deceased and her cause of death as unascertained, but we still have so many unanswered questions.

“Please, please help me and the family finally be able to mourn her properly with our questions around what happened to her answered.”

Despite huge searches of lakes, graveyards and woodland near her home, a body has never been found.

In March 2004, a local 18-year-old man was arrested in connection with her disappearance but later released without charge.

An inquest into her death in 2019 heard she most likely died on the day she was last seen, with many of her relatives believing Natalie was murdered.



Detective Inspector Jim Church, from our homicide review team, said: “It’s now been 23 years since Natalie went missing and we’re still working to get David and her family answers.

“From the day she disappeared her bank account has remained untouched, she didn’t take any possessions and the last communication she made with anyone was on that day.

“Unfortunately, despite our best efforts Natalie has never been found or heard from since the day she left her home.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“She was a new mum who loved her son and would never have left him or left her family without reason.

“Through my many chats with David, I know how much her disappearance has affected him and the whole family and all we want is to get her family some answers.”

News.title: Mega £2BILLION project boasting UK’s second-tallest residential building plus hotel, cinema and shops is revealed
News.content:
HUGE plans to build the UK’s second-tallest residential building is set to be approved.

The £2billion project will see a major development of seven new buildings, with one 69 storeys high.



The impressive new project will be located in South London‘s Vauxhall Square and the mammoth build will bring the UK’s second-tallest residential building to the area.

The UK’s current highest is located in Canary Wharf, which has a 75-storey residential tower block.



The development, planned by Applicant Vauxhall Square Limited, will also deliver over 1,000 flats.

The proposals also outline 1,164 co-living units and student accommodation for 699 residents.



While Lambeth Council’s Planning Applications Committee must approve the plans, it’s been recommended that they give the development the green light when they meet on September 8.

The swanky set of buildings will also be home to a hotel, a cinema and office spaces.

Plans also state that there will be community spaces as well as retail units and parking for cars and bikes.

A gym with a swimming pool is also set to be approved for the development.

News.title: Should Lindsay Clancy face a retrial?
News.content:
AFTER 38 hours of deliberations, jurors at the Lindsay Clancy trial couldn’t reach a verdict on whether the mother should be acquitted.

One juror held out against the other 11 and refused to unanimously agree if the 36-year-old should be held criminally responsible for the deaths of her three young children.



The judge formally declared a mistrial on Friday and Clancy’s lawyer has slammed the one jury member for “robbing” them of a not guilty verdict.

Clancy admitted to strangling her three children with exercise bands in 2023, but her lawyers argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and is not responsible.



Prosecutors have maintained the Massachusetts mum was acting intentionally and knew the difference between right and wrong.

The prosecution can request a retrial and the decision could be made during a status conference on September 29.

News.title: Reform promises to increase tax-free personal allowance to £15,000
News.content:
Reform UK is promising to increase the tax-free personal allowance to Â£15,000, if it wins the next general election.

Robert Jenrick, the party's economic spokesman, has pledged to introduce the tax cut within the first 100 days if he became chancellor saying it would provide "money that people really need right now".

It is seen by Reform insiders as the flagship policy announcement of its conference and perhaps their biggest tax policy between now and the general election.

Asked about two senior Reform aides being investigated by the party following a Channel 4 News undercover broadcast into claims about funding, Jenrick told the BBC Nigel Farage had acted swiftly and they had been suspended.

In undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totalled Â£500,000.

Electoral law sets out that to be a donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

Farage said on Friday that his party had "done nothing wrong" and had taken "no illegal money. In fact no money was taken at all."

Jukes denied wrongdoing and said he was stepping away from politics "in order to clear my name". Orr told Sky News he would cooperate fully with the party's internal investigation.

Orr is an associate professor of Philosophy of Religion at Cambridge University's Faculty of Divinity.

Responding to the Channel 4 News and Verbatim report, Cambridge University said it was "looking into these matters".

Jenrick told the Today programme that the party had taken legal advice and it did not believe it had done anything wrong.

Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported the party to the Metropolitan Police.

The Electoral Commission has said it is considering "all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit" and was in contact with the police.

News.title: Chris Mason: Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach
News.content:
Defections, those who leave one party and join another, have been a big part of the party's growth in the last year â not least the recruitment of former Conservative cabinet ministers Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman.

Elections have been as well - Reform's gains in the English local elections and the devolved parliament elections in Wales and in Scotland.

But so too has money. The backdrop to this conference was the swirl of questions about money even before Channel 4 News', and Verbatim Investigations', endeavours.

In the hour or two before its broadcast on Thursday night, senior Reform figures, including those directly caught up in it, projected a sense of being relatively relaxed about it. Awkward, embarrassing, but survivable.

Once it was broadcast, things changed. There was fury, I am told, and very quickly there was a sense of its gravity. "A few bottles of red were had, and we knew we had to act," is how one source described it to me. The conversations went on into the early hours.

Firstly, there was anger that it would drown out a conference that has been months in the planning. And yes, it has dominated conversation here in Birmingham.

Secondly, there was widespread concern about the image it projected, the impression it would leave.

Reform wants to project itself as a prospective party of government.

And yet the headlines allow critics to claim they are not just ramshackle and amateurish but can point to what looks like a pattern of activity, consciously pursued, to breach the law.

Absolutely not, Nigel Farage insisted to me, there was no such pattern.

But what of the ethos of the party? Journalist Tim Shipman in The Spectator writes , externalthat "it is the experience of everyone I have ever known near the summit of politics that political operations take their character and operating logic from the person at the apex of the triangle. Leaders set culture."

There is something in this. Take Rishi Sunak's Downing Street operation and Boris Johnson's. They were wildly different culturally, reflecting the very different characters at their helm. Would all the things that happened during Partygate under Johnson have happened under Sunak? Unlikely, I would have thought.

Some within Reform, who are full of admiration for Nigel Farage's chutzpah and gift as a communicator, are desperate to see a behind-the-scenes cultural shift that minimises the chances of further embarrassments. And, alongside that, a step up in the infrastructure and personnel to match.

Farage's team express frustration that this is precisely what they have been doing, but some are telling them internally they need to move more quickly.

Both James Orr, the party's head of policy; and Dan Jukes, Farage's right-hand man, will be missed profoundly by those inside the party.

Privately, some wonder if Orr may yet return.

Jukes, who has been a pivotal and loyal figure in Team Farage for years, was already dividing his time between the UK and the United States as his wife and baby are on the other side of the Atlantic.

Perhaps, some senior figures suggest, his immediate future might be in America. Does he return when the general election is nearer? Let's see.

Reform leave Birmingham winded and wounded by the last few days, their days in the sun overshadowed.

The question is how they deal with this and respond to it, in the coming weeks and months.

News.title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
News.content:
A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.

Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news.

"No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.

The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra Â£2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.

Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."

Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra Â£20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.

Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.

It also ranks highest for burglary, sexual offences, violence with injury, and criminal damage and arson.

Fuller said Cleveland Police had also experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force.

"It absolutely needs to change," she said.

Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".

She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."

Recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues.

"We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."

Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fuelling organised crime.

"When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said.

"They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."

News.title: 'I'd rather die than ring the police': Distrust and fear in Middlesbrough after A66 crash
News.content:
All but one of the residents who speak to us do so on the condition of anonymity. They are worried that showing their faces could place them or their homes at risk.

What message do the attacks send to people on this street, I ask one.

"Well, they should be scared, shouldn't they, that something's going to happen to their property if they say anything or get involved. So we don't."

Victoria, who moved here several years ago, says the escalating violence cannot be separated from the wider condition of the town.

"This is a social problem, especially in this area. Teesside has been massively neglected and ignored," she says.

The attack in Acklam is far from Middlesbrough's only recent case of a vehicle being used as a weapon. Back in May, a tractor was driven into a house on Priory Road, and since the A66 crash Cleveland Police has investigated at least two further rammings.

Detectives have also linked their wider investigation to a caravan fire on Attlee Road in Grangetown.

"It's getting worse," a nearby resident says. "They're always balaclava-ed up as well, do you know what I mean?"

He blames drugs.

"It can't be anything else. Why would you be like you are unless it was drugs?" he says.

Whether every incident is part of a single feud has not been established. But taken together, the rammings, fires and arrests have created a powerful sense that violence is being used to intimidate, punish and send messages.

What is most unsettling for these residents is the sense that nobody is fully in control.

Grangetown and South Bank are communities still living with the void left by the decline of heavy industry. Both now rank among England's most deprived neighbourhoods.

In South Bank, we see a group of teenagers tend three ponies tethered on the grass. Two perform wheelies on electric scooters while another uses a long stick to scatter rubbish.

On the adjoining estate, more than a dozen homes have boarded-up windows.

On a wall are the words "RIP 2UZZI", said locally to have been the nickname of Jakub Matusiak, who lived one street away.

One 17-year-old boy tells us he knew him. "He was my best mate," he says. "It's sad."

Elsewhere, three letters are repeated: "FTP" - an expletive directed at the police.

I ask the teenager if he would call the police if another young person approached him carrying a knife.

"No," he says. Before adding: "I've never needed the police in my life. I'd rather die than ring the police."

Again and again, the young people we speak to express a profound distrust of the police.

Cleveland's Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said what we'd heard was "horrifying".

"Yes, there are a small minority of people in the Grangetown area who blight those communities. But we will continue relentlessly to serve our communities."

The scale of the challenge facing the force and the community it serves is not new.

The area has some of the highest police-recorded crime rates in England and Wales.

Its leaders have been warning for years that its resources did not match the demands placed upon it.

But recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Since the crash, more than 200 additional officers have been deployed in Middlesbrough and surrounding communities. Their immediate task is to suppress the violence and identify those directing it.

There is also the question of restoring order and rebuilding trust and confidence.

News.title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
News.content:
Domestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it.

With two energy companies â the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK â due to undertake work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added.

On Saturday morning Milei's office said on X that it was launching sanctions proceedings against 45 people and companies. The announcement did not identify those targeted and it is not yet clear what impact they will have.

In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally.

The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the "Don-roe Doctrine", a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas.

Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics.

Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship".

News.title: Michael Owen doesn't tell his children he loves them - how big a deal is that?
News.content:
To the outside observer, Owen's love for his children is not in doubt.

The trailer for his new show, Meet the Owens, shows glimpses of what appears to be a happy home life with his wife and children. And in 2024, the former England striker spoke movingly about his son James's sight loss, saying: "If I could give him my eyes... I would."

Pushed by podcast host Laing to explain why he doesn't let the 'I love yous' flow freely, Owen told Laing that "I would love to be a little bit soft".

"I'm definitely getting softer," he said, "but still not soft enough to say anything like that."

Using the word "soft" to describe telling your children you love them reflects long-standing attitudes many fathers have towards parenting, both Dale and Dr Britto suggest.

They say it's a result of different contexts, such as culture, class, gender and a generational divide

"I think that's the dangerous part there," Dale says, "the belief of what men should and what men shouldn't do."

Many fathers believe their role is simply to "provide", but they can do so much more, he says.

"Men are much more than just providers... what about our emotional capacity and willingness to have conversations and be there as fathers? And maybe we can't provide, but you know what? Our presence is at full capacity."

He adds that he thinks people's style of parenting "always stems from somewhere", including whether they were often told they were loved as a child.

News.title: Police say these cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
News.content:
Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined.

These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see co-ordinated vandalism. Yet here, four surveillance cameras were attacked and cut down in the middle of the night.

The metal poles were severed, leaving the distinctive black oval cameras and accompanying solar panels lying on the ground. On some of the cameras was a red sign reading: "Notice. 24/7 video recording."

These cameras are run by a company called Flock Safety and this sabotage, which happened in late July, is a signal of growing concern over the nationwide spread of sophisticated AI-powered surveillance systems. Similar vandalism incidents have occurred in Minnesota, California and Georgia.

Proponents say they have made communities safer and have helped dramatically increase the rate at which crimes are solved. But recent examples of misuse have caused concern. Critics say the cameras, which take pictures of the rear of every car that drives past, are overly broad investigative tools that treat civilians like suspects.

They see the little black poles popping up in their neighbourhoods as visible reminders of state power, at a time when public confidence in institutions is historically low and many are concerned about the accelerating pace of technological change and the influence of AI on people's lives.

News.title: Counterfeit copies of experimental weight-loss jab flood black market
News.content:
Excitement around the creation of a new drug, especially one showing early promise in clinical trials, is often celebrated by those developing it.

But new weight-loss drug retatrutide has become a headache not only for Eli Lilly, the pharmaceutical company behind it, but for regulators in the UK and around the world.

The jab has not yet been approved for human use by any regulatory body.

But illicit, counterfeit dupes of retatrutide are currently flooding the black market.

Experts have told the BBC this is one of the first times they have seen copycat versions of an experimental drug, still in the throes of being tested, become so widely available.

Vials purporting to be "reta" as it's become known, are being sold in the UK in gyms, nail and beauty salons, hairdressers, on social media and even by flower sellers on the street.

"The world has gone mad," pharmacist and director of 24 HR Pharmacy, Sehar Shahid says. "People are effectively injecting an illegal drug and thinking it's safe.

"It's become so normalised people openly talk about their dealers, where's best to get it from and post all over social media."

One quick flick through my socials and I can order a batch of a drug billed as retatrutide in minutes - although I would have no proof what it's actually made of, what its effects would be and where it's come from.

Keen users are posting before and after "reta" pics on their TikTok feeds, describing how it has silenced food noise, helped them shed pounds and lose inches, with some saying it's completely transformed their lives.

The problem? Despite positive results in its most recent clinical trials, real retatrutide is still being tested for its safety and efficacy.

Only 50% of drugs in this Phase III stage of testing in the US are eventually approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), so there is no guarantee retatrutide will ever hit the market. The high rate of failure is primarily down to drugs not working as well in large, diverse human populations as they do in smaller early tests, or because they reveal unexpected safety hazards.

And the current, fake versions available may not resemble what's being developed in the safe confines of the laboratory.

News.title: Disruption at Port of Dover as masked men hold protest
News.content:
There has been major disruption at the Port of Dover due to a large group of masked men holding a demonstration.

Hundreds of protesters, dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads and were heard chanting "stop the boats".

Kent Police said it had been "engaging with protesters" and marched the crowd to Dover Priory railway station at about 11:30 BST. After that, people started to disperse.

Traffic was initially stopped from going in and out of the port but officials said approach roads were now "free flowing".

Paul King, Reform UK councillor for Dover West, said he had been told it was a "stop the boats protest".

A government spokesperson said they condemned "the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused".

Demonstrators told the BBC they did not want to talk to the media, although one said "send them back" and another said "stop the boats" when approached.

News.title: UK support for Falkland Islands 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims, No 10 says
News.content:
It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.

Two oil companies â Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum â are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.

A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government."

The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".

Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas.

"That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said, describing the UK as a nation "in decline".

On Thursday, President Trump hinted the US would not help the UK in any future Falklands conflict because Britain "had not been there to help me" during his war with Iran.

Trump's latest remarks on the islands come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review.

On Friday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK would "resolutely uphold" the self-determination of the islands.

Writing on X on Friday, Miliband said the Islands would remain British as that is the "overwhelming position of the islanders."

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable".

"Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he wrote in his own post on X.

In an earlier statement, Downing Street said it was "not the first time" the Argentine government had made economic threats against the Falkland Islands.

"We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources," it said.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "Britain does not surrender to bullies".

"If (Milei) wants a stronger Argentina, he should build its economy, not threaten others."

Although the US is formally neutral, Washington provided support for Britain's campaign to retake the islands after the Argentinian invasion in 1982.

Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.

The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

In a sign of the ongoing tensions between the two countries over the issue, Argentina players celebrated their victory over England in the World Cup by waving a banner in support of their country's territorial claim.

News.title: Lauryn Hill, Wyclef and Giggs among surprise guests at Jay-Z's long-awaited UK show
News.content:
Jay-Z's first headline solo show in the UK in more than a decade saw him celebrate hip-hop culture alongside a host of special guests, including Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and Giggs.

The US rap superstar rolled back the years for more than two hours - playing hits like 99 Problems, Empire State of Mind and Dead Presidents - as he took to the stage at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Friday night for the first of two shows in London this weekend.

The run is part of his Jay-Z 30 tour, which is marking the 30th anniversary of his debut album, Reasonable Doubt, and his culture-shaping career that followed.

Fans of his wife BeyoncÃ© had hoped she would join him on stage, like she did at two of his three New York shows this summer, as she was also celebrating her 45th birthday on Friday.

News.title: Tonnes of rubble including 'bits of old toilets' being dumped in village, residents claim
News.content:
Wrexham Council has also issued a temporary stop notice after a "significant amount" of material was deposited "without planning permission".

The council said it would also be serving enforcement and stop notices "to remedy the situation and have the land restored".

Tom Lawson, from Coedpoeth, said he was frustrated that the activity was not stopped by NRW when it was first spotted.

He estimated there were thousands of tonnes of material, which he said looked like "low-grade demolition waste", saying that he had seen tar and lead batteries in amongst the rubble.

He said he also feared the people responsible would "just walk away from it".

"It'll be left for the public to pay... it's just wrong," he said.

Wrexham-based company SOS Aggregates said it owned the land in Coedpoeth and had been depositing "grade 1A fill material" on the site to make a plateau on which to create the equine arena which would then be "landscaped".

A spokesman for the firm denied it had continued depositing on the site when the temporary stop order was in place, but said it had continued work once the order expired.

He said that they had told the council they would be submitting a planning application this week and that they were also seeking legal advice.

He said the company would also be providing evidence to NRW of the materials being used on the site.

The investigations in Coedpoeth come as another field on the edge of the nearby village of Minera has seen dozens of lorries depositing materials, which one local councillor described as "reeking of diesel".

Caravans have also been placed on the site opposite a cul-de-sac of bungalows on Nantlais.

The farmland was sold approximately two months ago, but according to the council no planning application has been submitted for development there.

SOS Aggregates said it had delivered recycled construction material to the site in Minera, but that it was not involved in work taking place there and did not own the land.

Wrexham Council has served a temporary stop notice due to "a breach of planning control and the change of use of the land to a gypsy and traveller site with associated engineering operations".

NRW said it was investigating the materials on the site and would take action if appropriate.

News.title: Moment mum catches suspected arson attack on CCTV
News.content:
A mum-of-two has said she was "disgusted" after watching CCTV of an arson attacker setting fire to her home.

Holly Cham, 33, from Bootle, in Merseyside, was away with her children when - in an incident caught on her security cameras - a stranger appeared to emerge from her garage, coming back into view as a fire took hold.

A 31-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of arson with intent to endanger life following a fire on 24 August, Merseyside Police said.

He was released on conditional bail pending further enquiries, the force said.

News.title: The Grand Tour's new presenters: 'I hope we prove the critics wrong'
News.content:
For a show built around the chemistry of its three former presenters, finding a replacement trio with such chemistry was always going to be as important as finding people who knew about cars.

Engelsman and Holland are an already established double act as the presenters of Throttle House, a motoring YouTube channel with more than three million subscribers.

The bigger unknown was who would become their third presenter.

That search eventually led the show's producers to Francis Bourgeois, a social media star better known for standing on railway platforms than behind the wheel of a supercar.

Engelsman says he and Holland had done chemistry testing with a number of people, but Bourgeois immediately felt different.

"As soon as Francis showed up, we were like: 'That guy'," Holland says.

Bourgeois remembers their first meeting taking place on a leather sofa in a hotel outside Basingstoke, where they mostly talked about what cars they owned.

By the time filming began, Holland says there was no need to consciously work out how to make the three-person dynamic function as "it just worked and clicked immediately".

While the chemistry came quickly, actually finding out they had the job was much less straightforward. Engelsman says there was "no immediate moment" when they were formally told they had been chosen.

"It was the most gradual thing," he says.

He and Holland initially thought they were simply part of a wider audition process, but then found themselves repeatedly being invited into writers' rooms and asked for their views on ideas for the show.

For Bourgeois, that uncertainty may have been helpful as he admits he'd "just fall apart and start crying" if he'd found out about the job.

There is a clear generational shift with the new presenters, all three of whom built their profiles on social media - and critics have been mixed on how successfully that translates to The Grand Tour.

The Independent's three-star review, external described the reboot as "all rather safe" and said the presenters feel "stilted".

The Guardian's review, external agreed and called the trio a "decent, if slightly anonymous, presence" who seem "quite meek and pleasant, and without any obvious dynamic".

But it did praise Bourgeois, with Stuart Heritage calling him "the most enthusiastic enthusiast currently working on planet Earth".

The FT also awarded the show three-stars, external and said that while the big budget spectacles are enjoyable to watch, they also feel "a little muted".

It added that "the real question is whether a series that has been driven by big personalities like Clarkson, May and Hammond can survive with a new team".

Hammond tells BBC News he tuned in for The Grand Tour's return and said it was great to see the new team getting going.

"That's the most important thing for them is to make their show. We made our show and we're really good at being us. They're going to be really good at being them," he says.

Hammond says the audience need to "give them the chance" to show that.

News.title: Woman whose XL bully dog killed her cousin given suspended prison sentence
News.content:
A woman has been given a suspended prison sentence after her XL bully dog attacked and killed her cousin.

Kelcie Reed, 24, of Bristol, previously admitted being in charge of a dog dangerously out control, causing the death of Morgan Dorsett.

The 19-year-old, from Shrewsbury, died from neck injuries caused by the attack, which happened at Reed's flat in south Bristol in February 2025.

At Bristol Crown Court, Judge Anna Richardson sentenced Reed to 18 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months. She will also be required to undergo mental health treatment.

Emergency services were called to the dog attack at a flat in Cobhorn Drive, Bishopsworth, but despite their best efforts, Morgan died from bites to her neck and face, a post-mortem examination ruled.

The dog, named Prince, which belonged to Reed and her boyfriend, was sedated at the scene and later "humanely destroyed", police said.

News.title: Rock stars gather on tiny Scottish island for world stone skimming championships
News.content:
Contenders from around the world are converging on a tiny Scottish island for one of the country's most unlikely international sporting events - the world stone skimming championships.

The annual contest on the isle of Easdale, in the Inner Hebrides, has attracted a record number of international entries, representing more than 30 nations, with some flying in from New Zealand and Canada.

Last year's competition was rocked by a cheating scandal after some contestants were accused of stone tampering.

Toss Master Kyle Mathews, co-organiser of the event, said an official tournament geologist had been appointed this year, leaving no stone unturned in keeping the 400 challengers in order.

The contest was first held in 1983, inspired by an alcohol-fuelled conversation in a pub, and has been held every year since 1997 apart from an interlude during Covid.

Traditionally a male-dominated sport, efforts have been made to make it more inclusive, with this year's event attracting a record number of women and under-16s.

News.title: Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry schedule, results, kick-off times and how to watch South Africa vs New Zealand
News.content:
From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging.

At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story.

The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it.

News.title: South Africa v New Zealand LIVE: Latest updates as Springboks and All Blacks battle in third Test
News.content:
Jets perform dramatic low flyover ahead of South Africa vs New Zealand

South Africa and New Zealand collide in the third Test of a heated Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series that continues to deliver thrills and drama.

The Springboks levelled affairs at 1-1 with a strong win in Cape Town last week, hitting back against the All Blacks – on and off the field, as it happens, with Rassie Erasmus issuing a strong response to suggestions that his side had been scrummaging illegally. In the last encounter on South African soil, the world champions will look to secure a drawn series at least with another success at FNB Stadium in Soweto.

The All Blacks showed, though, their capacity for try-scoring even while below their best seven days ago. A backline full of threat remains intact, and will look to again trouble a South African defence that has shown more chinks than usual so far in this series.

News.title: Man City v Coventry LIVE: Ndiaye makes debut but Fernandez on bench after record Premier League transfer
News.content:
Why Enzo Fernandez Will Either MAKE Or BREAK Man City

Manchester City host Coventry City in the Premier League as Enzo Maresca’s team look to continue their winning start to the season.

Erling Haaland got off the mark and Rayan Cherki also grabbed a brace in a 4-1 win at Crystal Palace last week, before a franctic end to the transfer window saw City equal the British transfer record to sign Enzo Fernadez from Chelsea for £125m and add Iilman Ndiaye from Everton in a £60m deal. Ndiaye comes straight into the team while Fernandez could make his debut from the bench.

Coventry’s start to life in the Premier League doesn’t get any easier after their opening day defeat at champions Arsenal and last weekend’s sucker punch against Hull, where Frank Lampard’s side lost 1-0 after conceding from a late counter-attack. The Championship winners are prepared for another tough afternoon.

“I think we all know that it will not look like last season and the quicker we realise that the better,” Lampard said. “Last season was an incredible season for us because we won a lot and everything becomes easier in that moment. So it’s important that we understand the rigours of the Premier League.”

News.content:

Elon Musk sent dozens of self-driving Cybercabs without steering wheels or brake pedals onto the streets of Austin, Texas, on Thursday, betting that Americans will overcome their fears of rides with “no control” and hop inside.

The rollout of the gold-colored Teslas, which give passengers no way to take control in an emergency, comes as the company prepares to launch the service in other cities. Tesla shares have suffered amid a slump in vehicle sales, but they rose more than 5% Thursday on hopes that the futuristic-looking taxis will catch on quickly.

“No steering wheel, no pedals,” Tesla teased on X before the launch. Musk followed with a post showing a giant Cybercab floating above the Austin skyline and later wrote, “A Storm of Cybercabs.”

An invitation-only launch event was expected to be held later Thursday.

It is unclear how soon Musk intends to roll out the Cybercab service, but he needs to move quickly.

Tesla trails self-driving taxi leader Waymo in the number of cabs deployed and trips completed. To catch up, it must demonstrate that its camera-only system can safely navigate streets and avoid pedestrians. By contrast, Waymo and another rival, Amazon’s Zoox, supplement cameras with radar and a laser-based technology called lidar.

Even if the technology works well, Americans still need to be convinced.

A Pew Research Center survey conducted in February found that seven in 10 U.S. adults were “not too” or “not at all” comfortable riding in a driverless car.

Tesla stock was battered last year after Musk took over President Donald Trump’s government cost-cutting campaign, dubbed DOGE, and embraced extreme-right political candidates, sparking protests at Tesla showrooms and boycotts by car buyers in several countries.

Tesla posted a second consecutive annual decline in vehicle sales last year. Its profits plunged, and it lost its crown as the world’s best-selling electric vehicle maker to China’s BYD.

Austin has had a self-driving Tesla “robotaxi” service since June last year, but those cars are equipped with steering wheels and brake pedals. The service, which has since expanded to five other cities in Texas and Florida, initially carried passengers with safety drivers aboard to take over in case of problems.

Tesla has more than 200 “unsupervised” robotaxis in those cities, meaning they operate without safety drivers aboard, according to the monitoring site RobotaxiTracker. Waymo has more than 4,000 such vehicles in 14 cities.

In the Pew survey, 16% of U.S. adults said they would be “somewhat” comfortable riding in a driverless car, while 7% said they would be “extremely” or “very” comfortable.

Separate Gallup polling conducted in 2025 found that skepticism about the safety of driverless cars had risen over the previous several years. More Americans said all or mostly human-operated cars were the safest option than in a 2018 poll.

It is unclear whether Musk is the right person to coax people into cars with no human controls. Another Pew poll conducted in January found that nearly six in 10 U.S. adults had a “very” or “mostly” unfavorable view of him.

Musk eventually hopes to send full self-driving software to hundreds of thousands of Teslas through a software update. That would allow Tesla owners to turn their cars into taxis for hire when they are not using them.

But regulators in the U.S. and overseas have signaled that he still has some convincing to do.

Tesla has not received approval for drivers to use even its partial self-driving software in most European Union countries. In the U.S., where the software has been downloaded and used, regulators have opened several investigations into its safety.

One probe is examining the software’s role in several Tesla crashes in fog, sun glare and other low-visibility conditions, including one in which a pedestrian was killed. Another is investigating dozens of incidents in which Teslas using partial self-driving software ran red lights or drove on the wrong side of the road, sometimes crashing into other vehicles and causing injuries. A third is examining why Tesla apparently violated regulatory requirements by failing to report crashes promptly.

Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen evoked memories of their 2021 title scrap as they clashed in practice for the Italian Grand Prix.

Hamilton and Verstappen, the latter already aggrieved with his one-time rival for appearing to get in his way earlier in the session, came together in the closing moments.

Hamilton was forced to take to the escape road at the opening chicane – the scene of their infamous accident five years ago – after Verstappen launched his Red Bull underneath the seven-time world champion’s Ferrari. The pair came within centimetres of making contact with one another.

“I got blocked by Max,” said Hamilton over the radio. “Yeah, he caused that,” counter-claimed Verstappen on the Red Bull intercom.

George Russell will head into qualifying as the favourite to secure a much-needed pole position after he finished quickest in final practice.

Russell, who was fastest in yesterday’s second running at Monza’s Temple of Speed, again led the way in the concluding session prior to qualifying later today.

The Englishman saw off Hamilton by a commanding 0.226 seconds, with Verstappen third.

open image in gallery Mercedes’ George Russell set a commanding pace in final practice (Bradley Collyer/PA) ( PA Wire )

Kimi Antonelli, who leads Mercedes team-mate Russell and Hamilton by 59 points in the championship standings, will serve a grid sanction for an engine change and start tomorrow’s race from the back of the field. He finished fourth in the order, 0.361 seconds slower than Russell.

World champion Lando Norris, who arrived in Italy off the back of consecutive wins in Hungary and the Netherlands, took fifth – four tenths off the pace.

Qualifying takes place at 16:00 local time (15:00 BST).
