Last weekend, a group of New Yorkers filed into a private screening room in Chelsea to watch It Ends — a new horror thriller from first-time director Alexander Ullom. The film follows a group of four college grads who go on a late-night drive, only to find themselves on a never-ending highway.

But this was no ordinary screening. The room had been stocked with supplies that seemed more suited to a nuclear bunker than a movie theater. Hosted by Neon, the film’s distributor, the event brought together a handpicked group of cinephiles for an endurance contest that required them to watch It Ends on repeat for up to 36 hours.

27-year-old Fola Olusanya was among the contestants, equipped with blankets, water bottles, Clif bars, cough drops, Tylenol and a handheld fan. She and the others had been challenged to sit through the 89-minute movie as many times as possible between Friday at 7 p.m. and Sunday at 7 a.m. Their reward? 25 cents per minute with the prize capped at $540 per person.

“I kind of tried to predict the worst-case scenario of being stuck in a movie theater for a few hours and just expanded the contents of what usually goes in my purse,” Fola told The Independent.

The “last man standing” competition, as Neon described it, required participants not to leave the theater for anything other than a bathroom break. Each person was given a $250 theater concessions credit, which excluded alcohol, and they were allowed to bring in their own snacks and drinks.

open image in gallery Neon's contest challenged participants to watch Alexander Ullom's directorial debut 'It Ends' on a loop ( Neon )

While spending a weekend in a movie theater might sound dreamy to some, Fola said watching the same film over and over again came with some painful side effects.

“The hardest part of the night was the crazy headache I had,” she recalled, adding that two of her team members suffered the same fate. “I don't really get headaches after movies at the theater, but maybe it was exhaustion, or an empathy headache because our [team’s] bond together got so strong.”

Neon selected teams of four in New York City and Los Angeles to take part in the stunt after they submitted video applications online. Those who managed to make it through the full 36 hours were promised a $500 bonus on top of the $540 they had already earned.

Fola’s group ended up completing five watches of the film and meeting director Ullom and members of the crew at the event.

“I know I could have kept going longer, but it was one of those headaches that made even laughing hurt, which sucked, because I was having a ton of fun,” she said, adding, “I knew I was kind of losing it by the end of the third watch because everything we said felt really funny, and I was super tired.”

However, delirious laughter might have been the key to enduring the movie marathon. A group of four who completed all 36 hours of the challenge said that humor helped them stay afloat during the wee hours in the Metro Private Cinema.

One of the winners, 24-year-old Veronica Gilligan, told The Independent: “Going into the screening, my group made an agreement that we would not be leaving before the 36 hours were up, and I’m proud to say we did, in fact, last the whole time.”

They completed 24 viewings of the movie and made $1,040 per person, Neon confirmed to The Independent.

“We laughed, we lived, we cried,” Yasemin, one of the winning group members, wrote in her Letterboxd review of the film. Another winner, Jake, added: “I think I memorized the whole movie. It’s baked into my subconscious now.”

As with any good rewatch, Fola found that her understanding of the film shifted with each viewing — something she said was partly shaped by talking it through with her friends.

“I definitely did not have the same reaction to the movie after each viewing,” Fola said, adding that the “shock value” of the thriller “wore off after time because I could anticipate it.”

“I think I also had time to dive deeper into different aspects of the movie during each watch — the editing, the cinematography and the characterization — and I had different reactions to each one,” she said.

Though it may have been a marketing stunt, the competition ended up mirroring the very themes at the heart of Ullom’s directorial debut: friendship and the intimacy that can emerge from a surreal, shared experience.

open image in gallery ‘It Ends’ follows a group of friends who become trapped on a never ending road trip ( Neon )

Actor Akira Jackson, who plays one of the four friends in It Ends, might as well have been speaking about the movie marathon when she told the New York Times recently: “This entire movie is about who you become when there’s nothing to regulate you and there’s nowhere to hide.”

“There were moments when the endlessness of the screenings became kind of annoying, mostly when we wanted to fall asleep, but it was never unbearable,” Veronica said. “A big part of why we all agreed to do the challenge in the first place was because we’re all such good friends, so it kind of felt like we were getting paid to hang out for two days straight.”

Fola too found herself relying on the group to get through the increasingly dreamlike experience. “I barely paid attention to the second watch because my group and I were dissecting what we’d seen, coming up with theories, and just chatting in general. Watches three to five were when we started reciting lines from the movie and dancing with the characters during a short sequence,” she said.

At some point, It Ends became less something they were watching and more something they were collectively living with.

“After 36 hours, we started to feel way more connected to the movie,” Veronica said. “We were quoting specific lines and creating inside jokes related to it.”

“By the end, we were pretty exhausted,” she admitted. “But I would do it again in a heartbeat.”

News.title: ‘It’s just a useless gimmick’: Telegraph readers react to Dyson’s latest gadget
News.content:
Would you spend over £400 on a toothbrush? Telegraph readers aren’t convinced.

The new Dyson CameraJet has just launched, retailing for £419.99, which brushes, flosses and mouth-washes in one, with the help of a camera.

After Rebecca Astill gave her verdict on the gadget, we asked Telegraph readers for their views and whether Dyson can convince them to trade in their old faithfuls.

They share the toothbrushes they swear by, from manual to electric models, and whether they see any reason to upgrade. Here’s what they had to say.

Why readers are unconvinced

The majority of readers seem unconvinced by the CameraJet, with John arguing that a toothbrush and a smartphone “sounds like two accidents waiting to happen. Squirted in the eye with mouthwash as you drop the phone down the toilet”.

“It’s just a useless gimmick,” argues reader Donald Mckie, a retired NHS dentist. “The average patient wouldn’t have a clue what they would be looking at in their mouth on a phone screen,” he adds.

“Dyson as a brand is an aspiration for many but I don’t know how this appliance would improve anyone’s oral health.”

In his view, “the tank for the mouthwash at 12.5ml is far too small, the industry average will be somewhere near 250-300ml” to last long enough and successfully dislodge sticky plaque.

He also questions the picture quality of the camera with water spray, saliva, lips, facial hair and toothpaste in the way. “People nowadays will expect pin sharp detail, which I doubt this will deliver.”

News.title: DiCaprio’s Amazonian warrior queen
News.content:
It was while she was in hiding after recovering from the sixth attempt on her life, that the activist Juma Xipaia got a call asking if she would agree to be the subject of a documentary. The first female chief of the Middle Xingu region of the Brazilian Amazon, Xipaia was well known in Brazil for her passionate attempts to protect her indigenous community from the effects of deforestation, illegal gold-mining and – in particular – the catastrophic environmental consequences of the $11 billion Belo Monte hydroelectric dam project, a wildly ambitious and destructive endeavour that has affected livelihoods, fish stocks, ecosystems and biodiversity, with legal challenges still ongoing today.

Thirty-four-year-old Xipaia’s outspoken resistance and exposure of corruption relating to the dam’s construction led to the threats on her life. The last attempt was by poisoning, via a food delivery company, which resulted in her being on a ventilator with 70 per cent organ failure. She was on the verge of death, when, she says, she had a dream that she was given a choice – to take the easy path of dying, or the difficult path of coming back, and because she’s a fighter, that’s the one she chose. And a week later she walked out of the hospital.

Leonardo DiCaprio described the activist as one of the most incredible people he’d ever met Credit : Lalo de Almeida/Folhapress, FSP

Like many activists representing indigenous communities she walked a tightrope between protecting the interests and traditions of her people, and not being perceived as standing in the way of progress in terms of the economic development that benefits Brazil as a whole, a paradox that was defined when President Lula da Silva regained power in 2023, and brought Xipaia into government.

Richard Ladkani, a film director who has made vibrant environmental documentaries such as The Ivory Game (about poaching) and Sea of Shadows (marine activists), was the man who called her. It was 2019, when Brazil was still under the brutal rule of Jair Bolsonaro and destruction of the Amazon was at its peak – an area of rainforest the size of Belgium was burned during his presidency, and thousands of illegal goldmines flourished, contaminating the forest, polluting the river with mercury (mercury is used to bind gold) and bringing crime and disruption to previously pristine areas.

Film-maker Richard Ladkani in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

“All summer long we had seen these dramatic apocalyptic images,” says Ladkani. “And I was posing for photos at the premiere of Sea of Shadows, with [executive producers] Leo DiCaprio and Jane Goodall, when Leo leaned over and whispered, ‘So Richard, what’s next?’

“And I said, 'We've got to do something about the Amazon.’”

DiCaprio came onboard as producer, and Goodall as an ambassador. Ladkani knew he had to find a powerful central figure to provide human and emotional context, someone who would be the voice of the Amazon. He drew up a list of possible candidates, until the Brazilian journalist Eliane Brum told him “do not make a decision until you have spoken to Juma Xipaia – when she speaks, the world listens. She can silence a whole room with her energy.”

‘For a long time I had been seen as a soldier, an army of one’

Right now, in a small restaurant in New York, Xipaia is not really in the mood to talk. It is February, and it’s snowing, and Ladkani, Xipaia and her husband, Hugo Loss, are here to publicise the resulting documentary, Yanuni – which took six years to make – at a screening attended by UN representatives and Brazilian diplomats. The recent news about Trump’s exploits in Venezuela has shaken them all and, more specifically, Juma has had a bad experience with American food which doesn’t really agree with her. She is a little reticent at first, but soon opens up with the help of an interpreter, and explains to me what it meant to be a cacique (chief), and how she was selected.

Indigenous leader Juma Xipaia and her husband Hugo Loss in the city of Aracaju, Brazil Credit : Lalo de Almeida/Folhapress, FSP

“I never chose to be a cacique,” she says, “but I couldn’t stay quiet in the face of exploitation of my people – there was violence, and women being harassed and raped.” She is referring to the collateral damage that importing thousands of workers to build a dam inevitably brings. “Usually the role of cacique is given to the oldest male in the community – my dad and my uncles and my brother were all caciques, but the elders knew that they could trust me never to negotiate our rights with corporations or politicians, never to compromise. For a long time I had been seen as a soldier, an army of one. I accepted the position for two years, with the goal of strengthening on our territories and bringing sovereignty to our people.”

Xipaia was born in 1991 and had an idyllic childhood, she says, growing up in Tucumã, a small indigenous community along the Iriri River, about 250 miles west of the city of Altamira. They lived in wooden houses and ate fruit and nuts from the forest and fish from the river, and in 2006 she moved to Altamira for her education. But threats were encroaching her community, with land opened up for mining and farming, and in 2011, a licence was granted to construct the Belo Monte Dam, to stop up parts of the Xingu River, one of the most species-rich areas of the Amazon.

Aged just 21, Xipaia spoke out against the dam at a public hearing, but despite lawsuits, protest from indigenous people and large sections of society, construction went ahead. Xipaia attended law school in Altamira and studied plans put forward by Norte Energia, the company that built Belo Monte, helping to expose corruption that was going on within. In 2015, at the age of 24, she became a cacique, the first female leader of her people. Other communities had been bought off by Norte Energia with gifts of stoves, fridges, TVs.

In November 2019, she led a protest of angry Brazilian landowners and farmers to disrupt the Amazon: Center of the World international conference in Altamira. But by now she had become a target, and by the time Ladkani called her she had survived six attempts on her life, including her car being rammed with children in the back, and a threat to kidnap her son. She went into hiding for a year and she didn’t want to talk to anyone.

“She thought, the only way I’m going to survive is if I stop talking, because when I talk, people want to kill me,” Ladkani says. But she was finally convinced to take a call from him, and from the first moment, he says, he knew he had found the voice for his film. “Her poetry is the thing that stands out – the way she can describe emotions and feelings and put things into context, I felt it was unique. And when she told me the story of how she almost died because of the poisoning, I was in tears.

“I told her I wanted her to be the voice in the film and also offered her the role of producer. Because I knew nothing of indigenous life and I needed her to lead the way.”

An aerial view of the Belo Monte hydroelectric dam in Altamira Credit : CARLOS FABAL

It was a struggle from the word go. Xipaia was not happy about a translator being involved because of security reasons; she couldn’t trust anyone. So Ladkani, who is Austrian, took intensive lessons in Portuguese and within six months was fluent. “It was a key thing to show that I meant business and took her concerns very seriously,” he tells me.

The security budget for the film was huge, they needed the best, most experienced people: safe houses, secure drivers. And the arrangements had to extend for a year after filming was completed – a total of seven years. “Leo was extremely important here because he raised the first third of the budget, and this encouraged other philanthropists to be part of it.”

Filming began in 2020. There was no script and Ladkani didn’t know what he was going to get from it, just that he needed to tell the story of the pillaging of the Amazon via Xipaia’s voice.

And in the end it was a wild ride: it started with Xipaia leading protests against Bolsonaro, but after Lula was elected in 2023, he established a Ministry for Indigenous Rights, of which Xipaia was made state secretary, implementing a series of bills for the protection of the forest and employing lawyers, biologists and engineers to combat the destruction of the Amazon.

Juma Xipata and Leonardo DiCaprio at the Yanuni Premiere during the 2025 Tribeca Festival in New York City. Credit : John Nacion/Getty Images for Tribeca Festival

The film documents her move from her village to set up home in Brasilia with her son; getting together with her husband Hugo Loss, head of special operations for Ibama (the Brazilian Institute of Renewable and Natural Resources), an elite outfit conducting raids on illegal mines; and the birth of their first child, who was called Yanuni.

It was a lengthy, exciting journey, an improvisation which resulted in thousands of hours of film. “I just had to go with the unpredictable. The strength of any documentary is when unforeseen things happen, because a twist in direction is the greatest thing of any film structure.

“And we had that multiple times. I had chosen a woman to be the voice of the Amazon and two years later she became the second most powerful woman in the Indigenous Ministry – I get goosebumps now at the sheer luck. That was the first twist, and then Hugo enters her life, who happens to be this charismatic soldier of an elite force who would take me to the frontline of the Amazon resistance, and then Juma becomes pregnant and gives birth to Yanuni. Holy s**t. If I had written that as a script, everyone would have thrown it out as complete fiction.”

‘I said, how dangerous is it? And he said, “Well, the risk of you dying is 50 per cent”’

Leo DiCaprio was a producer on the film (rather than his usual role of executive producer), which meant he was far more involved. “He not only provided the money, but he gave me meaningful support throughout the production,” says Ladkani. In November 2021 DiCaprio attended Cop 26 in Glasgow, where he met Xipaia for the first time. “That meeting was spectacular – Leo posted a picture of the two of them together and said that she was one of the most incredible people he’d ever met.” The resulting attention helped to protect Xipaia, because a public profile is to some extent a safeguard. “There she is next to DiCaprio, so she’s not just a voiceless indigenous person from somewhere in the Amazon.”

There were many technical challenges. Because of security, Ladkani couldn’t film in the normal way, with lighting and a crew. “I had a second cinematographer, a brilliant guy from Brazil, called Fábio Nascimento, and I took him with me when I could – but that was only 30 per cent of the time. The rest I shot alone. I downsized my gear and basically shot the film with a DSLR, like a photo camera, so I looked like a tourist. To an outsider, I was just a white gringo taking pictures.” Xipaia had a hidden microphone beneath her shirt. If Ladkani was ever confronted, he claimed to be a YouTuber.

“Security demanded that we shot the film incognito, and that became its strength, because I was embedded within the family to the extent that they stopped noticing me,” says Ladkani.

An illegal gold-mining ship destroyed by Ibama in the Brazilian Amazon – it is dangerous work, with agents risking serious injury and even their lives Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

Hugo Loss’s job involved protecting indigenous communities and flying over the forest and rivers of the Amazon routing out illegal goldmines, dredgers and excavators. His small team lands, arrests the miners and sets fire to all the expensive equipment, which is too bulky to confiscate. In the film we see massive plumes of thick black smoke rising above the forest. Penalties for environmental crime are insubstantial, but, says Loss, “It’s not for President Lula to change those things, it’s Congress, and it’s hard to change the law. But destroying the equipment is a real deterrent, because the machines are expensive, so it’s a risky investment.”

An illegal gold mine in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

Loss and Xipaia met when her village was attacked in 2020 by illegal goldminers; she was in Altamira, a two-day boat ride away. She put out a cry for help on social media and Loss, who was also in Altamira, saw it and responded right away. He picked Xipaia up in a helicopter and asked her to take him to the exact location of the miners’ dredger. The attackers spotted them and ran, but Ibama were able to seize their boat and secure the area. “He saved her village and her people and her parents from an immediate attack and they fell in love and have been together ever since,” says Ladkani.

“I’m usually very shy about these things but from the first time I saw her in the helicopter I couldn’t stop thinking about her,” admits Loss. “Three months later I was doing an Ibama operation on land to remove some illegal loggers and I saw a hawk’s nest and I took a picture of it and sent it to her,” says Loss.

“It’s the bird whose feather I wear in my headdress,” interrupts Xipaia, shyly. She admits that she had first met Loss before the helicopter ride, at a meeting, but he was leaving as she arrived. “He shook my hand and I made eye contact with him and something told me – I can’t really explain what – that he was going to be my husband.”

Loss holds a Master’s degree in social anthropology from the University of Brasília and is one of Ibama’s most experienced field agents, yet he spent a good part of his career sidelined by Bolsonaro, who had no interest in protecting the environment. In February 2023, under Lula, he was appointed Ibama’s coordinator of enforcement.

Loss has taken part in hundreds of operations. His job is a dangerous one. We watch him flying helicopters over swathes of forest to spot mines, or patrolling the rivers looking for dredgers. Recently one of his team was killed in an ambush, another got burns over 60 per cent of his body.

Hugo Loss, Xipaia’s husband, on a mission to destroy illegal mining equipment for Ibama, Brazil’s government enforcement agency

Ladkani asked to accompany Loss on a raid. “Hugo told me, it's too dangerous, the risk of you dying is too high. It’s a small team, and you would be taking the place of a soldier on the helicopter so we would be down one security man, which means our job is much harder, and by the way, if we get into a gun fight, we are not your bodyguards, we are there to finish a job. You would have to save yourself.

“I said, how dangerous is it? And he said, ‘Well, the risk of you dying is 50 per cent.’ I laughed – and then I realised he wasn’t joking.

Film-maker Richard Ladkani in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

“Of course I had to think about that – I have a wife and two daughters. My wife and I discussed it. She grew up in a war zone in Beirut, so she understands threats, and how you can mitigate risks as well. She is also the producer of this film. We have had a long journey together – making conflict zone films like Sea of Shadows and The Ivory Game was no joke. But this one felt like a different level because of the 50 per cent quote.” He smiles.”‘I did hostile-environment training and we augmented the security to a degree where I felt it wasn’t 50 per cent any more.”

An illegal airbase in the Brazilian Amazon being destroyed Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

So Ladkani joined the team, and the resulting episode is terrifying: they are patrolling the river when they find a huge illegal dredger, used for gold mining. They board the dredger, its crew of illegal miners are put in a small boat and dispatched, and Loss’s team set fire to it. Attempting to get away, they realise their boat is still attached to the dredger by a chain, and they have only moments before an oxygen tank below the deck of the dredger explodes. Loss has to shoot the chain, but he has to hit it while it is taut, or the bullet would glance off. “The oxygen tank is steel and if it had exploded we would have been killed by the fragments if we were within 100 metres of that boat – and we were six metres away. It was Hugo who shot the chain – it took 50 shots at least. When Juma saw that footage she broke down and sobbed,” says Ladkani.

Do you like your job? I ask Loss.

He smiles. “Yes I do.”

Back in the 1970s, when two major roads were originally carved into the Amazon rainforest, of which 60 per cent is in Brazil, it opened it up for settlers to devastating effects – the population of the Brazilian Amazon quadrupled and millions of acres of trees were cut down for timber or land clearance and farming, and the rivers became polluted. Thousands of garimpeiros (prospectors) arrived, bringing disease, destruction and violence.

Indigenous people from the Mura tribe in a deforested area inside the Amazon rainforest near Humaita, Amazonas State, Brazil Credit : Ueslei Marcelino/REUTERS

Despite the protected reserves created by Lula during his first tenure (2003 to 2011), when Bolsonaro took over, he vowed that he would not demarcate a single millimetre of Indigenous land.

There was reason to be hopeful when Lula was re-elected in 2023, especially when he created the Ministry for Indigenous People. But it was an uphill struggle, and Xipaia left the post of State Secretary after about two years, and retired to her territory, where she still is. “She realised that it would be years, if not decades, before change could happen and she felt that her power was with activism from the front lines rather than being in an office in the city,” says Ladkani. “And what really hurt was her children having to grow up in the city and not having the connection to nature that she had.”

Smoke from illegal fires lit by farmers rises in Manaquiri, Amazonas state Credit : MICHAEL DANTAS

There has been a lot of progress, Juma says, compared to the Bolsonaro years “when it was genocide”. “It is hard to quantify all the changes because even though there was a change in the administration, it is important to understand that the government structure is very colonialist, no matter who is in power, and everything takes time. I entered the ministry when it was just being born.

“It was hard working in an office every day and not spending time with my children, and my son Tuppak [eight] told me that he wanted to go back to the forest, he was having a hard time at school in the city. I did not want to rob my son of that kind of childhood – being in the territory and getting his knowledge from the forest.”

I ask Loss and Xipaia if, with the way things are now, they are more inclined to hope or despair. “Most of the time I don’t think about the future,” says Loss. “I just focus on doing my work, one operation at a time.”

A wildfire consumes land deforested by cattle farmers near Novo Progresso, Para state, Brazil Credit : MICHAEL DANTAS/AFP via Getty Images

Xipaia thinks. “It depends where I am. When I’m in the forest with my family, there is immense fulfilment which is hard to explain; it gives me the hope and energy to keep wanting to protect it, and I want the whole world to get to know it.

“When I walk through the forest and harvest food there with my family and my people, it reminds me of what my ancestors were doing. The innocence of children, the idea of clean water, food without toxins – this gives me hope.”

“I don’t feel despair,” says Ladkani. “I feel like we’re in a war. There are plenty of good people fighting back, and that gives me hope. And there are lives on the line that we need to care about, which is the indigenous people, who are the frontline of our defence. They are defending nature for us so we need to make sure that they are heard and seen and respected. And we hope that the film puts a human face to that.

“We can’t pretend that destroying the biggest ecosystem on the planet is OK. If we lose the Amazon, we all lose.”

Yanuni will be released later this year

News.title: Alexander Isak starts to justify £125m price tag with double
News.content:
Emersonn, Ipswich’s Brazilian striker, did not see the ball in the opening exchanges and, by the time he did, Liverpool had zoomed into the distance to such an extent that you felt it was going to be impossible for them to peg their visitors back.

“I hate having to talk about good performances when you do not get points,” O’Neil declared to a room full of raised eyebrows and you can only assume his message was to ensure that morale in the dressing room was not drooping.

What damage was inflicted with Liverpool’s first significant attack. Gakpo, the subject of an £80m bid from Manchester City, was never going to allow transfer speculation to disrupt his focus and he nudged a perfect little ball into Isak’s path in the sixth minute to show his wellbeing.

The next move announced the return of Isak. One touch gave him an avenue to shoot, the next was a shot with his right foot that was so hard from 16 yards, on an angle, it bent the wrists of Kjell Scherpen as it howled into the net. Critics will feel Ipswich’s keeper should have done better.

Your first thought was to think of the first goal Isak scored in English football in September 2022, a similarly venomous drive, against Liverpool at Anfield. He oozed quality that evening, his pace and skill had Jürgen Klopp’s defenders persistently fretting and this is what he was doing again.

It was no coincidence that three minutes later, he came up with another wonderful goal. This one owed much to the beautiful pass Gakpo presented to him, an inch-perfect through ball with the outside of his right foot, but Isak still showed great poise to bamboozle Scherpen.

News.title: Forced displacement in the West Bank could be ‘crime against humanity’, says UN report
News.content:
Israel’s forced displacement of more than 33,000 Palestinians in the West Bank could amount to a “crime against humanity” and involves “ethnic cleansing”, according to a report published by the UN.

A report by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said that Israeli actions in the area had sparked the “largest and longest displacement crisis in the West Bank since 1967” – the year in which Israel captured the territory.

The report said “large-scale, long-term and systematic displacement of over 33,000 Palestinians from refugee camps … during Israel’s Operation Iron Wall [which] raises serious concerns of the crime against humanity of forcible transfer”.

It added: “The documented use of airstrikes, armoured bulldozers and controlled detonations, to render entire camps uninhabitable, to force the displacement of their residents and to prevent their return, in the absence of imperative military necessity to justify such destruction and displacement, are not permissible under international law, appear to amount to collective punishment and raise concerns of ethnic cleansing.”

The 27-page report covers the period December 5, 2024 to January 31, 2026.

In January 2025, Israeli forces launched “Operation Iron Wall” in the northern West Bank in a bid to counter what they said were terrorist threats.

They destroyed hundreds of homes, cut off water and electricity, and barred humanitarian access to the Jenin, Nur Sham and Tulkarm refugee camps.

By October 2025, 52 per cent of structures in Jenin camp, 48 per cent in Nur Shams and 36 percent in Tulkarm had been destroyed or damaged.

The three camps are among 19 in the West Bank established to shelter Palestinians after the 1948 Nakba, and are administered by the UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA).

Although still referred to as refugee camps, they are in fact now densely packed towns.

News.title: When is Black Friday 2026? This year’s dates and what to expect
News.content:
Five tips for finding genuine Black Friday discounts and deals

Learning how to find the best Black Friday discounts can make a meaningful difference to your festive budget, especially if you’re a keen sale shopper. The following five tips are a good starting point.

1. Don’t over-fixate on Black Friday itself

Although the day of Black Friday brings some of the best discounts of the festive sale season, good deals are likely to be available both before and after it – and some items may sell out.

“When we look at our pricing data on a daily level, you have certain events such as Amazon’s October Prime sale [not yet confirmed for 2026] that are an earlier vector for change in prices,” says Vivek Pandya, a director at Adobe for Business.

“We typically see more significant discounts starting to emerge as we get into late October or early November, and these really kick up a notch as we get into Black Friday week.”

So, while interest in Black Friday deals will peak around the day itself, some of the best deals may have been available since the beginning of the week, or earlier.

2. Expand your search to everyday essentials

At Telegraph Recommended, we’ve picked up on a proliferation of discounts on everyday household items during recent Black Friday sales (and during other occasional events such as Prime Day). If you need a top-up of items such as cleaning products or pet supplies, this could be a thrifty time to buy them.

“These sales have become a spending spree on what retailers frame as ‘everyday essentials’, as well as bigger items and gifts,” says Pandya. Last year’s Cyber Weekend saw a 260 per cent spike in sales of “personal care” items including cosmetics, shampoos, fragrances and toothbrushes, according to Adobe.

3. Use a price tracker

Free price tracking tools such as camelcamelcamel can show you how the price of a product has changed over time. This allows you to identify when a Black Friday deal has actually brought a product’s price significantly lower than usual, or when the retailer’s pricing strategy has artificially made a deal appear to be generous.

Gabrielė Vitkė, product marketing team lead at data-gathering specialist Decodo, warns shoppers to watch out for “anchoring”, where a product’s price is set high prior to Black Friday, allowing the retailer then to reduce it sharply and advertise an eye-catching reduction.

“Discounts on items such as electronics and computing products can seem steep, sometimes exceeding 50 per cent against the list price,” says Vitkė. “However, our data shows that prices in this category rose in the run-up to Black Friday 2025, which is a sign of anchor pricing before the ‘discount’ is applied.”

News.title: Indonesia wildfires trigger 50,000 respiratory infections
News.content:
More than 50,000 people have contracted respiratory infections in Indonesia, as raging wild fires blanket huge swathes of the country in a thick, toxic smoke.

The vast archipelago is only a month into its fire season, but intense blazes have proven hard to control across Sumatra and Indonesian Borneo. There are fears the situation will only get worse, because the “Godzilla” El Niño is set to suppress rains that would normally have helped extinguish the flames.

“Our problems are not over. September is the peak of El Niño,” said Raja Juli Antoni, the forestry minister. “September is the main fight for us.”

Already the toxic haze has spread across Southeast Asia. On Friday Kuching, a city in Malaysian Borneo, was the most polluted city in the world on the IQ Air Index, followed by Jakarta and Singapore.

The wildfires have brought memories of record-breaking blazes in 2015. Then, the smoke was linked to roughly 100,000 excess deaths in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, according to one study. The World Bank said Indonesia alone saw economic losses of $16.1bn, or 2 per cent of GDP.

News.title: Global hunger is a threat to Britain’s national security, report says
News.content:
Global hunger poses a direct threat to Britain’s national security, and tackling it should be a government priority, a new report from the London School of Economics has warned.

It says hunger is a major driver of mass migration, extreme violence and war – events that threaten significant repercussions for Britain and Europe’s national security.

“Hunger prevention is an important part of national security policy, not an optional act of charity,” Stuart Gordon, professor of International Development at LSE and author of the report, told The Telegraph.

Recent hunger crises in places like Sudan, Afghanistan and across North Africa have contributed significantly to rising numbers of people moving to the West.

Between January and November 2025 alone, 12,684 migrants from Sudan – which is facing what has been described as the worst hunger crisis in Africa’s history – arrived in Europe, roughly three times as many as the previous year.

Last year, an estimated 155,000 African refugees arrived in Europe.

“Food insecurity tests one of the most basic expectations people have of government: that it will protect access to the essentials of life,” said Prof Gordon.

“Food price shocks can rapidly escalate into political instability when governments are perceived to have failed to protect access to basic subsistence goods,” he added.

News.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak slows at epicentre but widens elsewhere, modelling suggests
News.content:
Congo’s Ebola outbreak shows signs of slowing at the epicentre of the flare-up, but is widening as the infection spreads further afield, modelling suggests.

The daily tally of new cases in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) was falling at the end of August, but more cases were being found outside Ituri province, where the infection burst out.

Latest official figures say the outbreak has now killed more than 3,000 people out of over 6,100 confirmed cases, with the infection spreading faster than any previous epidemic of the viral haemorrhagic fever.

Modelling by Airfinity, a health analytics firm, suggests the true toll of cases could be more than four times higher than reported.

The outbreak remains on track to eclipse the 2014 West Africa outbreak later this month, to become the largest ever recorded.

Airfinity said that data from late August showed the seven-day averages of reported cases and reported deaths had fallen by 16 per cent and 18 per cent respectively.

The firm said it was “too early to confirm the decline will hold, and it may mask subnational variation: The outbreak has fluctuated before and a week of falling case and death counts does not rule out another surge.

“Even if the decline continues at this current pace, low case levels remain weeks away.”

Sports.title: Liverpool confirm departure of Richard Hughes days after difficult transfer window ends
Sports.content:
Liverpool confirm departure of Richard Hughes days after difficult transfer window ends

Richard Hughes has decided to leave Liverpool after just two years at the club and will join Saudi Arabian club Al-Hilal following a turbulent summer on Merseyside

View 2 Images Richard Hughes has left Liverpool (Image: Robin Jones/Getty Images)

Liverpool have confirmed the departure of sporting director Richard Hughes. The club chief was contracted until June 2027 but has decided to leave after just two years following a difficult summer.

‌



Hughes arrived from Bournemouth in the summer of 2024 and oversaw the hiring of Arne Slot as manager after Jurgen Klopp stepped down. He was behind the big-money transfers of Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz last summer, as well as the £123million signing of Bradley Barcola this summer.

‌



The 47-year-old has decided to leave shortly after the departure of Michael Edwards from Fenway Sports Group and following a difficult summer which saw Liverpool struggle to bring in new players for Andoni Iraola.

‌



Liverpool said in a statement: "The process of appointing a successor is under way and the outcome will be confirmed in due course."

Hughes said: “First and foremost, I would like to reiterate what I said upon my arrival – it has been a source of great pride to have been given the opportunity to serve this incredible and unique institution. That is something I will always be grateful for.

“My appreciation extends to ownership for their support and leadership, to club staff at all levels who give so much to make Liverpool FC what it is, to the players who make such an enormous contribution and to the fans who support the team in great numbers whenever and wherever games take place.

“I’ll always follow and support the club with great affection, and I wish everyone involved nothing but success for this season and beyond.”

‌



He will team up with Simon Francis - the man who replaced him at Bournemouth two years ago - in Saudi Arabia. Francis left the Cherries at the end of the season and has been overseeing Al-Hilal's transfer activity this summer, including the recent £60million signing of Gabriel Martinelli from Arsenal.

View 2 Images Richard Hughes has followed Michael Edwards out of the door at Liverpool (Image: Robin Jones/Getty Images)

‌



“The results we achieved in these areas during this period are testament to this contribution. Nevertheless, we respect Richard’s life choices and wish him and his family well in their next venture."

Hughes' exit continues a summer of change at Liverpool, with Edwards, the chief executive officer of football of FSG, having also left back in July. FSG made the decision to sack Slot after two seasons following a disappointing 2025/26 campaign and the arrival of Iraola as his successor has triggered a changing of the guard behind the scenes.

Sports.title: Jamie Carragher fires blunt warning to Bradley Barcola as Andoni Iraola gives update
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher fires blunt warning to Bradley Barcola as Andoni Iraola gives update

Bradley Barcola made his first appearance for Liverpool in their 2-0 win over Ipswich on Friday night, but his position on the bench may continue according to Jamie Carragher

View 2 Images Bradley Barcola made his Liverpool debut against Ipswich (Image: Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

Jamie Carragher has warned Bradley Barcola that he may struggle to force his way into the Liverpool starting XI after another impressive performance from Cody Gakpo.

‌



Liverpool beat Ipswich 2-0 on Friday night to record their first win of the season following successive 2-2 draws under Andoni Iraola. The result was settled inside the opening 10 minutes thanks to two goals from Alexander Isak.

‌



Isak rifled past Ipswich goalkeeper Kjell Scherpen to open the scoring before losing defender Jacob Greaves a second time to finish underneath Scherpen. Both assists came from Gakpo, who continued his fast start to the campaign, having scored at Newcastle and assisted Isak against Nottingham Forest.

‌



Gakpo's strong start to the campaign has come despite speculation over his future. The Netherlands international told Liverpool he preferred a move to Manchester City over Tottenham in the final stages of the transfer window, but the proposed £85million deal never materialised, with City instead landing Iliman Ndiaye from Everton for £65m on Tuesday's deadline day.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Gakpo started at Portman Road ahead of Barcola, who is being eased into action by Iraola following his £123million move from Paris Saint-Germain. And Gakpo's form could be a worry for the Frenchman.

"Barcola is going to struggle to get a game with this version of Gakpo," Carragher wrote on X with a fire emoji after the game. Barcola came off the bench in the 64th minute to replace fellow summer signing Victor Munoz and Iraola stressed the need for patience post-match.

"I think Bradley hadn't played a single minute since the World Cup so we needed to be careful. I think he is training well, in a good place, and I think that he has helped us," the Liverpool boss said.

‌



"I think 30 minutes is going to be good for his fitness, for his build-up, and we will continue because now we play a lot of games, so he will have a chance to play more."

View 2 Images Cody Gakpo assisted both of Alexander Isak's goals at Ipswich (Image: Getty Images)

Asked about the need for patience, Iraola added: "I think it's normal, he hasn't played any pre-season minutes. I think he's still in a good place. I don't think he will need something like a very special build-up, but we have to be aware that he hasn't been playing in a while and the demands of the games are very different from training, so we have got to consider this."

‌



Iraola was also asked about Gakpo's mindset after a move away failed to come to fruition. "I have no doubt with Cody. He has been very good all the pre-season, has started very well this season, producing numbers," he said.

"Today again, after the two assists, he finishes [the game at] No.9 to help us close the game. I think it's good to have Cody because he can play in the three positions up top and to have him in this place for this beginning of the season is good.

‌



"Cody knows how much we value him, I think there is no doubt. I rate him very highly. I will demand from him, obviously, because there is also a strong competition for minutes because we have good players in those positions and it's a matter of pushing each other.

"With Bradley, with Rio [Ngumoha], with Victor [Munoz], it's a matter that sometimes they will start, sometimes they come from the bench, sometimes they will not play. But this competition, I think is going to be good for all of them."

Sports.content:

Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola 'never doubted' Cody Gakpo despite nearly completing Liverpool exit

Cody Gakpo played a starring role, creating both of Alexander Isak's goals, as Liverpool recorded their first Premier League win of the Andoni Iraola era

View 2 Images Cody Gakpo celebrates with Alexander Isak during Liverpool's win over Ipswich

Andoni Iraola insists he never doubted Cody Gakpo even after the Liverpool forward nearly quit Anfield.

‌



Gakpo could have left in the final days of the transfer window after Manchester City launched a bid to sign him but Liverpool blocked the move after failing to find replacements.

‌



Holland international Gakpo provided both assists for two-goal Alexander Isak in what was Liverpool’s first win under Iraola.

‌



Liverpool boss Iraola said: “Cody knows how much we value him. There is no doubt. I rate him very highly. There might be, obviously, strong competition for minutes because we have good players there in those positions.

“It's a matter of pushing each other. With Bradley Barcola, with Rio Ngumoha, with Victor Munoz, it's a matter of sometimes they will start, sometimes they will come from the bench, sometimes they will not play, but this is competition.

Iraola added: “If he's fit, if he's available, if he's in a good shape, I think he will produce the numbers. My demand with Alex will not be about the goals. Probably, it will be about other things.

‌



View 2 Images Gakpo played a starring role in the win over Ipswich

“I will demand other things so we can play well. And if we play well, we are in good positions. The goals will come. I think he has to contribute to the collective. And when everyone helps, I think the goals and the result will come.

“Bradley has not played a single minute since the World Cup, so we needed to be careful. I’m happy because 30 minutes is going to be good for his fitness for his build-up, and we will continue because now we play a lot of games. So he will have the chance to play.

‌



"I think two points also don't reflect our two first games. So definitely, we couldn't lose anymore and I’m happy because I think we controlled it well today.”

Ipswich boss Gary O’Neil insisted he was happy with his team and “proud of his players.” He added: “After the first two goals, we recovered and matched them and were arguably the better team at times.”

Sports.title: Liverpool transfer call vindicated as Alexander Isak downs Ipswich - 5 talking points
Sports.content:
Liverpool finally secured their first win of the Premier League season by beating newly-promoted Ipswich at Portman Road.

Liverpool took control early on through Alexander Isak as he scored twice in the opening ten minutes. The Reds thought they were set to be handed a penalty after Dominik Szoboszlai was fouled midway through the second-half but VAR correctly intervened.

But the damage was already done in the first half by Isak, as Liverpool sealed their first success of the campaign, while it's now back-to-back defeats for Ipswich.

Here are all of the talking points from Portman Road:

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Isak back to his best

Barely six minutes into the game and Liverpool were ahead through Isak. A lot of the praise for the goal has to go to Cody Gakpo, who showed great feet in the centre of the park and picked out the Swedish forward with an inch-perfect ball.

He controlled and then hammered past Kjell Scherpen in the Ipswich goal, who may have thought he could have done better. But Isak will not care too much, having netted his second goal of the season.

Two became three barely three minutes later as he latched onto another brilliant pass by Gakpo, composed himself and slotted home. He's now matched his Premier League goal record from the entirety of last season and it would be foolish to bet against him beating that.

‌



He actually thought he had done after getting on the end of a Florian Wirtz cross but had drifted offside.

View 3 Images Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo linked up well at Ipswich (Image: Getty Images)

Gakpo call spot on

If things had panned out differently, Liverpool might not have had Cody Gakpo's services to call upon for this game. He appeared set for a move to Manchester City over the closing days of the window.

For one reason or another, the move did not come to fruition. Liverpool will be hugely thankful that it didn't. Gakpo's passes for Isak were brilliant - the first being an inch-perfect pass, the second being a brilliant, outside of the boot effort.

‌



Like Isak, Gakpo has really impressed over the opening weeks of the campaign and that was certainly the same at Portman Road.

Penalty decision explained

Liverpool thought they were going to be given a golden opportunity to extend their lead even further as Dominik Szoboszlai was taken down by Leif Davies.

The referee did not give the decision initially but looked as though he would change his mind upon review. But the hosts still had a reprieve, with the Liverpool midfielder offside in the build-up, rendering the controversy irrelevant in any case.

It might not have been the call that Liverpool wanted, but it was the correct one.

‌



View 3 Images Dominik Szoboszlai thought he had won a penalty against Ipswich (Image: Getty Images)

Barcola gets Premier League introduction

While Liverpool fans will have been keen to see their side win, another key moment that they were looking forward to was Bradley Barcola's debut. The Frenchman was named on the bench following his £123m move from PSG.

But he came on in the second period to make his bow. In honesty, he was on the periphery of the game but there were a few moments where he showed his electric pace in front of the away fans so they will certainly be keen to see that a lot more throughout his time on Merseyside.

First win, first clean sheet

Liverpool's defensive frailties have been well discussed this season. And they were on show once again at Portman Road. The hosts managed to get through on a few occasions, with it taking either an important intervention from Jeremy Jacquet or a save from Alisson to keep them out.

‌



Regardless, Liverpool finally have their first win and first clean sheet of the campaign and that will be a big relief to Andoni Iraola.

When it comes to Ipswich, their season will of course not be defined against games against Liverpool - or indeed last week's trip to Old Trafford - so they won't be too worried at all.

Sports.title: Russell tops Hamilton at Monza ahead of qualifying
Sports.content:
George Russell established himself as pole position favourite ahead of Italian Grand Prix qualifying as the Mercedes driver topped Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton in final practice.

Mercedes and Ferrari had appeared closely matched in Friday's two practice sessions, and once more led the way on Saturday as Russell's time of 1:22.219s put him just over two tenths of a second clear of Hamilton at Monza.

Russell is shouldering Mercedes' hopes of claiming pole, with his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, the championship leader, serving penalties for taking new engine parts that will leave him starting from the back of the grid regardless of where he qualifies.

Despite being more focused on his long-run setup for Sunday's race, Antonelli, who leads both Russell and Hamilton by 59 points at the top of the standings, was fourth behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

McLaren's Lando Norris, who has closed to within 83 points of Antonelli by winning the last two races, was fifth ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

Mercedes tried out using Antonelli to give Russell a highly-beneficial tow around the high-speed circuit, but the Brit's fastest laps came without the help of his team-mate.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton braces for a tight Italian GP qualifying as Mercedes continue to find more pace

Ferrari appear to have reduced their straight-line speed deficit to Mercedes after bringing to Monza their second engine upgrade of the season, but it appears the Italian squad will need to find something extra to claim what would be an extremely popular pole at their home race.

There was drama in the closing moments of the session as Hamilton and Verstappen almost collided at the first corner after a squabble for track position ahead of what should have been their final attempts at flying laps.

Hamilton snuck ahead of Verstappen as they approached the final corner, which angered the Dutchman, prompting him to attempt to race the Ferrari over the start-finish line and then dive up the inside into the first corner.

Hamilton bailed out to prevent contact, avoiding a repeat of the pair's famous collision at the 2021 Italian Grand Prix when they were battling for the drivers' title. The stewards noted the incident but decided an investigation wasn't necessary.

Image: George Russell topped final practice at Monza

Russell has endured a difficult season having started the year of favourite before being outperformed by his far less experience team-mate.

However, the 28-year-old appears to have found a groove at Monza, with pole position having the potential to reignite his championship challenge.

Sky Sports F1's Naomi Schiff said: "George will be very pleased with himself. This is such a psychological sport and with a team-mate leading the championship he does need to switch that momentum.

"This session has been the most positive for Mercedes. They aren't losing much anywhere on deployment through the lap."

Sports.title: Sky Sports and Audi launch unique 'Flying Lap' track guide series
Sports.content:
Get closer than ever before to the technical and physical demands of an Formula 1 race circuit in a series combining real-life driving in an Audi RS5 road car with advanced simulation data

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Powered by Audi: Martin Brundle takes to the iconic Monza track in a high-performance Audi, combining real laps with advanced sim data to break down racing lines, braking points, and elite-level performance.

Sky Sports and their official Innovation partner Audi have launched a new series, combining real-world driving with Audi's R26 simulation technology to deliver a storytelling experience from the race track never seen before.

At the heart of Flying Lap is Audi's cutting-edge simulation technology, placing the brand directly into the narrative of performance. By integrating Audi Sim data with Sky Sports' world-class production, the series brings fans closer than ever to the technical and physical demands of the circuit.

Fronted by Sky Sports pundit and former Formula 1 driver Karun Chandhok, each episode sees the driver take to an iconic track in a high-performance Audi road car, delivering a full-throttle lap guide enriched with immersive data visualisation.

As they navigate the circuit, viewers are guided through key sections of the track inside the high-performance all-new Audi RS5 with highlighted hotspots. At pivotal moments, the experience shifts seamlessly into a fully rendered virtual environment - where an Audi R26 F1 car screams to life.

Within this graphical world, Audi's simulation data is used to break down the intricacies of elite performance, from braking zones and racing lines to gear changes, cornering speeds, and overtaking opportunities. The camera moves dynamically around the virtual car - from exterior angles to the driver's cockpit - offering perspectives never possible before.

The format then transitions back to real-world driving, maintaining continuity as the Sky Sports driver progresses through the lap, creating a seamless fusion of physical and digital storytelling.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Powered by Audi: Karun Chandhok takes to the iconic Miami track in a high-performance Audi, combining real laps with advanced sim data to break down racing lines, braking points, and elite-level performance.

The first Flying Lap episode took on Miami, one of the fastest and most technically demanding circuits on the calendar, while the second headed to the iconic Silverstone in Great Britain.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Powered by Audi: Karun Chandhok takes to the iconic Silverstone track in a high-performance Audi, combining real laps with advanced sim data to break down racing lines, braking points, and elite-level performance.

The third features motorsport's Temple of Speed - Monza in Italy.

Launched across Sky Sports platforms from May 2026, Flying Lap represents the next evolution of the Sky Sports and Audi Innovation partnership - pushing the boundaries of broadcast innovation and creating new opportunities for storytelling beyond live coverage.

Sports.title: Newcastle United v Bournemouth: Premier League – live
Sports.content:
now 08.19 EDT HALF TIME: Newcastle 1-2 Bournemouth Bournemouth lead at the break and deservedly so. Jaissle will have plenty to say although that Barnes curler has given the hosts fresh optimism. Share

1m ago 08.18 EDT 45 min +3: Bournemouth’s press continues to stifle Newcastle and Thiaw flaps, giving away possession. A cross from Truffert is well dealt with by Miley as Rayan sniffs an opportunity. Share

3m ago 08.17 EDT 45 min +2: Barnes tries to pick out Elanga with a cross but Petrovic plucks that one from the skies. Share

4m ago 08.16 EDT 45 min +1: Can Newcastle find something before the break? They’re hogging possession now but can’t really get Wissa into the game. Share

5m ago 08.15 EDT 44 min: Hall launches a free-kick to the edge of the box but Silva heads away. Kluivert is fouled by Gonzalez as he tries to break. The visitors will be glad to see this through to half-time now. Three minutes to add on. Share

6m ago 08.13 EDT 42 min: Much more intent from Newcastle now. That second Bournemouth goal has really sparked them into action and, of course, they’ve already halved the deficit. Share

8m ago 08.11 EDT 40 min: Rayan’s cross hits Hall in the chest inside the six-yard box and Hornicek has to be alert. The ball had probably gone out before the Brazilian played it in though. Share

10m ago 08.10 EDT 39 min: Blimey, that was all a bit crazy. Glenn Hoddle’s 3-3 prediction could be spot on. Share Updated at 08.10 EDT

11m ago 08.08 EDT GOAL! Newcastle 1-2 Bournemouth (Barnes 37) Before the mood really drops, Newcastle hit back straight away. Just 27 seconds from the kick off, Barnes gets the ball down the left, cuts inside and curls a beauty into the corner past Petrovic. What a response! View image in fullscreen Harvey Barnes unleashes a pearler to half the defecit! Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA Share Updated at 08.14 EDT

14m ago 08.05 EDT GOAL! Newcastle 0-2 Bournemouth (Thiaw o.g. 35) It had been coming! Bournemouth break and Kluivert’s thumping effort from distance hits the post and rebounds off the goalkeeper. Scott follows up and his cross/shot off Thiaw deflects up and over Hornicek. But…. View image in fullscreen The ball loops over Hornícek for an own-goal for Bournemouth! Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters Share Updated at 08.13 EDT

16m ago 08.04 EDT 33 min: Both sides cough up possession before a cross from Dedic on the right is easy for Petrovic to pluck out of the air. Share

17m ago 08.03 EDT 32 min: The near post corner is sliced behind by Elanga for another. Tavernier has another go and this time goes short. Bournemouth work the ball across to Truffert but his left footer from distance is charged down by Willock. But… the ball comes back to Bournemouth. That’s the story of his half. Share

18m ago 08.01 EDT 31 min: Kluivert bursts into space and pings one from 25 yards. It deflects off Botman for a corner but that could easily have wrong-footed Hornicek and gone in. Share

20m ago 08.00 EDT 30 min: Silva looks a little unshaken as he runs his fingers through his immaculate hair. On we go. Share

21m ago 07.59 EDT 28 min: Ouch! Silva goes up for a header and is clattered into by Elanga. It’s a booking. Shoulder on head. Elanga not happy but it was a bit clumsy. Share

23m ago 07.57 EDT 26 min: Another really good chance for Bournemouth. They break down the left after good work by Scott and Truffert rolls the ball to Tavernier in acres of space. But from the edge of the area his left-foot strike is too measured and Hornicek saves easily to his right. More conviction in the shot and that was 2-0. Share

25m ago 07.55 EDT 25 min: Barnes swings in the corner which Petrovic punches behind for another. Hall jogs across to take this one but his delivery to the far post has too much juice and goes behind for a goalkick. Some mutterings in the crowd. Share

26m ago 07.54 EDT 23 min: More excellent pressing from Bournemouth. Elanga tries to wriggle free down the right but two men are on him. The winger gets another go though and this time wins a corner after his cross is turned behind by Smith. Share

28m ago 07.52 EDT 21 min: Good tenacity from Willock but it’s matched by Adams in a touchline squabble for the ball. Bournemouth press again and Scott glides into the area, beating a couple of men but his cross comes back of his own leg so no corner. View image in fullscreen Tyler Adams slides in to tackle Joe Willock. Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA Share Updated at 07.56 EDT

30m ago 07.50 EDT 19 min: Newcastle are pressured in midfield and give the ball away. Marco Rose must be delighted so far. Share

31m ago 07.49 EDT 17 min: Rayan does well down the right and Evanilson tries to pick up a clearance but his effort is blocked. All the efforts are coming from Bournemouth who seem to have Newcastle’s number in this fixture. They’re unbeaten in the last eight top-flight meetings against the Magpies. Share

33m ago 07.47 EDT Colin Young writes: “Some August sunshine adds to the sense of optimism...” “I’m gonna give you the benefit of the doubt and suggest you meant to write ‘autumn’, yes?” Good spot Colin. Yes, it’s September now isn’t it. I’m mentally still in August. Share

34m ago 07.45 EDT 15 min: Another Bournemouth effort as Silva flicks Hill’s throw-in towards goal but it’s straight at Hornicek. Share

35m ago 07.44 EDT 14 min: Newcastle need to settle down a bit here. Some iffy defending so far in the first 15 minutes and Bournemouth are smelling blood. Share

37m ago 07.43 EDT 12 min: Terrible mistake by Botman at the back gifts the ball to Evanilson on the edge of the box. It’s a golden chance to make it 2-0 but the striker curls his left-footer over the bar, perhaps slightly put off by Botman charging back to atone for his error. Share Updated at 07.43 EDT

38m ago 07.41 EDT 10 min: Newcastle appealed for a foul in the build-up but nothing doing there. Share

40m ago 07.39 EDT GOAL! Newcastle 0-1 Bournemouth (Tavernier 9) Bournemouth lead! A bit of luck involved but also great anticipation. Scott latches onto a ball into the box and goes for goal. His strike loops up and Tavernier reacts first to tuck the ball past Hornicek. View image in fullscreen Marcus Tavernier beats Hornícek to open the scoring for the Cherries! Photograph: Robin Jones/AFCB/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Marcus Tavernier was in the right spot to tuck away the opener. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters Share Updated at 08.12 EDT

41m ago 07.38 EDT 8 min: Dedic also offers pace and intent down the right and his burst again gets the crowd going. He looks to have won the first corner of the game but it came off him last after a charge into the box. Share

43m ago 07.37 EDT 7 min: Willock and Barnes break down the Bournemouth end causing a surge of excitement in the Toon Army but the move fizzles out. Share

44m ago 07.36 EDT 6 min: Hill hurls a throw into the box. It’s flicked on by Evanilson who darts to the near post but the ball drifts behind. Decent start by the visitors. Share

46m ago 07.34 EDT 4 min: Tavernier strikes a low one with his left foot. It evades the wall but that’s easy enough for Hornicek to dive on to down to his right. Share Updated at 07.34 EDT

47m ago 07.33 EDT 3 min: Evanilson thumps a shot which is blocked but Bournemouth win a free-kick just outside the D after Kluivert is fouled first. Early chance for the visitors. Share

47m ago 07.32 EDT 2 min: Elanga on the ball again but Tyler Adams times the tackle well as the winger tries to forge through the middle this time. Share

48m ago 07.31 EDT 1 min: The jet-heeled Elanga scampers down the right but loses possession as he tries to chop back. Bournemouth win the ball back and stroke it around for a while. Share

53m ago 07.27 EDT Here come the teams! Some August sunshine adds to the sense of optimism and excitement in the ground. Giddy on those rays, Glenn Hoddle predicts either a 3-3 or 2-2 draw. Share

1h ago 07.19 EDT It’s certainly not the case with all Premier League managers but Marco Rose sounds more than happy with Bournemouth’s transfer window. That’s due mainly to keeping hold of key men, particularly midfielder Alex Scott: “Here’s a very important player for us. Happy to have him,” says Rose with a smile. Share

1h ago 07.17 EDT Table-wise, it’s 7th v 14th today. Look at Hull in that maximum points gang! Share

1h ago 07.10 EDT Here’s Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle on why he’s picked the same starting XI. “The lads deserved to start again after the performance against Tottenham and that was the approach for today.” And on whether new signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo will make his debut this afternoon. “Well, it all depends on the match. How is it going. I cannot predict anything right now, but he’s fit. He looks sharp in the training sessions, but we also need to be smart when it comes to the load management. He didn’t play for 90 minutes since a long, long time now, so that’s the reason why he’s coming now from the bench.” Share

1h ago 07.02 EDT Glenn Hoddle is looking well as he parades the ground during TNT’s build-up. Good head of hair still. Nice cardigan. Giving off a Brit-abroad-at-a-Spanish-golf-resort-vibe. Can still pick a pass no doubt. “These are a very good side,” Glenn says of Bournemouth, pointing out that the Cherries could easily have six points had the closing game situations been different. Share

1h ago 06.57 EDT Pre-match post bag: “It’s a delicious early kick off for us here in Aus, so my only (Toon supporting) mates have decided to organise a viewing, which only happens with the three of us once a season owing to life getting in the way / preference to live vicariously via our NUFC Instagram chat,” writes Chris Paraskevas. “As much as we’ve made a promising start to life under Jaissle, things can turn very quickly, and Bournemouth also have a very strong record at St James’ and have been eager to bring us down to Earth in recent years. “To make matters worse, every time me and the boiz get together to watch a game, we inevitably get hammered. Happens every single season. At least the host “Sorted snacks and drinks already,” though even that is a little disconcerting, given he organised them at 12pm and by now... well, the good stuff’s gone.” Share

2h ago 06.47 EDT A big question: do the two German managers know each other? Bournemouth’s Marco Rose (49) is 11 years older than Newcastle’s Matthias Jaissle (just 38) but, yes, their paths have crossed. Here’s Rose: “I know Matthias from Salzburg because I was the manager there and he succeeded, not me, but the manager after me, or after the manager after me! I visited old friends at the training ground and we met. We had a talk, had a chat. I know he is a good coach, he has an idea of football and he brought that idea really quickly into the team of Newcastle. They are in a good spot, in good shape, play quite intense. They have a clear pattern with and against the ball, but the same things we have as well.” Jaissle said in the build-up: “Today’s game against Bournemouth will provide us with another good test. They’ve also experienced a summer of change but have a top coach in Marco Rose, who I know well from his time in Austria and Germany.” Share

2h ago 06.38 EDT Newcastle are unchanged from the side that won 2-0 at Spurs last weekend. That means £51m signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo starts on the bench. For Bournemouth, Tyler Adams comes in for Lewis Cook in midfield. Share
