Sports.title: Liverpool look for new sporting director after Richard Hughes formally leaves
Sports.content:
Liverpool are searching for a fourth sporting director in four years after confirming that Richard Hughes has stepped down from the role.

Hughes’s departure has been long expected, with the 47-year-old in line to take up a similar position with the Saudi Pro League club Al-Hilal. He informed Liverpool of his intentions to leave early this year, after the departure of his friend Michael Edwards as chief executive of football for Fenway Sports Group, the club’s owner.

With work already under way on Liverpool’s summer transfer targets – including the signing of Bradley Barcola in a £123m deal – and Hughes enjoying a close working relationship with the new head coach, Andoni Iraola, it was agreed he would continue in the role until the end of the transfer window.

Liverpool say no approach was received from Al-Hilal for Hughes to start work with them this summer and are satisfied the sporting director worked for them alone throughout this period.

The search for Hughes’s replacement is already under way and is being led by FSG’s president, Mike Gordon, who resumed the day-to-day running of the club after Edwards’ exit. The eventual appointment will follow in the footsteps since Edwards left the role in 2022 of Julian Ward, Jörg Schmadtke and Hughes.

Liverpool’s football structure will otherwise remain intact. That includes Ward as technical director for FSG and Pedro Marques as director of football development at FSG, the assistant sporting director, David Woodfine, the chief scout, Barry Hunter, plus the senior leadership team at the training centre.

Sports.title: ‘Reverse bucket list’: Arteta channels Wenger in defence of Arsenal window
Sports.content:
For many people connected to Arsenal, it has been a time to remember the old line from Arsène Wenger. “We live in a society of ‘news’,” the club’s former manager once said, and by that he meant new things – the shinier the better.

Nowhere is the obsession more obvious than in the transfer market, when a club simply has to add new faces. These days, it feels as though some fans prefer them to be signed as late as possible in the summer window to ensure a positive narrative after the deadline; to maximise the potential to generate momentum. Recency bias is powerful.

Wenger’s tone was disapproving. The next big thing is not always thus. What you already have should not be undervalued or taken for granted. It struck a chord with Mikel Arteta, which everybody in the room for his press conference to preview Sunday’s home game against Chelsea could feel because it moved him out of succinct answer territory.

The Arsenal manager enters the match having won three out of three this season – including the Community Shield victory over Manchester City – without conceding a goal. His club, of course, ended their long wait for the Premier League title last May when they chased away all manner of demons. They are hot favourites to win it again.

At Aston Villa on Monday night, Arteta introduced two of Spain’s World Cup winning squad – Mikel Merino and Martín Zubimendi – from the bench. Plus the marquee summer signing, Bruno Guimarães. Plus Eberechi Eze. Plus another high-profile new boy, Ezri Konsa. Arsenal’s strength in depth is really something.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal were able to add the skill and strength of Bruno Guimarães to an already strong midfield this summer. Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/Reuters

Their squad is surely stronger now than it was at the end of last season. Does Arteta feel that? “Yes I do,” he said. “We are better equipped. We have more players available. We have increased the quality and we have increased the leadership in the team as well, which is very important.”

So, why the angst among supporters after the transfer window closed, which was probably nearer to hysteria in some cases? “It’s human nature,” Arteta said. “When you talk to people and you ask them … normally, it’s: ‘OK, what is on your bucket list?’ People write a lot about the bucket list. And sometimes we forget the reverse bucket list, which is the things that you already have in your life that are incredible. But you put so much emphasis on them [the bucket list items] that nothing seems to be enough.

“It’s very important to value what we have, what we have created together. To have ambition is great, especially to evolve the things we already have within the club. But listen – don’t lose perspective to what we already have, which is amazing.”

Arsenal are indisputably better in defence with Konsa and in midfield with Guimarães. The worry is the front line where it has been one in (Christos Tzolis) and four out (Leandro Trossard, Gabriel Martinelli, Gabriel Jesus and Ethan Nwaneri).

View image in fullscreen The summer window has left Christos Tzolis, himself only recently arrived, as Arsenal’s most natural option on the left wing. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA

The reasoning for each departure was difficult to fault. Trossard is 31, he had one year on his contract and Besiktas offered £15.3m. Tzolis felt like a fine replacement for him. Martinelli scored once in the league last season, although he contributed four in the FA Cup and six in the Champions League. Arsenal got £60m from Al-Hilal for him; a club record sale.

As an aside, Arteta mentioned how Arsenal had “made a move last summer” – a reference to their lavish spending – and there has been an acknowledgement within the club that there had to be a balancing this time.

Jesus started nine games in all competitions last season, scoring six goals. He, too, was into the final year of his deal, and he was one of the club’s highest earners. At one stage, it looked as though he might look to see out his contract and in the end, a £8.6m deal with Barcelona rising to £12.9m suited all parties. Nwaneri barely played for Arsenal last season, going to Marseille on loan in January. Another loan, this time to Borussia Dortmund, made sense, particularly as there is a January recall clause.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Yet the weight of the outgoing numbers makes it hard to say Arsenal are stronger in this department and Arteta was in no mood to over-promise here. “It’s another question and we have to prove in that particular position whether we are better or not,” he said. “Let’s see. I understand the point of view [about the number of departures] but we have to understand as well the amount of minutes that those players played. And the ones that were injured last season, especially in the first six months. It is what it is.”There is the belief at Arsenal that Eze can in essence replace Martinelli on the left, albeit he is a different kind of player. Arsenal can perhaps play in a different way, with Riccardo Calafiori stepping up more from left-back. There is the hope that with a reshaped medical staff, the team can have a better run on the injury front – specifically with Bukayo Saka, Martin Ødegaard and Kai Havertz having uninterrupted seasons. The fear is that more problems will undermine them.

What has coloured the post-transfer window vibe is the failure to add a big-name attacker, to make a real statement signing. If Arteta did have a bucket list, then a game-changer for the front line would have been on it. Arsenal did try; they reached for stars such as Vinícius Júnior, Julián Alvarez and Morgan Rogers. Arteta even suggested that this kind of intent was progress. It is a tough sell when the glamour targets remain elusive.

View image in fullscreen Despite a summer-long saga, the transfer window closed with Julián Alvarez still an Atlético Madrid player. Photograph: Chema Moya/EPA

There was a point in July when Arsenal thought there was more of a chance they would get Vinícius than not. Then Real Madrid made him a new contract offer and he signed it. Alvarez just did not want to come, and the case of Rogers boiled down to the numbers. Arsenal offered £80m to Aston Villa for him and no more. Chelsea ended up going to £117m. They overpaid. But then they announced a deal with Villa two days later to loan Alejandro Garnacho there with a conditional purchase obligation, valuing the winger at £40m. Chelsea found a way to get Rogers. Arsenal did not. He will be a major subplot on Sunday .

There were moments when Arteta dropped his usual ultra-positive outlook and offered little peeks behind the curtain, including when he suggested that reporters speak to the sporting director, Andrea Berta, or the co-chair Josh Kroenke about why it was so difficult to close deals for the very elite.

“To get these deals done in this market is complicated,” he said. “I don’t know how it looks from the outside but we have put in everything that we possibly could to make those deals happen and we made most of them happen. We have been very efficient with what Andrea has done in the market again. It has been incredible, the support of all the club and that’s it. It’s not perfect but it doesn’t need to be perfect.”

Arteta believes that Arsenal have enough.

Sports.title: Isak’s rapid double sinks Ipswich to give Andoni Iraola first Liverpool win
Sports.content:
A first win for Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool, the introduction of the latest star signing in Bradley Barcola making for a successful Friday night. Better yet, continuing signs that Alexander Isak, last year’s model, is coming back to life, his two, well-taken early goals securing the three points. That Cody Gakpo, Isak’s supplier, might have been at Manchester City or Tottenham had the transfer runes been right, added further to a sense of renewal. Liverpool’s attackers were full of the speed and invention sorely lacking for much of last season.

Once Barcola arrived in the second half, those velocity levels increased yet further, Liverpool playing the attacking style, high on risk and entertainment, the appointment of Iraola promised. “We are starting to get to the way we want to play,” said Isak afterwards.

Travelling Liverpool fans were made to wait for their first glimpse of £123m Barcola, his being on the bench adding further suspense to a deal that took an entire summer to complete.

If Ipswich looked to show the “emotional discipline” their manager, Gary O’Neil, said they lacked in losing 5-2 at Old Trafford, little was in evidence in a ruinous opening spell that betrayed the decent performance they went on to put in.

How long will Iraola’s doctrines take to embed? Perhaps not as long as feared. Isak, the most expensive player signed under the outgoing sporting director Richard Hughes, looks – at last – to be flowering. To follow his strike against Nottingham Forest, he had scored twice by the 10th minute. “If Alex is fit and is available, he will produce the numbers,” said Iraola.

Assisted for both by Gakpo, the finishes were of the gold standard Liverpool invested so heavily in. “Cody was outstanding,” said Virgil van Dijk, sharing the credit. “I said it before the transfer window had closed, he’s important for us, and he will be important this season.” Iraola joined the appreciation society: “I had no doubt with Cody … he knows how much we value him.”

“The level is ruthless,” said O’Neil, otherwise exalted by his team’s response to adversity beyond those opening nine minutes. “If you make mistakes against players like Gakpo, Wirtz and Barcola, there’s a chance you will get punished.”

Just as at Old Trafford, two Ipswich goals were conceded in quick, damaging succession, the defence far too open and chaotic. After Víctor Muñoz had set off on a long run stopped only by Issa Diop’s last-man tackle, Julio Enciso controlled the ball, taking a beat by standing on the ball, as if calling for calm.

Isak, who had a third first-half goal disallowed for offside, made the runs into scoring positions that made his reputation, nothing like the sorry figure of his debut, lost season. Meanwhile, a no-look pass from Ipswich’s captain, Dara O’Shea, straight to Gakpo, betrayed a collective cognitive dissonance.

View image in fullscreen Bradley Barcola beats Dara O’Shea on his Liverpool debut. Photograph: Dave Shopland/AP

Florian Wirtz becoming involved with the tricks and flicks offered another pointer that last summer’s huge Liverpool outlay may not be so wasteful as it appeared in Arne Slot’s dog days. Iraola’s appointment came with a reputation for improving players. Should the Basque get the best from the German, in a similar price bracket to Barcola and Isak, then this week’s pronouncement he is happy with his squad will ring truer.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

An obvious gap in the Liverpool squad left by Hughes is a commanding defensive midfielder. Enciso often located space, though suffered for a lack of quality around him. Beyond the break, with O’Neil in full flow, barking at players and officials alike, Ipswich were more confrontational, less admiring of their opponent’s higher skill levels. “I hate having to talk about good performances when you don’t get points because you need to maximise them,” said O’Neil, painting a picture that will not match many other summations of the match.

Muñoz, stocky and adventurous, might well prove the answer to the right-wing vacancy left by Mohamed Salah, showing off a ready work ethic before departing in the double substitution that brought Barcola on. Isak also departed, returning after full time to an ovation from fans finally seeing something close to his potential.

With Gakpo pushed to centre-forward, Barcola’s first touches came off the left flank, one drop of the shoulder and sprint beyond O’Shea lifting the volume among the away supporters. “He hadn’t played a single minute since the World Cup so we had to be careful,” said Iraola. “He was always a threat.”

That burst of Barcola preceded another loss of Ipswich faculties as Leif Davis first pulled Dominik Szoboszlai, and then knocked him over for what appeared a clear penalty. Only an offside ruled by the video assistant protected the Ipswich defender’s modesty. The announcement of that decision brought the loudest cheer of the night from the home contingent.

Barcola, even amid the warp speed of the Premier League, showed lightning acceleration when creating a late chance for Gakpo. An impressive cameo and the expectation of far more to come from the player and his new team.

Sports.title: Uefa legal case may be beginning of the end for Infantino as Trump’s support evaporates | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
“Tell Mike it was just business. I always liked him.”

“He understands.”

“Tom, can you get me off the hook? For old times’ sake?”

“Sorry can’t do it.”

I never believed it would actually happen. Not really. Not until this week, when, for the first time, there was a sense, as The Godfather makes so abundantly clear, that you really can get to anyone.

Gianni Infantino is beleaguered. Gianni Infantino is re-beleaguered. Gianni Infantino has been beleaguered for almost six weeks, since news emerged of his grotesque undercover plan to sell off, for related personal gain, the shared global property he’s employed to preserve, protect and safely pass on.

There has been hopeful talk in that time of toxic status attained, a base being hollowed out, a rival presidential candidate next March. But power runs deep. Entrenched dictatorial power runs even deeper. Time passes. The doorway narrows. Infantino is already the man who sold the world, not once, but twice, most recently to Donald Trump in return for a peace prize, a scrunchie and a fawning presence around the sub-table of power.

Give it a month. Chuck in a Football Jesus turn at the lighted lectern a few weeks from now, arms whirling like a street magician, reeling off the usual stuff about caring and sharing, égalité, fraternité, fiscal stimuli. Look deep into those weirdly flat painted-on eyes, cold and hard behind the papier-mache mask of power. You don’t buy me out. I buy you out.

But something has shifted this week. It was never going to be the gnats around his ankles that did for Infantino: another thundering newspaper column, the latest stern denouncement from – whoah, hang on – former Manchester United utility defender Mikaël Silvestre.

Hard power is something else, however. And two things have now happened, both responses to the threat of a Uefa lawsuit, which I believe has no really serious notions of ultimate victory, but which may turn out to be an expert chess move, a zugzwang that leaves the king having to go somewhere, but with no safe spaces left to hide.

View image in fullscreen Josh Kushner said he ‘would not have gotten involved’ in Fifa’s plans had he known the full picture. Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters

The first response was Josh Kushner’s statement this week after being named as a party to discovery in Florida. Kushner was the money guy behind the Fifa Forward fiasco. Nuts isn’t it? The person you come to for finance and macro-favour just happens to be, by an accident of talent and destiny, the brother of the president’s son-in-law.

Kushner said he “would not have gotten involved” in Fifa’s plans had he known the full picture. He said this was all regrettable. Ostensibly mild and reasonable words, but with a sense of distance being carved out, of a cutting loose from the protective apron.

Kushner has also hired a nuclear option lawyer, Alex Spiro, who defended Elon Musk when he called a caver “a pedo” and Alec Baldwin when he accidentally shot someone. It’s a serious defensive move. As is, to a more rattled degree, Fifa’s counter-filing this week, which dismisses the whole episode as a “smear campaign”, then says the quiet thing out loud. Specifically, Fifa mentions discovery and a very urgent intention to resist it.

This is the real point. No one on the Infantino side wants discovery. Which is, to be clear, the sharing of related documents, from internal memos down to relevant emails sent from your smartphone on the golf course after lunch.

This, as Gianni knows, is always a worry to those in power. And you really don’t want to be a worry to anyone in any way connected to Trump. This is why, behind the sabre rattling, there is for the first time a sense of a thinning out, of nobody there on the ward, no cops on the doors, of the old man up there unprotected.

Even Trump’s early support for Infantino was a little over-juiced in the media. The president Truth Socialed his assurances in early August. It still felt a little qualified. “If for any reason” Fifa got rid of Infantino, well, this would be really bad. And nothing since.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There is a vague sense of a shrug here, of an amble away from the stage. We remember the good times for the Gianni-Trump bro-tocracy, laughing together like men in a Brooks Brothers senior knitwear advert, the gleaming bald impresario to power and his tolerant daddy-patron looking as ever like a giant man-size unit of American food, as though something deep-fried, honey-glazed and dished up at an out-of-town hotel conference buffet has somehow learned to walk around in a baggy suit and say things like “a very tall, very handsome man”.

View image in fullscreen ‘Zip it’: Fifa will want to avoid discovery to protect Gianni Infantino’s relationship with Donald Trump. Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPA

This is always brittle. Trump will walk you in, remember your name, glad-hand you by the stairwell. But once you’re gone you really are gone. There is no loyalty, and logically so, because Trumpian politics has no core belief, no substance, just a cold, hard matrix of winners and losers.

And if you lose, or look like you might, then by coincidence bad things tend to happen. The Guardian published a list a while back of Trump enemies who now find themselves subject to charges, exile, security clearances revoked, mortgage fraud investigated. And that list does include some pretty high-profile one-time golden boys.

Michael Cohen, the fiercest of Trump loyalists, who famously stated he would “take a bullet” for the big man? Legal difficulties and fallings-out intervened. Cohen has since been imprisoned, disbarred and sent into exile. The former US attorney general Jeff Sessions was among the first to call Trumpism “a movement”. He’s now not only out of the game, but has apparently been described by Trump, variously, as weak, confused, dumb, an idiot, a disgrace, and “mentally retarded”. There is a pattern here. If you’re in then you’re in. But don’t fly too close to those flames.

The decision of the court on allowing discovery could well be key. Make no mistake, Uefa is accusing Fifa and Infantino of “criminal mismanagement”. The key issue is an alleged undervaluing in the sale of the World Cup. Unrelated, and arguably standard industry practice, Infantino also stood to take a huge personal salary from all this.

It is a clear attempt to peer inside and see what, if anything, is in that box. Uefa wants discovery from Fifa, Thrive Capital and the Trump donor and deal adviser Greg Maffei, all of whom will have paper trails from that period when Infantino was granted intoxicating access to the halls of power. It puts you in mind of the Club World Cup trophy, a weird, frightening-looking thing, all razor-sharp odd nooks and crannies, the secret little drawer full of human toenails. Do you really want to know what’s in there? Is it safe to look?

“Please Mike, don’t do this, don’t do this to me”

“Today I settle all the family business. So don’t tell me you’re innocent.”

How is this going to play out? Infantino is doing what he can, touring his outer provinces and pressing the flesh. Saudi Arabia has offered qualified backing (“at this time …”). There’s a Fifa congress in November. Really, though, you wonder about votes, and to what extent votes are the thing here. It is hard not to muse on how it ended in football for Sepp Blatter and Michel Platini. That one-shot illegal payment allegation really did come out of the blue.

For now the process will simmer on. Legal challenges often fail or melt away. Uefa just needs to keep pressing, to make it clear that coals will be raked. Keep the pressure up and you never know what may fall out, or from where. Mr president, you can have my answer now. Our offer is this. Nothing.

Sports.title: ‘The noise was unbelievable’: the referee’s view of Mexico v England at the World Cup
Sports.content:
It was 6pm on 5 July in Mexico City, and Alireza Faghani, a 48-year-old Australian-Iranian, was asleep in the locker room, snoring. His assistants had turned the music down. Had it not been for the muffled roar of nearly 90,000 fans through the concrete walls of the Estadio Azteca, he could have slept until the following morning.

Faghani was the referee for Mexico v England in the last 16 at the 2026 World Cup. Mexico hadn’t lost a competitive game at the Azteca since 2013, at least in part because they’re used to the conditions. Situated 2,240 metres above sea level, the air contains less oxygen. Opponents struggle to breathe, let alone win.

This was Faghani’s third match of his fourth World Cup. A contender for the final, he needed a strong performance. Outside, pouring rain fell from the sky. Thunder cracked overhead. The storm had delayed kick-off by an hour, but it could do little to quell the fans, who banged their drums and sang their chants.

Eventually the noise jolted Faghani into action. He splashed water over his face and reviewed his notes again. As a referee in Australia’s A-League, he knew few of the players well, so he’d been studying their triggers, their temperaments and their tendencies in different match scenarios. “You know the key players, you understand their characteristics and how they normally behave in certain situations,” he adds.

The uncertainty around the kick-off time had disrupted his preparation for the match. Days earlier, amid warnings of extreme weather, Fifa officials had revealed plans to bring kick-off forward by six hours, only to shelve them after Keir Starmer, then the British prime minister, raised concerns that it would favour the hosts by giving England less time to adapt to the altitude.

During those hours of uncertainty, Faghani needed to adjust his pre-match physical and nutritional schedule accordingly. It was unsettling. “I don’t really have any superstitions, but I do like routine,” he says. “That routine gives me a sense of calm and helps me enter the field with a clear mind.”

View image in fullscreen Deafening noise generated by Mexico’s fans inside the Azteca added to the pressure. Photograph: Ezra Shaw/Fifa/Getty Images

But he tried not to spend too much energy on something he couldn’t control. “At this level, part of the job is staying calm and keeping your preparation as normal as possible, even when everything around you is changing.”

As kick-off approached, Faghani also resisted obsessing over his notes. He didn’t want to introduce bias into his decision-making. If you go into a match expecting a player to dive in a one-on-one situation, for instance, you might see a dive when there was genuine contact. Or you might see a player kick out when it was just normal movement. “That can be dangerous because you can start the match with a preconceived idea,” he adds.

So he visualised the opening moments. “I try to switch off from everything outside the dressing room and focus only on the match,” he says. Mexico had a tendency for rampant starts. England were hard in the tackle. “We expected a match with a lot of intensity, particularly in transition and in individual duels. The important thing was to be mentally prepared for the speed of the game.”

England kicked off to a chorus of boos, and those boos greeted their every touch. “The noise was unbelievable,” Faghani recalls. The same sound that had woken him up was now a distraction, and a threat to his impartiality on borderline calls – so he tried to block it out. “You are always aware of the atmosphere, especially with a home crowd like Mexico at the Azteca. Naturally, they react strongly to decisions involving their team, and you can feel that energy.”

In the opening stages, he wanted to let the match unfold without imposing himself on it. To assess the intensity, then decide how strongly he would need to intervene. “Every match develops its own personality, and one of the most important skills is recognising that personality as quickly as possible and adapting your refereeing to it.”

In this cauldron, however, Faghani was afforded no such luxury. With just seconds gone, Declan Rice stretched for a loose ball and caught an opponent in the head with his boot. With nearly a full match still to play, Faghani wanted to keep his yellow card in his pocket. Once he books a player, he loses that option to manage them later. Another yellow means a red, which fundamentally alters the balance of a match, damaging the spectacle.

View image in fullscreen Alireza Faghani shows a yellow card to Declan Rice (right) in the first minute. Photograph: Rodrigo Oropeza/AFP/Getty Images

But he felt he had no choice. He needed to communicate strongly to the players that dangerous challenges like this were unacceptable, otherwise he feared they would spread. So he flashed his yellow card into the air, igniting the Mexican fans. “It was a clear yellow card for me,” he says. “It also helped everyone understand the line from the beginning.”

Thomas Tuchel the England manager, berated the fourth official on the sideline. As both sides launched into tackles, the fans urging them on, Rice’s chances of seeing out the match seemed slim. “Very quickly I felt it was going to be an intense, emotional, and fast game,” Faghani says. “I knew I needed to stay calm, be strong when necessary, but also give the players space to play.”

Finding this balance “comes from reading the players and the temperature of the game”, according to Faghani, but he struggled under the pressure. “You are constantly asking yourself whether an intervention will help the match or interrupt it unnecessarily.”

As softer fouls were punished and harder challenges went unpunished, frustration simmered and spread. A Mexican defender threw his arms in the air after being penalised for tugging down Jude Bellingham. “It’s not a foul,” he yelled. “It’s not a foul!” Faghani sprinted over, stood face to face with the player, and blew his whistle – an overt, intentional demonstration of authority. “In that environment, I felt it was important to deal with dissent immediately,” he says. “I wanted to send a clear message that communication was welcome, but there was a limit. Sometimes strong body language is more effective than using cards.”

View image in fullscreen Alireza Faghani intervenes as Jordan Pickford tries to stop Raúl Jiménez placing the ball on the penalty spot. Photograph: Antonio Nava/ ZUMA/Shutterstock

Faghani repeated the tactic moments later when another Mexican screamed at him for delaying a quick throw-in. It seemed to have worked. The dissent dissipated, and in its place came flowing football from the Mexicans.

It was two English attacks that led to the game’s first decisive moments, though, with two Jude Bellingham goals. Mexico responded with a goal of their own. 2-1 to England. Faghani clenched his fists, knowing the pressure was only rising from here. But first he allowed himself a brief moment to drink in the skills on show. “You definitely appreciate the quality, but only for a second. As a referee, your mind immediately goes to the next responsibility – restart, player reactions, positioning, and staying focused.”

England held on until half-time. In the locker room, Faghani was mildly satisfied with his performance. “Overall, I felt we found a good balance,” he says, speaking about the line of intervention. “My mindset was simply to maintain the same concentration and consistency in the second half.”

Not even Faghani, however, could have anticipated what was to come.

In the 52nd minute, Jesús Gallardo, Mexico’s left-back, sprinted down the left wing. Jarell Quansah, England’s right-back, sprinted towards him. Between them, the ball rolled slowly over the turf. They were converging on it at full speed. If Gallardo got there first, he would be through on goal, with Raúl Jiménez waiting in the box. From the centre of England’s half, Faghani watched Quansah slide in, taking the ball and Gallardo. Gallardo rolled on the floor in agony and the Mexican fans roared, but Faghani carried on. “In real time, it looked like I could allow play to continue,” he says. Mexican coaching staff shot off their seats, gesticulating furiously at Faghani to stop play. Others shoved England staff.

At the next break in play, Mexican players swarmed the referee. He gestured for them to move away. Then his VAR, Nicolás Gallo Barragán, told him to pause the restart while he checked the incident. Faghani’s stomach dropped. He couldn’t help but replay Quansah’s challenge in his mind, wondering what he hadn’t seen. Then Barragán instructed him to use the pitchside monitor.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Sport in Focus Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Whistles rang around the stadium as Faghani jogged over. Mexican players yelled at him as he reviewed the incident, demanding a red card. But soon they became white noise, Faghani recalls. “Once you’re at the monitor, your focus becomes very narrow. You concentrate only on making the correct decision.”

It took just three replays from the same angle for Faghani to change his mind. From behind Quansah, he hadn’t been able to see the defender’s boot make contact high on Gallardo’s shin. “I saw the challenge but I didn’t have a clear view of the point of contact,” he says. “But now it was clear.”

View image in fullscreen Mexico fans celebrated like their team had scored when England were reduced to 10 men. Photograph: Manuel Velasquez/Fifa/Getty Images

As Faghani thrust his red card into the air, the Mexican fans celebrated as if they’d scored a goal. On the sidelines, Tuchel adjusted his tactics. Faghani gulped down air. “You could feel the physical demand more, particularly after repeated high-intensity runs,” he says.

Precisely when he didn’t want one, the game demanded another. Anthony Gordon sprinted towards a flick-on from Harry Kane, closing in on the Mexican goal. As the Mexican goalkeeper rushed from his goal, Faghani sprinted towards the play, fighting to be close enough to see any contact between him and Gordon.

Gordon touched the ball before the goalkeeper wiped out his legs. Faghani saw and heard the contact, almost in slow motion, then pointed confidently to the penalty spot. “That’s part of the physical preparation at this level,” he says. “You work hard to arrive in the best possible position, but once the incident happens, you have to become mentally calm very quickly and judge only what you see.”

Now the England fans roared with emotion. Harry Kane converted, giving England a 3-1 lead. Walking slowly back to the centre circle, Faghani tried to fill up his lungs and compose himself. Thirty minutes remained, and he knew a Mexico onslaught was coming.

The onslaught soon produced a penalty. Hooking away the ball from the England box, Harry Kane kicked a Mexican leg. Despite appeals from the Mexican players, Faghani let play continue. “Initially, from my angle, I wasn’t convinced there was enough for a penalty,” he says. “I heard the appeals, of course, but players’ reactions can’t determine your decision. You have to trust what you see.”

Moments later, Barragán told him to pause play to review the incident. Faghani’s stomach then dropped a second time. Seconds passed. Then some more. Once again, Faghani tried not to think about what he might have missed. Under extreme pressure, he wanted to be calm enough to review the incident accurately on the monitor. “Second-guessing yourself for a minute doesn’t help. You need to stay composed and ready for the next step.”

At first, at the monitor, he couldn’t see what Barragán had seen. He certainly couldn’t see a clear and obvious error. He considered sticking with his on-field call, something he’d done earlier in the tournament.

Then Barragán slowed down the footage and walked him through Kane’s contact with the Mexican player’s boot. Kane had caught the boot without kicking the ball. Slowly, the foul revealed itself. Then it was all Faghani could see. “The communication helped me understand exactly what VAR wanted me to look at,” he says. “Once we identified the relevant contact and I saw the best angle, the decision became much clearer.”

Mexico scored. 3–2 to England. Twenty minutes remaining. Plenty of time for big calls. To get them right, Faghani needed to reset, fast. To let go of the disappointment of missing two crucial calls. “You have to move on immediately,” he says. “VAR is part of the refereeing team, and the objective is to get the final decision right. You cannot allow one decision, or even two, to affect the next one.”

View image in fullscreen Dan Burn of England blocks a bicycle kick from Raúl Jiménez. Photograph: Jam Media/Getty Images

England hung on. No more goals. In the final minutes of normal time, the Mexican bench pointed at their watches, demanding that Faghani account for every second of stoppage time. When the board showed 11 minutes, Faghani sighed. His muscles were weary, his thoughts cloudy. However hard he breathed, he couldn’t fill up his lungs. By this point, the pressure was almost unfathomable. He knew that a single lapse could reshape history and end his tournament.

Fortunately for him, that lapse never came. In the 102nd minute, he blew his whistle and ended the match. English players fell to their knees. Faghani wanted to join them, to close his eyes, to release the tension. Later, in the locker room, he listened to music and chugged down water, reflecting on a job well done.

Down the hall, however, Tuchel took aim at him. “The referees are just not good enough, fourth officials are just not good enough. That’s the bottom line,” he said. He singled out the decision to award the Mexican penalty, questioning whether the intervention had met the threshold for a clear and obvious error. “VAR overturns [but] is this a clear and obvious error for the penalty? For sure not. They overturned a situation where [the referee] doesn’t even give a foul.”

Faghani, however, refused to dwell on the criticism. Hours later, once the Azteca had fallen silent, he headed for a light dinner and then to bed, where he quickly fell into another deep slumber. This time, he slept peacefully.

The Impossible Job: The Truly Unbelievable World of Football Referees by William Ralston (Viking, £22). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com

Sports.title: Alexia Putellas begins WSL ride as London City outclass Manchester United
Sports.content:
There are few scenarios since Millwall Lionesses broke away from Millwall and became London City Lionesses that would have felt more surreal than the idea of Alexia Putellas captaining the side to a statement win in a WSL season-opener in Bromley just seven years later.

Here we are though: referees have to get used to the formerly talismanic Barcelona captain stooping to pick up the coin after the toss, as is her custom; players must get used to eyes and cameras looking past them to focus in on the influential No 11; and the two-time Ballon d’Or winner has to get used to playing with teammates not drilled in a very specific style of play from such an early age that it becomes an inherent part of them.

Of course it is a step down to go from the three-time European champions to a team embarking on their second season in the WSL, but off the pitch, with the owner, Michele Kang, committed to giving female athletes the best of everything, the difference will be more negligible, even before the approved new world-class training facility is built.

Regardless of what you think of her movements in women’s football, or about private finance investment in it, Kang, who walked the perimeter of the stadium prior to kick-off taking photos with fans in her ‘Kang 27’ emblazoned home shirt, is the antithesis of the owner of last night’s opposition, Jim Ratcliffe, and his dismal references to his women’s teams.

View image in fullscreen Michele Kang did the rounds at a sold-out stadium, the first time London City Lionesses have done that since starting to play at Bromley. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Putellas led the team out to a ­raucous welcome at the sold-out home of Bromley FC, her steely stare only broken to crack a quick smile and share some words with the mascot gripping her hand.

In this corner of London’s outskirts, the midfielder experienced her first proper taste of her new reality. At 32 and with her very best years likely behind her, it was a solid rather than showstopper performance. She was outshone by teammates such as Rosa Kafaji and Lucía Corrales, who unfortunately went off on a stretcher late on after overstretching for the ball.

“Everybody knows what [Putellas] can create and bring to us,” said the London City manager, Eder Maestre. “It’s not just the things she’s capable of doing, it’s the things she facilitates for other players too.

“Having this kind of player in the squad is very important because she represents the highest standards and having her involved in it is not only because of her performance, but also because of the leadership she can bring in terms of helping us to reach that standard. But it is not only about Alexia, she is only one player, and I think the most impactful thing was the way everybody connected, the chemistry that we are building around the players.”

View image in fullscreen Alexia Putellas was solid rather than spectacular on her WSL debut. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Maestre has been tasked with gelling a squad stacked with new players, including the former England goalkeeper Mary Earps, who was on the bench with Elene Lete starting.

Maestre explained: “Mary had some issues in pre-season so that was why there was inconsistency in game involvement. We have two strong goalkeepers. Today, Elene deserved to be in the lineup. She was very strong in her actions.”

Maestre has said the identity he wants to create for the side is “related to all those things we felt when we were playing football as children”.

That ethos was evident in their play, with London City on the front foot from the off. Despite not always being pretty, they looked like they were having fun as they pressed and attacked aggressively, and when they broke the deadlock nine minutes in it was not surprising.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Alanna Kennedy provided the pressure, rising above a hunkered-down Julia Zigiotti Olme who could only turn the ball into her own net.

View image in fullscreen Delphine Cascarino (left), who set up London City Lionesses’ second goal, was named player of the match. Photograph: John Walton/PA

It was a cruel introduction to life in the WSL, and its spotlight, for the new Manchester United manager, Eva Olid, particularly with Chelsea and Arsenal up next, but on this showing and after a lacklustre summer transfer window, few games would have offered a kind introduction. United were outclassed in Bromley, conceding 60% possession.

They did at least manage three shots, but by the time they did any hopes of a leveller were crushed by the home side, when Mapi León’s corner was worked towards Delphine Cascarino and the French forward’s cross was delightfully flicked into the far corner by Daniëlle van de Donk.

“It’s a process,” said Olid. “I think it was something more mental in the first half, we could feel like the players were not believing.

“At half-time I say that this is not us, we need the ball to be ourselves … in the second half, we were building through the middle, finding the free player, playing between the lines. That is us, and I can feel my team in the second half. It’s my job to help them to believe that we can always be the team of the second half.”

There was a late consolation for Olid’s humbled charges deep into added time, when Simi Awujo powered in the loose ball after a free-kick was cleared into empty space, but it could not dampen the enthusiasm of an emphatic performance from Maestre’s side – a performance that is a very solid foundation to build on.

Sports.title: José Mourinho sick as a Parrott as Real Madrid sunk by Real Betis and Irish supersub
Sports.content:
Real Madrid’s perfect start in La Liga ⁠ended on Friday when Real Betis beat them 1-0, with the ⁠substitute Troy Parrott ⁠scoring ​nine minutes from time and goalkeeper Álvaro Valles saving a stoppage-time ⁠penalty from Kylian Mbappé.

The clash began at a high tempo but the pace ⁠dropped after the interval in the heat in ​Seville. The Republic of Ireland star Parrott, introduced ‌in the 68th ‌minute, broke the deadlock in the 81st when ‌he reacted quickly after Thibaut Courtois parried a header into his path.

Mbappé struck the crossbar four minutes later before the substitute Carlos Espí met a cross from Vinícius Júnior with a spectacular bicycle kick, only for the equaliser to be ruled ​out for offside following a VAR review.

Nelson Deossa then nearly sealed the victory for hosts Betis with a long-range effort after spotting Courtois ⁠off his line, but the goalkeeper recovered to ​make ​the save.

José Mourinho’s Madrid got one ​final opportunity when Natan brought down ​Vinícius inside ‌the area, ​deep ​into stoppage time, but Valles saved Mbappé’s spot-kick to preserve Betis’s lead and secure the three points.

“My team played a great game, and sometimes you lose and you don’t know why,” Mourinho said. “We dominated, controlling everything, lots of attacks, lots of chances. If we had drawn we would have been left frustrated, so imagine how we feel after losing.

“I don’t know how we lost because we played very well collectively. I cannot fault the attitude of any of my players. We deserved to win but deserving to win does not ⁠give you points. I’m very happy with ​my players, all ​of them. I cannot fault ​any of them individually. As for the penalty, when ​one of us ‌steps up to ​take it, ​we all stand together.

“The Betis players are more streetwise than the Madrid players, who are very honest. With the backing of a fantastic crowd, they manage to gain these kinds of advantages.”

Paris Saint-Germain looked to be on their way to their first Ligue 1 win of the season when Marquinhos put the hosts ahead in the 31st minute, but Monaco rallied with goals from Flavio Nazinho in the 58th minute and Stanis Idumbo in the 72nd. Monaco lead the table as the only team to win their opening three games.

“We clearly deserved to win. That is my opinion,” said Luis Enrique.

“I saw the game and it was the typical game in which we were better than the opposition and created a lot more chances, but the opposition goalkeeper was the best player on the pitch.”

The US striker Folarin Balogun was left out of Monaco’s squad after the collapse of his proposed transfer to Everton this week, while Lamine Camara played after his move to Chelsea was called off at the last minute.

View image in fullscreen PSG’s Fabián Ruiz (left) challenges for the ball with Monaco’s in-demand Lamine Camara. Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/AP

PSG had already drawn 2-2 with Rennes and Lille in their first two games and also lost the French Super Cup to Lens 1-0 last month.

The first league defeat came hours after PSG announced contract extensions for coach Luis Enrique and several players. João Neves, Lucas Beraldo, Senny Mayulu and Willian Pacho all signed new deals through to 2031, while Fabián Ruiz had his contract extended until 2028.

Lyon beat Auxerre 3-1 earlier on Friday and are second in the league, two points behind Monaco and level on points with Lille, who won 1-0 at Toulouse on Thursday thanks to an Ayase Ueda goal.

Assane Diao bagged a brace as Como rolled to a 4-1 win at Genoa in Serie A. Nico Paz and Martin Baturina also added goals. Cesc Fabregas’ side lead the Italian standings by one point ahead of a pack of six teams who have yet to play this weekend.

Como will make their Champions League debut against Leipzig on 10 September, with Manchester United to visit in October and PSG in January.

In Germany, Stuttgart romped to a 4-1 win over Köln in the Bundesliga.

Sports.title: Richard Hughes, mastermind of Liverpool's £700m transfer rebuild, QUITS to move to Saudi Arabia
Sports.content:
Big-spending Richard Hughes has officially left his post as Liverpool sporting director. The Scottish transfer chief informed the club of his desire to seek a new challenge earlier this year but agreed to stay in situ until the end of this summer window. Hughes and Liverpool also agreed that he would work for only the Premier League club and not simultaneously conduct business for Saudi Arabian side Al Hilal, where he is expected to join. The Reds hierarchy are satisfied Hughes honoured this agreement. Hughes spent more than £700million at Anfield on big-money players like Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola. He was also the man that identified Arne Slot and Andoni Iraola as head coach after Jurgen Klopp's exits. He joined the club from Bournemouth in June 2024. But he leaves with some fans frustrated at his business which has left Liverpool exposed in certain positions. Richard Hughes has left Liverpool with the transfer chief set to move to Saudi Arabia Alexander Isak was signed under Hughes' watch for an initial £125million in September 2025 Bradley Barcola made his debut for Liverpool against Ipswich Town on Friday night Hughes said of his departure: 'First and foremost, I would like to reiterate what I said upon my arrival – it has been a source of great pride to have been given the opportunity to serve this incredible and unique institution. That is something I will always be grateful for. 'My appreciation extends to ownership for their support and leadership, to club staff at all levels who give so much to make Liverpool FC what it is, to the players who make such an enormous contribution and to the fans who support the team in great numbers whenever and wherever games take place. 'I'll always follow and support the club with great affection, and I wish everyone involved nothing but success for this season and beyond.' Hughes (centre) played a key role in bringing manager Andoni Iraola (right) to Liverpool LIVERPOOL'S BIGGEST DEALS UNDER HUGHES Alexander Isak - £125m Bradley Barcola - £123m Florian Wirtz - £116m Hugo Ekitike - £79m Jeremy Jacquet - £60m Fenway Sports Group president Mike Gordon added: 'Richard joined us at the start of a period of change, embracing that responsibility by leading our football operations department and overseeing recruitment while also providing valuable support to our coaching staff. 'The results we achieved in these areas during this period are testament to this contribution. Nevertheless, we respect Richard's life choices and wish him and his family well in their next venture.' The news comes a day after Liverpool claimed their first win of the season by defeating Ipswich Town 2-0. Isak, who cost the club an initial £125million in September 2025, scored a first-half double against the Premier League new boys. Bradley Barcola, signed from Paris Saint-Germain for £123m, made his debut on Friday night.
