Sports.title: Anthony Joshua's conqueror Andy Ruiz is PUMMELLED with punches and brutally beaten on his return to the ring after two years - but incredibly insists he WILL keep fighting
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua's conqueror Andy Ruiz is PUMMELLED with punches and brutally beaten on his return to the ring after two years - but incredibly insists he WILL keep fighting

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Andy Ruiz, the man who condemned Anthony Joshua to his first ever professional defeat, suffered a horrific loss of his own on Friday night.

The 36-year-old Mexican was left bruised and bloodied as he lost to Poland's Damian Knyba on his return to the ring after two years out.

Knyba unleashed heavy punch after punch in the seventh round but Ruiz managed to ride it out, after being saved by the bell, to lose by a unanimous points decision.

Ruiz, who is now signed to British promoter Eddie Hearn, vowed to carry on despite losing his comeback fight to Knyba. The Pole now has a record of 18 wins and one defeat.

Rewind to June 2019, and Ruiz shocked the boxing world by upsetting the odds to knock Joshua out in the seventh round at Madison Square Garden.

Ruiz was a late stand-in for Jarrell Miller, who had failed a drugs test, and wasn't seen as a threat to Joshua's chances of remaining unbeaten and hanging on to his then IBF, WBO and WBA world heavyweight titles.

ANDY RUIZ IS SAVED BY THE BELL 🤯🤯🤯#TheFight | #RuizKnyba | Live NOW on DAZN and TNT ▪️ pic.twitter.com/JVQjG3KQM3 — DAZN Boxing (@DAZNBoxing) September 5, 2026

Andy Ruiz kneels down in front of the referee after being on the receiving end of heavy blows

Ruiz feels the full force of Poland's Damian Knyba during Friday's fight in New Jersey

Ruiz famously defeated the then undefeated Anthony Joshua back in June 2019

Joshua exacted revenge six months later and Ruiz has gone on to have just four more fights since due to injury problems, beating Chris Arreola and Luis Ortiz before drawing with Miller and now suffering his third loss.

Ruiz said after Friday's defeat in New Jersey: 'It was just a long layoff, and it was a great opponent.

'I didn't want to take an easy fight, so that's why I took Damian. He's a big guy. But we've got to take risks. I've still got it in me, man. I've just got to stay active and I want to fight again.

'Every time I tried to come in, he'd hold me really tight, and I just couldn't let my combinations go.

'He played a good game plan, but I'd love to run it back and do things a lot different.'

The judges scored the fight 117-110, 114-113 and 114-113 in Knyba's favour.

It wasn't the night Hearn was hoping for after signing Ruiz this summer but much of his current focus is on trying to finalise Joshua's highly anticipated fight against British rival Tyson Fury.

The bout has been proposed to take place in November after years of negotiations but the location of the fight appears to be a major sticking point.

Hearn and Joshua are said to want the fight to take place at Wembley Stadium in London while the Fury camp are reportedly leaning towards Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Sports.title: Virgil van Dijk suggests Cody Gakpo is suffering after cancelled £80m Man City transfer and loss of his unborn son - despite his remarkable return to help Liverpool win
Sports.content:
Virgil van Dijk suggests Cody Gakpo is suffering after cancelled £80m Man City transfer and loss of his unborn son - despite his remarkable return to help Liverpool win

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Virgil Van Dijk insists no-one knows what Cody Gakpo has been through and hailed the Dutchman after his two assists helped Liverpool to their first win of the season.

Gakpo has had a turbulent and heartbreaking summer that started with his partner losing a pregnancy during the World Cup. He then nearly completed an £80million move to Manchester City.

But on the pitch, the forward has started this season in electric form, scoring one and assisting three. Two of those were to set up Alexander Isak for a brace at Ipswich on Friday night.

And captain Van Dijk said: 'I don't think anyone knows what he has been through, so it is not easy for the outside world.

'But the reality is he is here with us, and he wants to be important for us. He showed it already over numerous games, including already the last two games before tonight and then today again. Now it is on to the next game.'

Van Dijk pleaded with his compatriot to stay and, asked about Gakpo's importance so far this term, said: 'I don't think only this season. Obviously over the last seasons. I'm glad he stayed and on to many more good games.'

Cody Gakpo starred for Liverpool, producing two assists against Ipswich Town

On goal-scorer Isak, Van Dijk added: 'He had a terrible injury and I think a lot of people would take a lot of time to come back from it. That was very unfortunate. But he worked so hard behind the scenes.

'We know there is obviously pressure with him coming to the club for a big amount, and everyone wants him to perform. I think he had a great World Cup and he had a great pre-season in my opinion and I think he had a good start to the season, so I think he is only going to get better.'

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso are the king of the Premier League and the pretender to the throne. This is the story of how their remarkable shared history led them to the same touchline - as very different managers
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso are the king of the Premier League and the pretender to the throne. This is the story of how their remarkable shared history led them to the same touchline - as very different managers

The photograph has been famous for some time. Two 10-year-old boys stand on a grassy slope at a youth football tournament in France, staring into the camera. It is their first tournament abroad with Antiguoko, a club from their home city of San Sebastian, in the Basque Country. They will go on to win the tournament.

On the left, Mikel Arteta beams into the camera. He looks smart, in a dark anorak. He is holding what looks like a notebook or a map in a plastic holder. He looks neat and together and stylish even then. He looks as if he cannot wait for all the adventures that life is going to bring him.

On the right, Xabi Alonso looks more uncertain. He wears a wistful, thoughtful expression. He is looking at the camera as if it is a curiosity. He is carrying a rolled-up poster in one hand and what looks like a pennant in the other. His anorak is undone and billows around him. They are different characters but a certain intensity is already apparent in both.

And now the boys are men. And the first thing to say about them is that they have grown up good men, a product of their families and their city and their region.

‘I know I am hardly neutral expressing my opinion on him as a friend and former team-mate,’ Jamie Carragher says of Alonso, ‘but anyone who spends time with Xabi will appreciate that the manner in which he carries himself and presents his vision of the game oozes class.’

Arteta can divide opinion more than his old friend but his instincts are sound and he tries to be fair and just, not only with his players but with everyone he meets.

He is liked by staff and players at Arsenal and if it sometimes feels that he lacks levity, that is because levity is not something he aspires to.

Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso, aged 10, during their time at Antiguoko, a club in San Sebastian. The pair will face off on the touchline at the Emirates this Sunday

The coincidence of Alonso and Arteta growing up together, playing football on Playa de La Concha in San Sebastian, playing for the same youth team, growing into players who faced each other for Liverpool and Everton and now will face each other as managers of Chelsea and Arsenal at the Emirates on Sunday, is endlessly striking.

Both men have led their clubs to successive wins in the early stages of the new season and early predictions are that they and their respective teams are the most likely sides, along with Manchester City, to contest the title this year.

Sunday’s Emirates clash will be their first meeting as managers but it seems likely to be the start of a fierce rivalry.

To add to the fascination of their shared background, Andoni Iraola, the new Liverpool manager, played for Antiguoko at the same time but Alonso and Arteta have risen faster and more prominently. And if their backgrounds unite them, the different paths their careers took exposed them to contrasting influences that have shaped the football their teams play.

Both men have been outstandingly successful already. Arteta took over as Arsenal boss at the end of 2019 when the club was at a low ebb. He brought the club together, dragged it out of the despond that followed the Arsene Wenger years and had the hunger and the drive to survive three consecutive runner-up finishes to beat Manchester City to a first title in 22 years last season.

Those three successive second-place finishes would have destroyed other managers but not Arteta. He did not lose belief in himself or his players. He stuck to his playing principles, he resisted revolution, he kept evolving the side. He played under David Moyes at Everton and cites Moyes’ influence as a lesson in to how to build a club.

Alonso made a spectacular start to his own coaching career, taking over at Bayer Leverkusen in October 2022 and doing the unthinkable by leading them to the first Bundesliga title in their history in 2023-24 without losing a game. Leverkusen’s win halted a run of 11 straight Bayern Munich title triumphs.

Mikel Arteta has turned Arsenal into the dominant force in English football, never losing belief in himself or his players despite three straight second-place finishes

Alonso, meanwhile, will try and replicate his enormous success at Bayer Leverkusen with Chelsea

When the two boys left Antiguoko within a few months of each other in their teenage years, Arteta went to Barcelona and gradually came under the orbit of Pep Guardiola.

Most significantly of all, he became a disciple of Johan Cruyff, the great Dutch player who became one of the most imitated and followed coaches of all time and introduced a kind of ‘total football’ to Barcelona.

‘They changed the world for me,’ Arteta says of his time at Barcelona. ‘It’s like the sky had opened and this was a different sport.

'Johan was the influence of everything when I was at the La Masia academy, all the coaches who were at the academy it was the same. He was the one that injected that vision and that passion and understanding for the game.

‘From there, the game has evolved. Pep took the game and his vision to a different level. Johan is the greatest football person. I fell in love with that Barcelona team of his, I was six or seven, and I fell in love with that team, that way of playing. I had posters, kits, and if Barcelona were losing 1-0, I was going mad and my dad would send me to bed.

‘I learned a lot about the culture of a club when I was there and now, at Arsenal, it’s about the culture I create.

'It’s like drizzle. It’s always raining. You have to have a jacket because if you decide you are going to go without a jacket, you are soaking wet. If you don’t do it every day, the structure cracks.

‘I have high demands but I am realistic, too. What do I expect from one of my kids? That he goes to his room and everything is tidy and he always flushes the toilet and his toothpaste is always in the right place and they eat and they are always dressed? It’s not like this. We want everything perfect but this game is very imperfect.

‘I like to be challenged but if you work with me at Arsenal in the environment we have created at the club, I need you to love what you do because that is why we are here and we have to be contagious.’

Arteta's vision of football was shaped by Barcelona. He idolised Johan Cruyff, and worked for years with Pep Guardiola

Alonso, however, was shaped by a more diverse group of managers, including Rafa Benitez at Liverpool

Alonso’s influences are more diverse. Arteta idolised Cruyff, admired Moyes and worked with Guardiola at Manchester City but Alonso has played for both Guardiola and Jose Mourinho, both Rafa Benitez and Carlo Ancelotti. He has already managed in Germany and Spain, where his reign at Real Madrid was short-lived. Some credit him with being more flexible and pragmatic than Arteta.

‘The data and the information is not everything,’ Alonso says. ‘You have to have knowledge and intuition. You have to have man management. I have had great managers and from each one, I have learned. I have lived with them through good and bad moments and understood why they have made their decisions.

‘It’s not copy, paste. It’s about being authentic, being your own self. Building my own ambition as a coach, taking the best from each one. That is the way you are going to be able to trust me. I want to be open-minded to everything, not just one idea, have different ideas, sticking with your principles.

‘In different countries, you live different things. The more you know, the better you can get. The German way – for the last 20 years, something has been happening in German football. I think it started in 2006 with the World Cup in Germany and the influence of Jurgen Klinsmann.

‘What the German Federation started doing with grassroots and new managers and young managers. The profile of the manager is very brave and intense, physical but with a tactical approach. Julian Nagelsmann, Thomas Tuchel and Jurgen Klopp but there are others, too. I thought it was great what they were doing.’

So if Arteta largely sticks with a 4-3-3 system that has consistently served him well, Alonso mixes styles according to the challenge in front of him.

The basic formation he favours is 3-4-2-1 but against Brighton last weekend, Chelsea won the game 4-3 while recording only 26 per cent of possession. When new goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez was on the ball, 97 per cent of his passes were hit long. As he settles in at Stamford Bridge, that process will be refined.

Sunderland’s Granit Xhaka has played for both managers. He is more complimentary about Alonso than Arteta, which is hardly a surprise given he was the star man for Bayer Leverkusen in their title-winning season and endured some difficult times at Arsenal before and after Arteta’s arrival.

‘Mikel has his philosophy and that’s it,’ Xhaka says. ‘You know this: always change the sides, find the free man, let him jump, for example. Play always with a back four and never change to a back five for example, or never change like a 4-4-2 with two proper strikers. So you had this 4-3-3, with one six and two eights.

‘Xabi is a little bit different. I think that Xabi can play a back four, but he can play as well a back five. What he wants is always two No6s, not running everywhere, or more of the time be in the position. But if you are a coach you need your own philosophy, your own tactics, your own ideas.’

‘Mikel has his philosophy and that’s it,’ Granit Xhaka says of Arteta, under whom he endured some difficult times at Arsenal

‘Xabi is a little bit different,' adds Xhaka of Alonso, who is perceived as a more flexible coach than his boyhood friend

It is the most eagerly anticipated game of the season so far. Chelsea under Alonso look like the great entertainers, despite that possession statistic against Brighton. They will score plenty and concede a few, too.

Alonso appears to have allowed Cole Palmer to rediscover his best form and line him up in a formidable front three with Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro. They will present a test for Arsenal’s redoubtable defence.

Arsenal already look like the team to beat again this season. Their squad is even deeper and even more impressive than it was last season. They have improved from a position of strength. They look, at last, like a team that believes in itself after getting over the line and winning the title.

This is Arteta’s league now. He is the manager of the champions, he is the longest-serving manager in the top flight by a distance, he is the man.

But if there is a pretender, if there is a manager who has the qualities to threaten his dominance, it is the man who was once the boy standing next to him in the photograph all those years ago.

Sports.title: 'I didn't watch Villa when I was injured... it was too difficult': BOUBACAR KAMARA opens up on his 'tough' comeback from injury, what life is like under Unai Emery and why he's optimistic Aston Villa's best days are ahead of them
Sports.content:
Boubacar Kamara puffs out his cheeks and grimaces ever so slightly. The Aston Villa man is one of the best midfielders in the business but still the crash-bang-wallop of the modern Premier League takes his breath away.

Villa’s much-changed team are still looking for their first point and goal of the season after defeats by Brighton and Arsenal, and they travel to Hull on Saturday with the promoted team seeking a third successive win.

Unai Emery has lost six key players and brought in 11 new ones but at least he still has Kamara, probably Villa’s most important player and firmly on the road to full recovery after the second serious knee injury of his career.

But what a challenge it is. According to data from analytics company Skill Corner, in partnership with the SCOUTED platform, the Premier League outstrips every other league in five key physical metrics – distance covered, speed at which a player changes direction, top speeds, explosiveness and intensity.

According to Frank Lampard, one of the greatest midfielders of the Premier League era, the increasing emphasis on athleticism is probably irreversible.

When we put it to Kamara that the modern Premier League is becoming ever more like the NFL, he nods emphatically. ‘Yeah – that’s right,’ he says. ‘Is it as physically demanding as it has ever been in my career? Of course – by far.

The rough and tumble of the Premier League still takes Boubacar Kamara's breath away. ‘Every contact, everyone fights for the ball,' he says

The Frenchman has cemented his reputation as one of the finest midfielders in the Premier League since joining Villa in 2022

‘Every contact, everyone fights for the ball. The striker fights, the goalkeeper fights, everyone wants to win the ball, everyone has become stronger. In some moments during the game, it’s only fighting.’

It is a fight Villa need to win. At Brighton, they were felled early in the bout and never climbed off the canvas, losing 4-0 in a feeble performance.

And though Emery’s men threw a few more punches against Arsenal, it was still the champions who landed the knockout blow to secure a 1-0 victory at Villa Park. Emery’s men have not registered a shot on target this season.

The battles are becoming harder every year. In three full seasons under Emery, Villa have finished fourth, sixth and fourth, qualifying for the Champions League twice, as well as lifting the Europa League.

Even though their work in the transfer market leaves much to be desired, they have also been severely restricted by UEFA rules that seem tailor-made to favour Europe’s wealthiest.

‘It’s really difficult – every year the Premier League is so tough,’ Kamara reflected. ‘You have 10 teams fighting every year to get in Europe.

‘But to keep this mentality and consistency, and to finish every year in the top four or top six, and also to play in Europe every three days, going far in those competitions… it’s really not easy.

‘We saw last year and two years ago that at certain times of the season we were without certain players at crucial times. So when we saw the table at the end of the year we were proud, and we believe we can do even better this season.’

Emery’s long training sessions and even longer stints in the analysis suite have already raised eyebrows among those new players used to lighter regimes at previous clubs.

Life under Unai Emery is intense, and not for everyone. But so many of Villa's players have reached new heights under the Spaniard

Kamara suffered a serious knee injury in an FA Cup tie with Tottenham back in January

The Villa boss leads every day’s training and twice a week, in the afternoons, he will conduct 90-minute briefings. Sometimes, those are followed by individual chats with players.

It is intense stuff and there are unlikely to be many of the new faces in the starting XI at Hull. Yet as Kamara warns, the new players need to get up to speed – and fast.

‘With the meetings, you don’t have a choice – you need to sit and watch,’ Kamara says. ‘In training, every day you have the same task.

‘When new players arrive, they do extra work with Unai’s assistants. They teach them what they need to do so their adaptation can be as quick as possible. We have so many good, intelligent players in the team, too.

‘We will see what the manager wants. In some games, he wants us to play low block with good transitions. In others, he wants us to press high, keep the block high and play a lot of passes. Every game, we change our structure.

‘When we’ve shared the dressing room for three or four years with the same players, we are sad for a day or two but after that we are happy for them.’

As difficult as this start has been for Villa, simply having Kamara around is a bonus.

When he is in the team, Villa’s results are significantly better than when he is not. In that context, it was a huge achievement both to win the Europa League and finish in the top four last season, given Kamara did not play a game after injuring his knee at Tottenham in January.

Not only did he miss Villa’s march to Europa League glory, culminating in the win over Freiburg in Istanbul in May’s final, he also lost the chance of representing France at the World Cup. It was the same story before the 2022 tournament. Kamara is 26 and has yet to represent his country at a major tournament.

'It was difficult the first one or two months after my surgery,’ admits Kamara. ‘You can’t work, you have to stay at home'

‘Mentally it was difficult the first one or two months after my surgery,’ he admits. ‘You can’t work, you have to stay at home, ice treatment, do some exercises.

‘This is why I didn’t watch Villa play during that time, either at the ground or on TV. You want to play then you look at your knee and realise you can’t.

‘You keep going, work, and try not to think about football, think more about family, my kids, my friends. But it’s tough.

‘Before the game in Istanbul, I walked on to the pitch and I wanted to play, but I knew I couldn’t. Afterwards, I sat in my spot in the dressing room and I was a little bit sad, because I couldn’t do anything.

'So yes, in some moments it’s difficult but I tried to keep focused and now it is time to look forward again.’

Sports.title: 'The most competitive league in the world? Don't be ridiculous. It's rigged': Angry insiders doubt whether Aston Villa, Newcastle, Everton and Co can ever break the Premier League's glass ceiling and challenge the 'arrogant', free-spending 'Big Six'
Sports.content:
More than anything, it’s the utter sense of resignation that strikes you. There is anger, too.

After a summer that has seen our big Premier League clubs spend and exchange players with all the dignity of the Wolf of Wall Street trading floor, the mood among many of our rank and file top-flight clubs is unanimous.

‘It feels like it’s over for us,’ says one Premier League executive. ‘They say this is the most competitive league in the world. Don’t be ridiculous. It’s not allowed to be. The rules make sure of that.’

The spend in the Premier League this summer was a record £3.49billion. Half of that was spent in deals between top-flight clubs. It’s a story of a league that is now so extraordinarily wealthy that – outside of Paris Saint-Germain, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid and Barcelona – the only clubs rich enough to buy its players are its own.

What that says about the competitiveness of the big European competitions going forward is one thing – English clubs dominated last year – but it’s the increasingly skewed landscape of the Premier League that is now concerning many.

Across English football this week – from executives to coaches to scouts and recruitment specialists – the mood has reflected an environment that has perhaps changed for ever.

Chelsea paid £117million to take the England international Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa

While Arsenal took Newcastle talisman Bruno Guimaraes for £75m

Recruitment from the pyramid of the English game, for example, is now desperately low. Of those players taken from the Championship by Premier League clubs this window, the vast majority were from the three clubs relegated last season.

‘Clubs no longer have the patience to see investments in EFL players pay off over time,’ explains one recruiter at a big club. ‘They want results immediately and they want impact and star names. There is an arrogance from our big clubs and it’s damaging.

‘Signing players is about taking a chance but modern clubs would rather spend £130m on a big name or take someone from clubs lower down in the Premier League who have already done the hard work for them.’

That in itself is an emerging trend. Clubs like Brentford, Bournemouth and Brighton have established recruitment models that are the envy of the so-called 'Big Six'. They sign unknown players for small sums before selling them to top-end rivals for vast numbers. Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton to Spurs is a good recent example.

It’s a practice that on the surface works at both ends. Big clubs get oven-ready players and the smaller clubs make handsome transfer profits. But it’s also a trend that serves to keep the status quo in place on the field. It’s here that the frustration turns to anger.

‘There are well-run clubs doing things the right way who have owners with money yet they are not allowed to spend it,’ adds another Premier League executive. ‘Brentford and Brighton got more points than Chelsea last season. But they are not allowed to spend as much even if they have it.

‘You should never confuse sustainability with competitiveness. We are not competitive. We are not allowed to be by the rules that are essentially endorsed by the big clubs.’

Current spending rules are complicated but broadly speaking allow clubs to spend 85 per cent of what they earn on players, wages and football staff. If you play in Europe, it’s 70 per cent under UEFA’s regulations. It’s this that causes the resentment.

Clubs like Brighton sign unknown players for small sums before selling them to top-end rivals for vast numbers. Jan Paul van Hecke to Spurs is a good recent example

Brentford got more points than Chelsea last season. But they are not allowed to spend as much as them

‘Brighton have got very close,’ says a source who has worked at three top-flight clubs. ‘But they are stuck in a cycle of relative success which is not really success at all in terms of winning things. They are a great club. Well run with a fabulous stadium and training ground.

‘But there is no point anybody buying them because no matter how much money is pumped into it, they wouldn’t be able to spend it on the pitch. Clubs like them and Bournemouth have such limited capacity for growth.’

Another source puts it rather more bluntly. ‘The rules were once worthy and designed to stop people behaving like idiots,’ he says. ‘Sadly the rules have now become a device to stop there ever being a level playing field. The big clubs earn big and spend big. The others don’t and can’t. It’s fundamentally rigged.’

Last November’s vote on new spending rules by top-flight clubs was carried by 14-6, the very minimum required. The dissenters were, not surprisingly, Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds.

At the same time, a proposal to introduce a system of 'anchoring' – where spending by any club could not exceed five times the money earned in the previous season by the league's bottom club from prize money, TV fees and collective commercial income – was supported by only seven clubs and therefore thrown out. The dissenters viewed it as in effect a wage cap.

'The votes are hard,’ reveals someone from inside the room. ‘You have the top six clubs who vote the way it suits them and then the ones who think they may have a chance of becoming one.

‘Everton are a great example of that. The new stadium they think will lead to new revenues and new commercials. And then the new clubs who have been promoted will understandably vote that way too.

‘They just want their £100m for coming up and don’t wanna p*** off Man United as they may need to loan a player from them. It’s a mess and all of this is accelerated and compounded by the media.

‘They say, “They haven’t spent” or “They have had a bad window”. We will spend right up the limit but the truth is that our limits are different and that isn’t fair is it?’

‘Brighton have got very close (to the big teams),’ says a source who has worked at three top-flight clubs. ‘But they are stuck in a cycle of relative success which is not really success at all'

Everton believe they can crash the Big Six thanks to their new stadium, which will lead to new revenues and new commercial opportunities

In an interview with the True Faith Newcastle United Podcast this week, the Magpies’ chief executive David Hopkinson attempted to outline the way forward for a club awash with Saudi Arabian riches that it cannot spend.

Having lost Anthony Gordon, Bruno Guimaraes and Sandro Tonali this summer, Newcastle are perhaps the best example of a club that feels it’s being held back on a short lead by the league in which it plays.

Hopkinson talked of growing revenues by 50 per cent between now and 2030. He talked of new commercial revenue streams and sponsorship deals but that figure feels wildly optimistic. ‘We are going to catch up from behind,’ he said bullishly. ‘We have a plan.’

Inevitably that plan must include a new stadium at some stage. This is what has launched Tottenham into the stratosphere when it comes to income and this is what Everton are hanging a blue hat on too. ‘We need more stadium capacity because that capacity is revenue,’ Hopkinson said.

Buried within all this, however, was something else that impacts directly on supporters and not in a good way. It’s another direct trickle down of the League’s restrictions on spending.

Hopkinson talked of ‘VIP hosting opportunities’ and a demand for a ‘higher priced product’. Often what this means is a move to ease out regular fans in a bid to squeeze in those willing to pay through the nose for what they view as a premium corporate match-day experience.

It is symptomatic of a need to push at the edges of what clubs feel they can get away with in a bid to eke a few more quid from their paying customers.

‘We have had to put regular ticket prices up so that means our fans suffer,’ says a third Premier League chief. ‘We have to do anything we can to try and create a little more revenue that we can then invest in the squad. But it’s still nowhere near what the big clubs can do.

Newcastle's chief executive David Hopkinson is bullish about his club's hopes. ‘We are going to catch up from behind. We have a plan,' he said this week

But the club sold midfielder Sandro Tonali to Tottenham this summer, along with Anthony Gordon to Barcelona and Guimaraes to Arsenal

‘And this pressure to compete can promote clubs gambling with what they have and pushing at the margins. It leads clubs into trouble.’

Maybe the best example of this is Aston Villa, a club whose manager Unai Emery spoke eloquently about the limitations of the rules last season.

‘Financial control rules came to football to avoid bankruptcies and payment defaults with a good purpose,’ said Emery. ‘But this good tool will become a limitation.’

Villa have been successful under Emery. They won the Europa League last season and are about to play Champions League football for a second time in recent years. But their wage bill has rocketed in that time – breaching 90 per cent wages to turnover ratio at one point – while they, along with Chelsea, Nottingham Forest and Newcastle, have all been found to be in breach of UEFA’s spending rules last July.

It’s this that contributes to the kind of boom-bust experience of some of our more ambitious clubs. Successful one season, less so the next. Villa have, for example, lost more than half of their Europa League winning team in the recent window.

Villa – in the process of increasing the capacity of Villa Park from 43,000 to more than 50,000 – voted in favour of the new rules last November and amid all the rancour a question that often goes unanswered is what spending rules in England’s top division actually should look like.

One suggestion from a southern club was for all squads to have the same wage bill ceiling. The 'anchoring' system would have been a step towards that but that idea never got very far.

Meanwhile, another of our insiders adds: ‘I don’t think subsidies are the answer. I agree with the big clubs on that. Why should Tesco give its profits to the corner shop?

'But I do think owners should be allowed to inject money as equity that can then be spent on the football. It’s not debt. Debt comes with interest and must be repaid. It’s damaging. Equity is not the same at all. It should be allowed.’

‘Financial control rules came to football to avoid bankruptcies and payment defaults with a good purpose,’ says Aston Villa boss Unai Emery. ‘But this good tool will become a limitation’

Finally, a third small suggestion from a club in the midlands.

‘We suggested the wages of a home-grown player be added on the balance sheet as a positive,’ a staffer explains. ‘In other words, not included on your expenditure. That wage could then be spent on another player. It would act as a reward for growing your own. It never got past first base.’

When the Premier League announced their amended spending rules last season, they talked of ‘competitive balance’ and ‘promoting opportunities’. Looking across the landscape today, it’s hard to see evidence of it.

With the league having virtually annexed the fifth Champions League spot for the foreseeable future, seasonal revenues of at least £100m from that competition serves to widen the gap further.

Underpinning it all, meanwhile, is a nagging feeling among many with Premier League experience that the bubble has to burst at some point. The current TV deal is worth £6.7bn and runs until 2028 but with the way football fans consume their favourite sport ever changing, there is likely to be a shifting in the sands at some point.

Those numbers cannot be relied upon for ever and already this season the Premier League are experimenting in Singapore with producing and selling their own content direct to viewers.

Speaking on the Athletic FC podcast this week, Tim Bridge of the Deloitte Sports Business Group said: ‘I feel as though the League is banking on the ability to have the next new revenue kick – either a new broadcast contract or new commercial partner.

‘If that happens, then it’s rosy. But there is an awful lot being predicated on that (positive) future change and that feels new for the Premier League. I would suggest an appropriate approach for the 20 clubs would be to work more closely together to think about what the League is going to look like in 2035.’

This weekend, Dan Ndoye's Nottingham Forest will have hopes of beating Tottenham. In the long-term, however, it is hard to see much interference in the general order of things

Villa lost more than half of their Europa League-winning team in the recent window

Given that we are only five years on from the failed attempts by England’s big clubs to join a European Super League, the prospects of such a collegiate approach being taken feels unlikely.

And so the Premier League rolls on. So the gap between the top and the middle grows wider.

This weekend, Nottingham Forest will have hopes of beating Tottenham and Everton may have a real go at Manchester United. In the long-term, however, it is hard to see much interference in the general order of things, not when the richest six clubs earn more than the rest of the other 14 put together.

‘At past Premier League meetings we have scoffed at the way some Championship clubs work,’ one of our Premier League sources adds. ‘They have been reckless, blowing their own brains out.

‘Are we now on the way to doing the same?’

Sports.title: Tyson Fury attacks Anthony Joshua and questions his 'love' of England over his speech calling for a block on spending in white-owned shops - in bitter feud over moving their fight away from the UK
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury attacks Anthony Joshua and questions his 'love' of England over his speech calling for a block on spending in white-owned shops - in bitter feud over moving their fight away from the UK

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Tyson Fury has picked apart Anthony Joshua's 'love' of England and desire to fight his great boxing rival on home soil - by dredging up his speech appearing to call for a block on spending in white-owned shops.

Fury, 38, and 36-year-old Joshua are embroiled in a bitter tug-of-war over their heavyweight superfight - largely centring on a debate around hosting it at London's Wembley Stadium or broadcaster Netflix's choice of Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Yesterday, Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn said Wembley talks had 're-opened', weeks after the fight looked set to be signed off in New York in November - in what has become a crusade towards keeping the event at 'home' for the two fighters.

But today, Fury was keen to make clear Joshua is not motivated by a love of his country. Earlier this year Daily Mail Sport revealed Joshua had in fact quit the UK to move to Dubai - even as thousands tried to flee amid rising panic in the Middle East warzone.

And Fury, a tax exile to the Isle of Man himself, brought up a 2020 speech at a Black Lives Matter march, where Joshua read out a letter from his friend Reece Campbell to urge attendees to stop spending money with white-owned shops and businesses.

'Show them where it hurts,' Joshua had said. 'Abstain from spending your money in their shops and economies, and invest in black-owned businesses.'

Anthony Joshua's 2020 Black Lives Matter speech has been brought back up by his great boxing rival Tyson Fury

A shirtless Fury was relentless in his criticism of Joshua and his perceived dodging of the fight

Fury re-posted the video of the speech, writing: 'This is the man who loves England, absolute s*** bag! Total peice of s*** bully with zero guts! Don't let them deceive you! & Living in Dubai.'

In an address to camera, Fury accused Joshua of trying to derail their fight to avoid being embarrassed: 'If I agreed to tie both hands behind my back and wear solid cement boots, Anthony Joshua would never get in the ring with me because I'll annihilate him.

'And he's a piece of s*** bully, and that's his game—bullying people like he tried to do to Daniel Dubois, and he got knocked spark dead out.

'The latest news from them is, "Tyson don't want to fight in England". Why the f*** wouldn't I want to fight in England, you sausage? "Tyson only wants to fight in America". Are you joking or what?

'Tyson is not in charge of this fight. Tyson didn't put the money up for this fight. Tyson is not the paymaster. Netflix are and Turki Al-Sheikh. Lovely. If it's in England, even better. I'll knock the motherf***er out even quicker. Prime time England, 10 o'clock, Wembley Stadium, 100,000 people. Why the f*** wouldn't I want it in England? Doesn't make any sense, does it?

'Like I said, who do you think you are? You and your little pathetic puppet Eddie Hearn trying to save you. There's no escaping, you know. I'll come to Watford (Joshua's hometown) and I'll set about you. I'll batter you in your own front garden, you piece of s***.'

'There is no getting out of this one. There is no getting out of this one. Get ready for this fight. I've had enough of your sauce to last me 11 years. I'm battering the f*** out of you, you useless dosser, piece of s***. That's what you are. And you know it as well, and everybody else knows what you are: a coward.'

Fury posted this video where Joshua called for 'abstaining on spending' from a friend's letter

Roaring out his title of the 'Gypsy King', Fury added: 'You's are going down, and the cash cow is getting knocked out. Because after this, he won't be able to show his face in public ever again.

'You're a useless dosser, a big bodybuilding piece of s***. Too many weights, not enough speed. When I crack a big right hook off it, you'll go over like spaghetti legs Deontay Wilder. But he's 10 times the man you'll ever be, because he's got a pair of b*****ks like King Kong, and you've got a pair of b*****ks like two f***ing garden peas, you piece of s***.'

Joshua has still not signed his contract for the Battle of Britain fight. Promoter Frank Warren, who suggested that in reality boxing's longest hatching deal had to be finalised by this weekend, told Daily Mail Sport's Jeff Powell: 'AJ hasn't signed yet.

'Tyson signed in January. He's training in Miami for the fight in early November and doesn't care where it takes place.'

The original agreement stipulated England, putting Wembley Stadium on alert.

But Netflix, the mega-paymasters for the broadcast, have joined their Saudi partners in insisting on New York's fabled Madison Square Garden so as to maximise US revenue.

Joshua will need at least a two-month training camp for a fight of this magnitude and ideally nine to ten weeks.

It comes after Joshua was given 10 days to agree a deal on August 26 with Warren previously warning: 'Unless AJ commits by the end of next week I'm afraid this will slip away like so many of those great fights which never happened.'

He added: 'At some point everyone has to say the most important thing is that it happens. Not this bulls*** about money.

'That everyone wants the fight. Does AJ really want it? I don't know. He's been through that tragedy of the car crash which killed two of his closest friends. Only he knows what he wants.'

Much of the discussions around Wembley centre on a willingness to allow a late start time - and late curfew - to suit the American TV market. Mayor Sadiq Khan this week stated that he is keen to host the fight and find a solution.

Sports.title: Man Utd extend transfer talks after failed deadline day move for midfielder
Sports.content:
Man Utd extend transfer talks after failed deadline day move for midfielder

Manchester United failed to make a single signing on transfer deadline day, with one particular deal collapsing late on, and talks to agree terms are continuing

View 2 Images Manchester United are still in talks over signing another player for Michael Carrick (Image: Getty Images)

Leicester City and Manchester United are still in talks over Louis Page despite being unable to agree on the terms of a deal during transfer deadline day. Hopes of him moving to the Premier League effectively ended when Russell Martin included his midfielder in their starting XI for a League One match on the same night against Plymouth Argyle.

‌



Page, 18, had previously missed their opening match of the season. He will now be staying until at least January.

‌



United, however, are said to remain confident of signing the England under-19 international. Page made 18 Championship appearances last season.

‌



Our sister title the Manchester Evening News reports that lines of communication remain open between the two clubs. They understand that their issue earlier in the week concerned payment terms for the initial fee that Leicester City would receive, as well as the makeup of the add-ons.

Eight players could miss Everton vs Man Utd Premier League clash including £70m signing READ MORE :

It is understood that the League One club wanted a fee in excess of the £10million plus £2.5million in add-ons deal that Manchester City agreed for Jeremy Monga. A deal which would have seen Page stay at Leicester for the remainder of this season was understood to be close before the 11pm deadline.

‌



Arsenal have been credited with an interest in the midfielder. However, he is said to be sold on the pathway and vision that United presented.

Page's father, Don, was born in Manchester, and they still apparently have family in the area. Like his son, Page Sr was a footballer, playing for several teams in Greater Manchester, including Altrincham, Hyde United, Rochdale and Wigan Athletic.

View 2 Images Manchester United made a deadline day attempt to sign Leicester City midfielder Louis Page. (Image: Plumb Images, Leicester City FC via Getty Images)

‌



FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Martin acknowledged after Tuesday's match that Leicester rejected a bid from United on deadline day. He said: "The owner (Aiyawatt 'Top' Srivaddhanaprabha) was here today [and] we sat in the office and received a very big offer from Manchester United.

"Myself, Jon [Rudkin] (chief football officer), James [McCarron] (sporting director) and the owner, Khun Top, sat in [the office] and he said no.

‌



"So whatever's going on with the noise around the club and all that stuff, he was strong, and he wanted the player to stay and be part of us. It would have been so easy for him to sell Louis and take a lot of money, but he didn't.

"It's a brilliant thing for us. Louis, you can see the level of quality and potential he possesses is amazing. He's really helped us since coming into the team. I'm really grateful that he's still here."

Sports.title: Andy Gray's return to UK commentary confirmed for first time since Sky Sports sacking
Sports.content:
Andy Gray's return to UK commentary confirmed for first time since Sky Sports sacking

Andy Gray is making a return to commentary duties in the UK after a 12-year absence, having left Qatar and his role at beinSPORTS at the end of the 2025/26 season

View 2 Images Andy Gray has returned to UK commentary (Image: Carl Recine/Getty Images)

Andy Gray will return to UK commentary, 12 years after he was sacked by Sky Sports in the wake of a sexism scandal.

‌



Gray has been in exile from the UK, working for beIN SPORTS in Qatar, for the past several years alongside his long-time colleague Richard Keys. The pair moved to the Middle East following their sacking by Sky Sports for making sexist comments in 2011.

‌



The pair left Sky Sports under a cloud after being caught on camera making derogatory and misogynistic comments about assistant referee Sian Massey-Ellis and the fitness of women to officiate matches. But Keys and Gray have now moved back to the UK from Doha and are embarking upon the next stage of their careers, having launched a podcast together.

‌



Gray, 70, has now landed a gig on talkSPORT, and will work as a co-commentator on Liverpool's Champions League game against Atletico Madrid on Wednesday night. He will partner Jim Proudfoot at Anfield for the radio broadcast, 12 years after he briefly worked on the FA Cup with BT Sport.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

"I'd like to think, somewhere, I could do a bit of commentary," Gray told the Daily Mail last month. "Not television, maybe, but radio. Just to see what it feels like again. I would like that."

‌



Keys added: "I would be happy for you if that happened. I think you deserve it. To hear him back, analysing a football match, that would be special. He's the best I've ever known."

Gray played for Aston Villa, Wolves and Everton in a 17-year career before coming a well-known voice on Sky Sports. But he was forced out of the job after a live microphone caught his exchange with Keys about Massey-Ellis.

Keys was recorded saying: "Somebody better get down there and explain offside to her (Massey)," to which Gray replied: "Yeah, I know. Can you believe that? Female linesman. Forget what I said – they probably don't know the offside rule."

‌



View 2 Images Richard Keys and Andy Gray have returned to the UK from Qatar (Image: richardajkeys/X)

Keys then stated: "Course they don't" to which Gray responded: "Why is there a female linesman? Somebody's f***** up big."

Addressing what he said in 2011, Gray told the Daily Mail: "I can't imagine saying today what I said then, I just can't. I think we were two of the first people ever cancelled. I had 20 reporters outside my house for weeks."

Article continues below

He told Piers Morgan in 2022 that he considered taking his own life amid the backlash. “I suddenly found myself in a really dark place,” he said. "The house surrounded by people. And I knew I had done something wrong, of course I did, but I couldn’t compute it.

“My head was gone. If it hadn’t been for my wife, I don’t know what would have happened. I really don’t. Rachel was amazing. I was close to going down the garden, where I used to have a pond, with a little bottle and a few pills. I was that bad, one day – that bad, yeah... really weird, but I’m through it now.”

Sports.title: Alejandro Garnacho alarm bells ringing after Bruno Fernandes revealed Man Utd's true feelings
Sports.content:
Alejandro Garnacho alarm bells ringing after Bruno Fernandes revealed Man Utd's true feelings

Alejandro Garnacho's career has severely stalled in recent years

View 3 Images Alejandro Garnacho's attitude was called into question by Bruno Fernandes (Image: Ryan Pierse, Getty Images)

Alejandro Garnacho is at a crossroads in his football career. Once a highly-rated talent with heavy expectations of excellence placed on him, those days seem like a lifetime ago.

‌



The Argentine's form has been on a downward trajectory since the Ruben Amorim era at Manchester United, but questions about his attitude date back to his teenage years.

‌



His career at Old Trafford came to an end when he joined Chelsea for £40million in the 2025/26 campaign, as he went on to endure the worst season of his career, scoring just one goal in 24 Premier League games.

‌



The 22-year-old became surplus to requirements under Xabi Alonso this summer, with Garnacho inking a loan deal with Aston Villa - a move that could make-or-break his career. The winger has been told that he cannot ignore the magnitude of his stint at Villa if he wants to reignite his standing in the game.

Former Villa midfielder Ray Houghton said Garnacho's family have a responsibility to get through to him and make him understand that he won't continue to keep getting chances to impress at the highest level.

Michael Carrick hints he could fill problem Man Utd position without spending a penny READ MORE :

Man Utd striker transfer confirmed despite summer window closing READ MORE :

The 64-year-old told GOAL: "I've got every respect for the kid, but I think the alarm bells should be ringing. His closest people, his family and friends, should be telling him that. What they should be saying to him is: ‘Look where you've been, look what's happened to you and look where you are now, there's a reason this is happening, and it's down to you now.

‌



"This is another club that's going to give you a chance. You've got to seize it. No more excuses. No more saying, 'Oh well, there's something else at that club and someone else at that club.' That's all gone now. It's down to the individual now."

View 3 Images Alejandro Garnacho has played just 16 minutes in Aston Villa's opening two games (Image: Getty Images)

Houghton predicted that Villa boss Unai Emery will give Garnacho "tough love", but warned the winger that he'll be cast aside if he doesn't deliver. He added: "It's down to him as a player to seize it, grasp it and when he gets his chance make sure he's ready to take it. Emery, he's been brilliant at Villa. I love him.

‌



"I think he's a fantastic manager. I love his passion. I love his desire and if anyone's going to get the best out of him, I think it would be him. I think he'll give him some tough love but there'll be an expectation and you've got to live up to that expectation and you've got to deliver. If you don't deliver, he won't hang about with you. He's not that type of manager."

While opportunities to impress will be available, with the club competing on four fronts, it's up to the player whether his career takes another dramatic decline or if the football world is reintroduced to the star whose potential once seemed endless.

Sports.title: Arsenal vs Chelsea injury news as eight players could miss huge Premier League clash
Sports.content:
Arsenal vs Chelsea injury news as eight players could miss huge Premier League clash

Arsenal vs Chelsea is the standout Premier League fixture this weekend, with both clubs winning their first two games coming into the match at Emirates Stadium

View 2 Images Xabi Alonso and Mikel Arteta have late selection decisions to make on Saturday after their teams' last training sessions (Image: Getty Images)

Arsenal and Chelsea both have late selection decisions to make before meeting at Emirates Stadium in the Premier League this weekend. Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso acknowledged that their teams' final training sessions on Saturday will determine who makes their matchday squads.

‌



The Gunners are worse for wear and could be without as many as five first-team squad members. Multiple players picked up knocks and limped off the pitch during their 1-0 win away to Aston Villa on Monday night.

‌



Arteta's side have just six days to recover from that match. Chelsea, however, had the same Sunday-Monday turnaround last week.

‌



Bruno Guimaraes is among those whose fitness remains uncertain following his appearance as a substitute at Villa Park. Speaking at his pre-match press conference on Friday, the Arsenal boss said: "Yeah, he had a knock against Villa. "He's being assessed, but probably tomorrow (Saturday) he'll be OK for training."

Xabi Alonso rubs salt in Arsenal wounds over Morgan Rogers transfer ahead of clash READ MORE :

8 controversial Mike Dean moments from row with Arsenal manager to celebrating goal READ MORE :

A similar concern surrounds Cristhian Mosquera, who was forced off clutching his thigh before Ezri Konsa came on to make his Gunners debut against his former club. Arteta said of the substitution: "It was more precaution than anything else. So we'll have to see tomorrow (Saturday) in the session to see how he feels."

Declan Rice was also seen limping as Martin Zubimendi replaced him with five minutes remaining. However, the England international was back in training on Thursday and was not mentioned by Arteta during his pre-match briefing.

‌



Jurrien Timber has also returned to training with his teammates and could feature in the matchday squad. Arteta said: "Yeah, he is in really good condition at the moment. As I said, he's been on the pitch for a few weeks, and he's training with us now. We'll decide tomorrow after training [if he will make the squad]."

William Saliba, however, faces a longer spell on the sidelines. Arteta acknowledged: "We don't really know the number of weeks Wilo is going to be out because it's about a healing process and everything is a bit different.

View 2 Images Xabi Alonso and Mikel Arteta previous coached against each other two years ago during the Emirates Cup (Image: David Price, Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

‌



"We know we have to respect certain timings. The progression has been really positive in the last few weeks, but we need to wait and see how that one reacts when we start to put some load into it."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

As for Chelsea, Moises Caicedo's availability is causing concern for Alonso. Speaking during his press conference on Friday, the manager said: "We will check tomorrow (Saturday), as tomorrow is the last decision for the squad on Sunday."

‌



Marco Palestra remains another absentee. Alonso, though, did not refer to the summer arrival during his press conference. Yet, speaking on Wednesday at the Gran Gala del Calcio, held inside Milan's Teatro alla Scala, while collecting an award for making the Serie A Team of the Season, the player said: "I'm fine, it's still a few days away, but I feel much better."

He was absent from training with his teammates on Thursday, however. Jordan Henderson is also set to be absent. Alonso acknowledged last week that they are still awaiting confirmation that he has been given "the green light to play soon."

Sports.title: David Moyes drops bombshell about Everton owners after disastrous window
Sports.content:
David Moyes drops bombshell about Everton owners after disastrous window

Everton endured a miserable summer transfer window, with the collapsed £40million move on deadline day for Monaco striker Folarin Balogun leaving David Moyes with a headache

View 2 Images David Moyes has been left with a tiny squad (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

David Moyes has admitted that he has never spoken to Dan Friedkin, the chief executive of Everton owners the Friedkin Group, following a shambolic end to the summer transfer window.

‌



Everton have been left with a threadbare squad after failing to sign a striker on transfer deadline day. The Toffees sold Beto to Fiorentina and then saw Folarin Balogun reject a move to become his replacement, while late bids for Manchester United's Joshua Zirkzee and Aston Villa's Tammy Abraham also failed. It leaves Thierno Barry as Everton's only senior striker.

‌



While Everton did get some cheer, with Jack Grealish returning on loan from Manchester City, the sale of Iliman Ndiaye to City for £65million further weakened their squad.

‌



The farcical end to the window, in which Balogun U-turned on a move from Monaco after arriving at the Everton training ground, has put the club under scrutiny. Moyes' admission that he has no contact with Friedkin only adds weight to those criticisms.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Man Utd striker transfer confirmed despite summer window closing READ MORE :

Liverpool transfer call vindicated as Alexander Isak downs Ipswich - 5 talking points READ MORE :

“My real contact is Angus [Kinnear, Everton CEO]. Angus is the one who I would go to see," Moyes said ahead of Sunday's game against Manchester United. "Rishi [Majithia, TFG representative] is the next one and then the head of the Friedkin family in America. I don’t really get any direct conversations with them, but I do through Rishi, he is the one I would speak to.”

‌



Speaking in a press conference, as reported by the Liverpool Echo, Moyes was diplomatic when assessing the wreckage of the window, saying the collapse of the £40m deal for Balogun "wasn't anyone's fault".

“It was a difficult transfer window generally," he added. "I know how it culminated in the end but it was a difficult window all the way through for us. The last couple of days were difficult because we were pushing hard, we had made bids for several players on bank holiday Monday and it would be hard to believe the outcome got to where it was.

"Lots of things just didn’t fall in line but we probably shouldn’t have been as late as that, we should probably have tried to get the work done a lot earlier than that.”

‌



View 2 Images Folarin Balogun pulled out of a move to Everton (Image: Getty Images)

Asked if his job had been made harder by the transfer window, he said: “Look, I think the Everton job is always a hard job and it’s a club that is used to having some difficult times. I can understand how difficult it must have been for Dychey [former manager, Sean Dyche] and many of the managers in front of him, through different periods.

“It is going to be difficult. We don’t have a huge squad of players, it is not a number we would ideally want, but sometimes you need to do something special in football and we will attempt to do something special. I’ve never wanted a huge squad, I’ve always preferred it when the squad is tighter, but maybe not as tight as this.”

‌



Moyes has a huge amount of experience and is ready to fight on with reduced numbers. “My aim is just to be as good as we've tried to be in the recent seasons," he said. "I think some things will hinder it. There'll be days we don't get it right. But I'll tell you what there won’t be, I'll do my best not to make any excuses for what's happened. And the players are fully aware of that.

"There are no excuses from the players on what we've got, what we need, and there's two or three players who probably get mentioned quite a lot - they are going to have to come with the fore, they're all going to have to be the ones who see if they can really deal with this football club.

“And for me personally, it's a great job, I love Everton and always have done. It's actually invigorated me over the last year, getting back at it again because I was probably going to say I wasn't going to do it again, or I might have taken an international job or I might have done something else.

Article continues below

"I actually think we've had a good year and a half together, I really do. I think if you looked over the year and a half you'd have to say there'd been a lot more positives and negatives. So now, there’s a little bit of a bump in the road. I need to try and get over the bump quickly and start looking how I can make it go smoothly.”

Sports.title: Ex-Arsenal star Jay Emmanuel-Thomas on rebuilding life after jail – 'It's a long journey'
Sports.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Ex-Arsenal star Jay Emmanuel-Thomas on rebuilding life after jail – 'It's a long journey'

The former England youth international has looked to surround himself with good people as he gets his life back on track

View 3 Images Jay Emmanuel-Thomas has had an eventful life and career since coming through the ranks at Arsenal (Image: Scott Baxter/Getty Images)

Former Arsenal and QPR forward Jay-Emmanuel Thomas is rebuilding his life after spending time behind bars but he’s determined to look forward, not back. The 35-year-old pleaded guilty to a cannabis importation charge and was sacked by his club Greenock Morton, but he's returned to football since his release on parole in July 2025.

‌



Emmanuel-Thomas is determined to surround himself with good people and give back to the community. He recognises his time in prison wasn’t as difficult as it has been for some but he has thrown himself back into football, playing in non-league and Baller League.

‌



The next step for the former England youth international will come in the boxing ring. He is due to fight Nile Ranger in a charity bout as part of Pro Project Promotions’ A Night to Remember III, where former Arsenal goalkeeper Graham Stack has assembled a line-up of seven bouts between current and former footballers with the goal of raising £500,000 for charity.

‌



“Obviously it's never a good scenario,” Emmanuel-Thomas told Mirror Football. “Eleven months or dealing with situations and solicitors and legals and court and it's very overwhelming.

“But the aim was to, once out of that dynamic, be able to focus my energy into the right stuff, the right people and just make sure that I can get my feet back on the ground and get back to doing the right things. You've got to just make sure that everything that's happening around you is also positive - it's a long journey, but it helps.”

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Arsenal deal for Bruno Guimaraes rated one out of 10 in brutal transfer ranking READ MORE :

Emmanuel-Thomas has no problem admitting his sporting background meant he had an easier time behind bars than some. However, he also knows everyone’s story is different.

“I can openly say I was treated differently. I was given extra special perks,” he added. “[People] did what they could to make me feel comfortable. But also personally, how I treat people and how I spoke to them, it was an easy conversation and communication to have with the officers.

“I didn't have a bad experience. It's not a great place but I know it could be a lot worse and a lot different. I still wouldn't want anybody to have their freedom taken away because it's not a nice feeling.

‌



“A couple of people [from inside] still speak to you because they're just… some people just make a mistake and they have to pay the price for it. They’ve got to do their time.

“And then from there, when they come home, it's about them also making a change and making a difference. And if I can help them, even just to take them away from what they would usually be involved in, it would be good, that's the aim.”

View 3 Images Emmanuel-Thomas won the FA Youth Cup with an Arsenal side including Jack Wilshere (Image: Getty Images)

‌

After coming through the Arsenal academy, Emmanuel-Thomas made five senior appearances under Arsene Wenger. One of those came on the biggest stage when he came off the bench against Chelsea for his Premier League debut, testing himself against a daunting Blues centre-back pairing of John Terry and Alex.

He went on to rack up more than 200 EFL appearances with some of his best football coming at Bristol City, before testing himself abroad. Thailand and India might not be the most eye-catching leagues to the casual fan in the UK but that doesn’t mean they didn’t offer some genuine life experience.

‌



“I loved playing football overseas, experiencing different cultures,” Emmanuel-Thomas said. “The culture, the food, the people, the way they live. It's very different.

“You get to see their home traits and their behaviours, mannerisms, it's very different to how we live in London or where I've lived in the UK, Scotland, so and so forth.

“They've got lovely weather, it's hot all year round, the concept of it all is really good and the football quality is good, nice stadiums, there's a lot going on. In India I had 50,000 fans per game, big numbers. So, yeah, it was a good experience, and I really enjoyed it.”

‌



View 3 Images Emmanuel-Thomas will take on Nile Ranger in the boxing ring (Image: Aria's Bistro)

If football in Asia was a culture shock, it’s nothing compared to stepping into the boxing ring. However, the veteran might have a secret weapon as he prepares to take on Ranger.

One of his school friends is Anthony Yarde, a light-heavyweight star who had two world title fights during an impressive career. Yarde has been training him up for the October bout and has already left an impression.

‌



Emmanuel-Thomas has also known opponent Ranger since the pair were teenagers in the football academy system and the pair have plenty in common. They had similar upbringings in London and have both faced the challenge of returning to the game after time in prison but Emmanuel-Thomas believes both can use the experience for good - with their charity fundraiser only part of it.

“My [time in prison] was a lot more recent and his was obviously a while back but it's still the same mentality to overcome it and move forward,” he added. “Obviously he's known to have a bad reputation, a lot of problems with clubs and blah, blah, but at the end of the day, we are just young boys from the ends and we're just trying our best.

“Yeah, he makes mistakes, but at the end of the day, as a person, I've never had an issue with him. He's always been good to me. We talk and I know people say he's hard of hearing, but at the end of the day, he's still human, he's still learning, so, fair dos to him getting involved in this.

‌



“When you're young and you’re given the sums of money we were earning without any guidance or anything financial to help... We weren't brought up with money so you’re not quite sure what to do with it apart from to go and enjoy.

“So it's difficult. But, yeah, so we make some mistakes. We probably bought things that you probably shouldn't have bought, spent amounts of money that you look back at it and you thought, 'Oh...'

“But I look back at it and say, you know what? A time was had, I made a decision and I’m dealing with it. So that's where I'm at. I don't regret anything that I've done. It's just about being able to fix it now. It's just a journey, isn't it? So we have to just make it work.”

Sports.title: Four players Man Utd were glad to see leave after 'bad attitude' and 'unprofessional' claims
Sports.content:
Four players Man Utd were glad to see leave after 'bad attitude' and 'unprofessional' claims

There's rarely a quiet season at Manchester United, particularly when it comes to high-profile players who can prove a challenge to manage

View 5 Images Michael Carrick has worked hard to restore the culture at Manchester United (Image: Michael Campanella/Getty Images)

Some big personalities have joined Manchester United in decades past, and some have left swiftly to the relief of those at the club. In recent years, Alejandro Garnacho and Jadon Sancho were told they had "bad attitudes" and were "lazy" by managers and squad players alike.

‌



Other, more experienced stars who felt the wrath of their teammates and pundits included the iconic Cristiano Ronaldo and Romelu Lukaku. Current manager Michael Carrick starred alongside Ronaldo during his playing career and hopes to avoid any major dressing-room issues, as have often plagued the club in recent years.

‌



The United boss has started off with one win and one loss for the 2026/27 Premier League season and also has the return of Champions League football to look forward to. He will aim to maintain the feel-good factor around Old Trafford following his initial interim period last season, during which he led a struggling team to third place and European football.

‌



Here, Mirror Football has taken a look back at four former United players that the club were glad to see the back of.

Man Utd loan out Chido Obi as youngster risks following concerning Old Trafford pattern READ MORE :

Fenerbahce issue Mason Greenwood statement as UEFA investigate ex-Man Utd star READ MORE :

Alejandro Garnacho

Garnacho had a bright start at United, making 10 goal contributions in his first full season as a senior Red Devil. However, club captain Bruno Fernandes suggested that the Argentina international lacked a good attitude during his progression into the first team under Erik ten Hag.

Speaking in November 2022, Fernandes told BT Sport: "He was good but he knows we expect a lot from him. He's still really young, doing really well. At the beginning of the season, he was not at his best.

‌



"On the [pre-season] tour he did not have the best attitude. That's why he didn't get his chance until now. He's getting his chances because he's training better, he's having the correct attitude."

View 5 Images Alejandro Garnacho was accused of not 'having the correct attitude' (Image: Gareth Copley/Getty Images)

These words had the opposite effect on Garnacho. He fell out of favour under new manager Ruben Amorim and even criticised his decision to keep him off the pitch during the Europa League final loss against Tottenham.

‌



Garnacho said: "Until we reached the final, I played every round. And I played 20 minutes today – I don't know. I'm going to try to enjoy the summer and see what happens next.

"Obviously it's hard for everyone. Our season was s***. We didn't beat anyone in the league. We lacked a lot of things. When you don't score goals, you always need more."

The 22-year-old departed United and signed for Chelsea in a deal worth £40m. Garnacho failed to impress in west London and this summer joined Aston Villa on loan with an obligation to buy for a similar sum.

‌



Cristiano Ronaldo

View 5 Images Cristiano Ronaldo's return to United ended on a sour note (Image: ADRIAN DENNIS/AFP via Getty Images)

Ronaldo will forever be remembered for his first stint in Manchester, but his homecoming in 2021 ended in disaster. After a year where he scored 24 goals and brought back nostalgia for many, he fell out with Ten Hag and had his contract terminated before the 2022 World Cup.

The striker took part in a controversial interview with Piers Morgan where he stated there was "no evolution" at the club since Sir Alex Ferguson left. Christian Eriksen spoke out following Ronaldo's exit and claimed that "football will go on" without the Portugal international.

‌



He said: "First of all we are sad that Ronaldo is not part of it, his legacy and his name at any club is special, for me to be fortunate to play with him in my career was very nice. The football goes on. You feel that the next game after, people will forget what it was like before and now our focus is really like he is not here."

Highlighting an improvement in the dressing room, Eriksen added: "The atmosphere is good, we have a lot of people coming back from the World Cup, the last guys are coming back and everyone is coming together. The atmosphere is good. It helps winning games and also before we went away for the World Cup, we had a few good games and good wins and it makes it easier to come back and start like this."

Jadon Sancho

View 5 Images Jadon Sancho fell out of favour under Erik ten Hag (Image: Michael Regan/Getty Images)

‌



Sancho joined in a £73m deal from Borussia Dortmund in 2021 and arrived to much fanfare. However, he ended up on loan three times and left the club at the expiry of his contract this summer.

Once again, the player butted heads with Ten Hag, with Sancho left out of the matchday squad for his "lazy" tendencies in training. Speaking after a 3-1 defeat to Arsenal in 2023, the manager said: "Jadon, on his performances in training we did not select him. You have to reach a level every day at Manchester United and we can make choices in the front line. So for this game he was not selected."

Sancho hit back on social media, effectively claiming in a post that was later deleted that the Dutchman was lying. He said: "Please don’t believe everything you read! I will not allow people saying things that is completely untrue, I have conducted myself in training very well this week. I believe there are other reasons for this matter that I won’t go into, I’ve been a scapegoat for a long time which isn’t fair!"

‌

Sky broadcasts more than 1,400 live matches across the Premier League, EFL and more with at least 215 live from the top flight alongside Formula 1, darts and golf.

The Guardian reported that United players urged Sancho to apologise for his actions after he was left out of the team and training with the under-18s. One of Ten Hag's coaching staff, Benni McCarthy, told 947 Joburg how the situation played out between manager and player.

He said: "I spoke to the manager and I said to him that you know the delicacy and I think Jadon feels that if he apologises then he's going to be classed as someone who doesn't train hard, that doesn't work hard, who that everything that was said against him was true and if you are from the streets, no one wants to apologise, you admit you are not training well, you are lazy, everything you are accused of. Jadon wasn’t going to have that. The manager just said that all he wants is an apology.

‌



"I spoke to Jadon as a coach, as a mentor, as a friend, and as someone who grew up on the streets and knows the code. But Jadon just wasn’t seeing it. He said, 'I ain’t apologising because if I do, I’m apologising for being lazy, always being late, not giving my best. That’s what I’m apologising for,' and those were his reasons."

Romelu Lukaku

View 5 Images Gary Neville insisted Romelu Lukaku was overweight (Image: Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Romelu Lukaku arrived at United in 2017 for around £75m after an impressive stint at Everton. While his debut campaign brought 22 goals and seven assists up top, the Belgian forward's numbers began to dip in his second season and Gary Neville was quick to point out why after he left in 2019.

‌



After Lukaku's exit to Inter Milan was confirmed by the club, the former United defender claimed the striker was an unprofessional member of the team because he was unable to keep fit. Discussing Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's plans to instil a "new culture" at Old Trafford, the ex-England international told ESPN in 2019: "My view on Romelu Lukaku is that if Manchester United are trying to set a new tone and culture through the club, which Ole is trying to do, any lack of professionalism has got to be stamped upon.

"He didn't want to be here anyway. I think he is a really good player - he'll score a lot of goals and do well at Inter Milan."

Expressing his distaste at Lukaku's fitness, Neville added: "But the idea of a player being overweight for me is unforgivable. You can play badly, miss shots on goal, hit a bad cross or give goals away as they're mistakes in football but you can't be overweight.

Article continues below

"We were never overweight, not fit or not prepared. How can you be overweight!? There's no excuse. Romelu Lukaku has admitted himself that he was overweight so he has removed all doubt."

After stints at Inter, Chelsea, Roma and Napoli, Lukaku is now plying his trade at Fenerbahce in Turkey.
