Sports.title: Why Leclerc is likely to tow Hamilton in Italian GP qualifying
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc is expecting to give Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton a tow in Italian Grand Prix qualifying, with Kimi Antonelli ready to help Formula 1 title rival George Russell at Mercedes.

Slipstreaming has always been paramount at Monza’s ‘Temple of Speed’ when it comes to single-lap performance, and this still is the case in 2026 despite F1’s new machinery’s less drastic downforce set-ups, plus active aerodynamics reducing the effect of the tow.

Back at Spa-Francorchamps, Isack Hadjar helped Red Bull team-mate Max Verstappen clinch second place in qualifying after giving him a tow on the run to Blanchimont, proving that slipstreaming indeed remained effective.

At Ferrari, drivers take turns to choose in which order the cars go out in Q3. This time around, Hamilton will get to make the all-important decision – though longtime tifosi favourite Leclerc makes it clear he won’t sacrifice his own chances.

“We've always had the same philosophy over the years, where one time Lewis has the priority to choose where he wants to start, and one weekend is on me,” Leclerc explained. “This weekend Lewis will have the priority, so I guess he'll go for the slipstream.

“Whether we are going to compromise one qualifying rather than the other, I don't think that will happen, but of course if we can help each other, trying to start the lap at the optimum distance between each other, that will be done, and I'll try to find another slipstream of someone else, hoping to put myself in the best possible place.”

Antonelli: “We have agreed on a few things”

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

At Mercedes, the situation is simpler, with championship leader Antonelli given a new powertrain, exceeding his yearly quota for internal combustion engines, batteries and control electronics units – which should lead to a back-of-the-grid start.

In this context, Antonelli is expecting to be required to give team-mate Russell a tow – although the Briton is a title rival – as it could make the difference against Ferrari in the battle for pole position.

“It has been discussed with the team. And, yes, we have agreed on a few things,” the Italian confirmed.

“Let's see how the session develops. But if the team will ask me to do so, I will do it. Because, obviously, I'm not fighting for... You know, of course, I will still be happy to do pole, but, of course, I'm starting at the back. So, if I could do anything to help the team, I will do it.”

Antonelli currently enjoys a 59-point advantage over Russell and Hamilton in the drivers’ standings, with officially 11 more rounds to go – including Monza and the uncertain Qatar and Abu Dhabi events.

Additional reporting by Ronald Vording

Sports.title: F1 Italian GP: Russell beats Leclerc to top second practice
Sports.content:
George Russell has topped second practice at Formula 1's Italian Grand Prix, nudging Ferrari's Charles Leclerc off the top of the timesheets.

Russell set a 1m22.559s lap in the second half of the session as part of a mid-session shootout between the Briton, Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and Russell's Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli, who filled the top three.

Following tepid laps on hard tyres, also led by Russell, the second practice session came to life after 20 minutes when the frontrunners upped the pace by donning Pirelli's soft tyres, which had only been sporadically used in FP1.

On the red-rimmed tyres, Antonelli set a fastest first sector before diving back into the pits as he was blocked by traffic in the Parabolica, Monza's famed final corner.

On his next attempt, Antonelli was spared of traffic to fire in a 1m22.700s lap to go top, with team-mate Russell then taking over the lead with a 1m22.686s lap.

Leclerc, who had led the way in the first session, responded with a 1m22.679s effort, before Russell immediately claimed the lead back with a more comfortable 1m22.559s.

That time would remain untouched until the end as teams largely switched to long runs, with Leclerc and Antonelli thus finishing second and third.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

Reigning world champion Lando Norris, winner of the last two grands prix, was fourth just four tenths behind Russell, while Hamilton was fifth in the second Ferrari narrowly ahead of Oscar Piastri in the other McLaren.

Arvid Lindblad made a strong impression for Racing Bulls, briefly holding third in the opening stages before setting the seventh-fastest time. Oliver Bearman was an encouraging eighth for the struggling Haas team.

FP2 was Max Verstappen's first outing of the weekend after he handed his Red Bull to reserve driver Ayumu Iwasa for a mandatory rookie outing. As is often the case for Red Bull on Fridays, Verstappen was constantly chasing an agreeable balance on his RB22, with a front wing flap change not appearing to improve matters.

Verstappen could only muster ninth as the leading Red Bull driver, with Racing Bulls stand-in Yuki Tsunoda rounding out the top 10. Tsunoda gets a second weekend with his former team as Liam Lawson deputised for the injured Isack Hadjar at Red Bull. In FP2, Lawson placed 12th behind Alpine's Franco Colapinto.

The only incidents of note were a spin for Leclerc in the second chicane, losing the rear of his Ferrari on the high sausage kerbs, and a dangerous impeding case involving Aston Martin's Lance Stroll. As Stroll came out of the pitlane, the Canadian carelessly veered into the path of Norris, who had to take avoiding action. The incident will be investigated by the FIA race stewards after the session.

There was also some concern at Audi over an ill-sounding V6 engine in the back of Gabriel Bortoleto's car, forcing the Brazilian to abandon his run plan early.

Sports.title: Briatore questions Monaco GP appeal integrity in explosive Italian GP press conference
Sports.content:
Alpine Formula 1 boss Flavio Briatore has questioned the fairness of the appeal procedure against the Monaco Grand Prix results, claiming one judge has a close relationship with McLaren.

Pierre Gasly was one of several drivers penalised in Monaco for exceeding the pitlane speed limit, which was later found to be the result of an incorrect measurement by FOM. Gasly lost his third place, but Alpine launched a right of review against the penalties, with the FIA race stewards agreeing to rescind the Frenchman's penalty.

McLaren and Red Bull appealed against that decision, as the other drivers involved had already served their penalties and didn't have the opportunity to get those rescinded.

Following a lengthy procedure, the FIA's International Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the appellants and reinstated Gasly's two five-second penalties, dropping him to seventh as Red Bull's Isack Hadjar reclaimed a podium spot.

Read Also: Formula 1 Gasly loses Monaco GP podium as penalties reinstated following McLaren and Red Bull appeal

In a statement the Alpine expressed "its disappointment and frustration" with the ruling. But in the FIA's Italian Grand Prix press conference on Friday, executive advisor Flavio Briatore went much further, suggesting the hearing had been unfair as he claimed one of the four judges, Italian-American Filippo Marchino, had links to McLaren.

"I think it's very unfair. We accept the decision, but what is very strange was there were four judges on the panel and one of the judges acted like a prosecutor," Briatore said. "It was four judges, and this one was really a prosecutor against the FIA, against us, against FOM.

"Afterwards we found out what is the reason why this guy was so nasty. It's very linked with McLaren. We have a nice picture of this guy [giving a] speech for McLaren in 2018 at MSO Beverly Hills. He has a foundation, it's called One Drop Foundation and McLaren gave two or three McLaren cars, and this was quite unfair.

Flavio Briatore, Executive Advisor of Alpine F1 Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

"We accept the decision, we accept everything, but it's quite strange to have one guy in the panel linked to the team. This is unfair. The judge normally needs to be independent completely."

Sitting alongside Briatore, McLaren team principal Andrea Stella was visibly taken aback by those accusations.

"I find that this conference is going in a direction that is quite insulting for McLaren, for the reputation of a team that deserves a lot of respect," Stella shot back. "And if anybody makes these kinds of allegations, which seem quite serious, they are going to have to take the responsibility for what they are saying in a public forum.

"The hearing, the whole International Court of Appeal was conducted to the highest standards, and we should not question this case like it's been done."

Commenting on the Monaco appeal outcome, which also moved up McLaren driver Oscar Piastri up from fifth to fourth and earned the two additional championship points, Stella said: "It's a decision that definitely we welcome. It's very important, because it adds clarity in relation to the application of Article 1.1.1 of the International Sporting Code of the FIA, which is foundational for anything that derives from there.

"We appealed because we wanted to make sure that this clarity was sought. We had concerns which were beyond the fact that we might have lost two championship points. Probably these two championship points are not going to make any difference. We were concerned about the application of sporting equality and fairness. This is important and this is not only important for McLaren.

Andrea Stella, McLaren Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

"In fact, not only Red Bull applied, but all teams were present in the hearing because this was a very important moment in terms of clarification as to how we apply the rules, as to how we apply consistency, and also in the specific case, consistency is related to the methodologies that are valid through our race weekend."

Briatore returned to F1 in June 2024 as an executive advisor to then-Alpine CEO Luca de Meo. Earlier in his career, the Italian helped steer the Benetton and Renault teams to consecutive world championships, with Michael Schumacher and Fernando Alonso respectively.

But he was subsequently handed a lifetime paddock ban for his instrumental role in the 2008 Singapore 'Crashgate' scandal. Briatore had been implicated in a plot that involved his driver Nelson Piquet Jr crashing deliberately to cause a safety car intervention that helped his team-mate Alonso win. That lifetime ban by the FIA was overturned in 2010, with the Italian a regular paddock presence as a dealmaker until his official return with Alpine.

Sports.title: Why Norris wanted to set up his own single-seater race team
Sports.content:
Lando Norris says he hopes establishing his own junior team and driver programme can help guide underfunded talent all the way to the Formula 1.

On Wednesday Norris announced two separate projects; a single-seater race team called LN4 Fusion and the LN4 Legacy programme which aims to support a young driver's career through the FIA's ladder.

LN4 Fusion will be run by former long-time Prema team boss Rene Rosin, with Dan Hazlewood running the team's UK arm, and is working on fielding cars in F2, F3 and British F4.

LN4 Legacy Programme, led by former Alpine sporting director Julian Rouse, is a fully-funded programme aimed at supporting young talents all the way to the top. Norris says he was keen to give back to the sport in the face of the spiralling costs of single-seater racing.

"The legacy programme is more to pick out individuals, people that we believe can get to Formula 1 and try and help them one at a time. That's our initial goal," Norris explained. "The fact that drivers have to kind of go out of their way to do it is, I think, an acknowledgement of how difficult it is."

Given the finances involved, LN4 Legacy Programme is starting by backing one yet-to-be-named junior driver, but Norris is hoping he can raise the backing to scale up the programme in the future.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Kym Illman / Getty Images

"The scale we're talking about, you're talking tens of millions to start projects like this. And you need good backing from a lot of investors, things like that. And that can easily be and will be a longer-term project," he said.

"We've got to start somewhere. And I'm happy that I'm trying to help at least one to begin with, and then we'll work on two and then three and then four and five."

On the team side, Norris said former Prema chief Rosin was the ideal candidate to lead LN4 Fusion after racing against the Italian's powerhouse team for years, and Rosin surprisingly became available after ceding control of the family-owned team last winter.

"I've known Rene for many years, since I started to go into single-seaters," Norris explained. "We wanted to put together a group that is experienced and knows how to lead a team and not just create one good team, whether that's just in F3 or just in F2, but be able to put together a project and something long term.

"I've also been able to experience over the course of the last seven years what makes a good leader, what makes a good team. A lot of it starts with the person at the very top and he is that person. He was the inevitable choice."

Norris revealed Rosin had received plenty of interest from various corners to join LN4 Fusion, with the project getting a positive reception from around the industry.

Doriane Pin, PREMA Racing, Rene Rosin of PREMA Photo by: Sam Bloxham / Motorsport Images

"The reactions have been great. Rene said he got over a few hundred job requests within the space of an hour or so of the announcement," Norris said. "So, there's a lot of attraction from a range of drivers, but also mechanics, engineers, all the people that make a team. I'm proud that we've been able to put something very special together."

Norris credited the team he had built around him for helping him take on projects like this, meaning he can still focus on his day job at McLaren and pitch in whenever he is available.

But he was also conscious that it will take much more than his project, or fellow world champion Max Verstappen's GT3 race team, to make a lasting impact, as he called upon the FIA and on F1 management to help bring the exorbitant costs on the single-seater ladder.

"If you want to help bigger areas and economies that are just worse to kind of start racing and allow people to start their dream, it's much bigger than just me doing my job and trying to help out on that," he said. "That takes the sport itself. That takes a lot more work from F1, from FIA, from karting companies.

"It's just simply too expensive, so you cannot rely on people just to fund more people. You have to find other ways to make it more friendly for people to start racing and especially financially. You've got to lower the costs somehow of teams, of the ability to go testing, of just signing up to do Formula 2. F2 is over €2million euros, I think, to start.

"You've got to start somewhere. My ability is starting with one and that's already a big project. Hopefully, over time and with more partners coming on board and more money, more support, we can turn it into a way of helping more people from around the world."

Sports.title: F1 Italian GP: Leclerc heads Ferrari 1-2 in opening practice
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc led a Ferrari 1-2 to set the fastest time in first free practice at Formula 1's Italian Grand Prix.

Leclerc's time of 1m23.008s, set on medium tyres, was quick enough to pip team-mate Lewis Hamilton on a hot summer afternoon at the historic Monza circuit.

Leclerc set his time halfway through the first of three practice sessions, boosting expectations from the partisan home crowd in Italy.

Sporting a throwback livery paying tribute to Michael Schumacher's first season with Ferrari in 1996, Ferrari came to its home track with its latest suite of upgrades. Those updates include a refined low-drag rear wing and the Scuderia's second permitted engine upgrade that aims to help slash its power unit deficit to Mercedes.

Read Also: Formula 1 Ferrari to bring upgraded engine to Italian GP under ADUO

Reigning world champion Lando Norris had been leading the early running before the session was interrupted by Colton Herta's stricken Cadillac. The American was asked by his team to park the car with hydraulic issues, bringing out the red flag.

Test driver Herta had been hunting another superlicence point with his practice outing, but due to his lack of mileage the former IndyCar ace will not get one for his Monza run.

The session resumed with 34 minutes on the clock, with Mercedes' George Russell dipping below Norris' time before Leclerc took charge with a 1m23.008s on medium rubber.

Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Hamilton followed Leclerc through in second, shipping 0.173s to his team-mate on the same medium compound, as Russell reclaimed third with a 1m23.312s lap on soft tyres, three tenths down on the leading Ferrari.

Liam Lawson, who returned to Red Bull as regular driver Isack Hadjar continues to recover from his wrist injury, set fourth ahead of championship leader Antonelli.

Antonelli faces a back-of-the-grid penalty for a full power unit change, meaning the championship leader is fully focused on optimising his race set-up.

The Italian demoted Norris to sixth ahead of Racing Bulls man Arvid Lindblad and Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto. Alpine duo Franco Colapinto and Paul Aron, performing rookie FP1 duties in Pierre Gasly's car, rounded out the top 10.

In the second McLaren, Oscar Piastri was 11th ahead of Yuki Tsunoda, who received a second opportunity to fill Lawson's temporarily vacated Racing Bulls seat.

Herta and Aron were just two of four rookie drivers out on track in FP1. Ayumu Iwasa took place in Max Verstappen's Red Bull and Williams young driver Luke Browning got a run in Alex Albon's car as teams took the opportunity to satisfy one of the four mandated rookie FP1 runs for the season on a non-sprint weekend.

With temperatures soaring above the agreed threshold of 31 degrees and expected to do so for every on-track session, the FIA declared a heat hazard for this weekend's running, forcing drivers to either wear cooling vests or carry additional ballast.

Sports.title: Gasly loses Monaco GP podium as penalties reinstated following McLaren and Red Bull appeal
Sports.content:
Alpine Formula 1 driver Pierre Gasly has lost his Monaco Grand Prix podium finish after all, as his penalties for pitlane speeding stand, the FIA’s International Court of Appeal (ICA) has ruled.

Gasly was one of several drivers who were pinged for pitlane speeding during the race in the principality, but it emerged the pitlane measurements were inaccurate, with a discrepancy of 77cm between the first two timing loops – hence the unusual number of penalties.

While the likes of Oscar Piastri and George Russell lost out by serving their penalties during the race – incorrectly served in Russell’s case, with the Mercedes driver consequently incurring a drive-through sanction – Gasly’s couple of five-second penalties were added to his race time, dropping him from third to seventh. The timing meant Alpine was able to request a right of review.

FIA stewards subsequently overturned the penalties on 12 June, meaning Gasly was reinstated in third position. But this wasn’t an option for the drivers who served their penalties during the race.

Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar and McLaren’s Piastri lost out, dropping from third and fourth to fourth and fifth. Both teams therefore appealed the decision before the ICA; the move was supported by Racing Bulls, whose drivers both lost a spot in the classification, and Motorsport UK.

The Court ruled on Friday that the penalties do stand, so Gasly is back down to seventh, with fellow countryman Hadjar inheriting the third place the Red Bull racer celebrated post-race.

Pierre Gasly, Alpine, Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Erik Junius

Part of the ICA’s reasoning was that Alpine couldn’t prove with full certainty that Gasly had travelled a longer distance in the pitlane than (inaccurately) measured, so its shorter time between the timing loops could reflect “a shorter path, greater speed, or a combination of both”.

However, the ICA confirmed that other drivers having served their penalties “cannot be an obstacle to the cancellation of an illegitimate sanction, because those penalties were served at the discretion and choice of the team. Admitting the contrary on the grounds that it would create sporting unfairness would in return be inconsistent with sporting fairness.”

Alpine has expressed “disappointment and frustration” with the decision, still adamant that Gasly did nothing wrong and was undeserving of any penalties.

“The team expresses its disappointment and frustration with the outcome reached by the FIA International Court of Appeal relating to the result of the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix,” a team statement read.

“While we disagree with the decision, and still fully maintain that Car #10 did not exceed the Pit Lane speed limit at any point during the race, the team acknowledges the decision of the judging panel from the recent hearing in Paris.

“While the result is not what we had hoped for, as we feel that we have been unjustly punished, the team is firmly focused on continuing to improve its performance on track and remains in a close and very competitive Championship fight.

Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

“This outcome will not deter the team’s efforts and motivation in achieving its objectives by the end of the season.”

Meanwhile, an FIA statement insisted that its stewards weren’t necessarily to blame for making a wrong decision, though the federation pledged to review its processes.

“The FIA notes the decision today from the International Court of Appeal (ICA) in relation to the hearing of Tuesday, August 25 (case ICA-2026-06-07-08-09),” the statement read.

“The ICA decision upholds the appeals of McLaren F1 Team and Red Bull Racing against the decisions of the stewards contained in document 99 of the Monaco Grand Prix, effectively overturning those decisions.

“The FIA is reviewing the methodology and operation of the current Formula 1 timing system and the related regulatory matters. It will also be reviewing other judicial procedures and operations including the right of review and the appeal processes.

“The FIA is fully supportive of the Stewarding process and the independence and objectivity of the diverse panels of Stewards who are an integral part of global motorsport.

FIA flag Photo by: Mark Sutton / Motorsport Images

“Stewards’ decisions are taken in a different environment to that of the Court, whereas the Court has access to extensive and additional legal counsel input, arguments and evidence.

“The FIA Stewards constantly review their processes and take part in extensive professional development. Every decision of the ICA is carefully examined by FIA Stewards ensuring a process of continuous improvement.”

Sports.title: Domenicali on shortening races, sprints and F1’s future
Sports.content:
Formula 1 does not want to stop and contemplate the numbers of a particularly positive historical phase. This is the message Stefano Domenicali wanted to reiterate at Monza, ranging from the technical future of the championship to the evolution of the calendar, via the relationship with manufacturers, sprint races and the need to reach an increasingly young audience.

“The risk is becoming self-referential,” F1’s CEO explained. “We must not be satisfied with the success we have today. We must continue to understand why we have become so big and keep our feet on the ground, knowing that there are still many dimensions in which we can grow.”

One of the central themes concerns the regulatory future. F1 and the FIA will soon begin to consider the characteristics of the next generation of power units and single-seaters, in an industrial context that has changed profoundly compared to when the current rules were defined.

“When the regulatory change we are experiencing today was addressed, it seemed that the future was defined by electrification. Today that is no longer the case,” Domenicali stressed. “It is up to us to understand how to react and interpret this change in the right way.”

The point is to find a balance between the needs of the major manufacturers and the need for F1 not to depend completely on their industrial strategies. “On the one hand we must guarantee the presence of the manufacturers, but on the other, if they were to have different priorities, we must understand how to manage to be independent. If the manufacturers decided to leave today, we would have a big problem.”

Hence the possibility of moving in the future towards less complex technical solutions. “A less complex project, obviously while respecting cost and performance targets, helps to be independent.” Domenicali also indicated two points he considers fundamental: “I strongly believe in keeping sustainable fuels at the heart of the technological project and in moving towards a lighter car, because we want to see drivers who can really push to the limit a machine that must be in their hands.”

Domenicali is opening to shortening F1 races Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

Shorter grands prix

Also on the table is a broader reflection on the sporting product. Among the ideas that have emerged in recent months is that of slightly reducing the distance of grands prix, a possibility on which Domenicali has not closed the door. “My position is very simple and starts from a technical consideration. If we are talking, as it seems, about a few laps, for me it also goes in the direction of the fact that young people tend to be less and less present for long things. I don’t think there would be a negative effect if we are talking about reducing by two or three laps. If it became something more significant it would be a different discussion, but in this perspective I am not opposed.”

It is the same philosophy that accompanied the introduction of sprint races, initially met with some perplexity even by Domenicali himself. “I am the first who, as a Formula 1 dinosaur, had doubts when we proposed this. But the data did not contradict it: promoters, media and fans, in the vast majority, have digested the format and consider it dynamic.”

Sprint races will therefore continue to be part of F1, although Domenicali ruled out a scenario similar to MotoGP, with one every weekend. “They will be [at] fewer than half” of the events, he specified. “Young people increasingly appreciate a weekend in which there is already something that counts on Friday. Long-standing fans, and I include myself among them, may also be interested in a practice session, but for the general public having qualifying already on Friday means having more content.”

An evolution that Domenicali links directly to the change in the audience. “Today we have around 40% of the people who follow us coming are female and an average age that has gone from around 57 years to 34.” A transformation to which, in Italy as an example, the Kimi Antonelli effect is also contributing.

“I have to tell the truth, the numbers are surprising me because they are growing strongly,” Domenicali said. “Kimi has brought not only competitiveness on track, but also a wave of people who did not follow Formula 1 before. He is a young man who faces an enormous responsibility with a lightness typical of young people. He has a naturalness and freshness in which kids his age can recognise themselves.”

Turning peak interest into lasting success

Domenicali, however, insisted on the need to turn these peaks of attention into a lasting relationship. “We must avoid it being a growth spike that then leaves us. The great challenge is to understand how to keep connected those who show up for the first time. There are communities that do not know us and we have an obligation to build a Formula 1 culture.”

This scenario also includes the geographical expansion of the championship. Domenicali cited China, South America, Far East and Africa as areas with significant room for growth. “Africa is giving important signals on which we want soon to communicate something significant.”

Hill leads Zanardi during the 1993 South African GP Photo by: Motorsport Images

Finally, there remains the issue of the more immediate calendar, with Qatar and Abu Dhabi still confirmed but under observation. “The calendar, at the moment, is the one you know. We are monitoring the situation because, if safety and operability are not guaranteed in full, we will have to take other decisions. The teams are absolutely up to date, the dialogue with them is continuous.”

Even in a phase of expansion, therefore, Domenicali identifies the ability to react quickly as the main solution to future risks: “Things change so quickly that, if you are not able to react, you lose a lot of time in an instant. The risk we must not run is that of stopping looking for competent people, fresh ideas and new points of view. When you keep fishing in the same pond, the fish is always the same.”

Sports.title: Verstappen told Red Bull his car has “less power than a Fiat Punto” in practice | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen made his dissatisfaction with his car clear in final practice for the Italian Grand Prix.

“Mate I have less power than the Fiat Punto,” he told race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase as he prepared for his final run. “I can’t do anything, I can’t even race with them.”

Verstappen made his comment shortly before his run-in with Lewis Hamilton at the Rettifilo chicane late in the session.

Verstappen told his team several times during the session he needs to use the slipstream of another car to have a competitive straight-line speed at the track.

“It’s just slow driving by yourself,” he said early in the session. Following another run he told Lambiase: “I need the tow. You can see the difference again, this is slow.”

“I have no power in the laps,” he added on another run. “I can’t even stay close.”

Verstappen hit a top speed of 331kph on his fastest run as he passed the pits. As is typical with the current cars, his speed tailed off long before he reached the braking zone for the first corner.

The Red Bull driver ended the session third-fastest behind George Russell’s Mercedes and Lewis Hamilton’s Ferrari. His team mate Liam Lawson was 12th fastest, six-tenths of a second off Verstappen.

Sports.title: Russell fastest ahead of scrapping Hamilton and Verstappen in final practice | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell was quickest again in the final practice session ahead of qualifying for the Italian Grand Prix.

He led Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen, who almost collided at the Rettifilo chicane in the final minutes of the session.

The incident began after Verstappen’s race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase told him he could pass Hamilton as both drivers prepared to start their final laps. Verstappen passed Hamilton heading into Ascari, but the Ferrari driver re-passed him approaching the next corner.

Verstappen immediately tried to re-pass Hamilton on the straight but fell back behind the Ferrari, either out of choice or because his car ran low on energy before his rivals. When they reached the chicane, Verstappen dived down the inside while Hamilton swerved onto the run-off area to avoid contact.

“He caused that,” claimed Verstappen. “I got blocked by Max,” said Hamilton.

The pair were separated by a tenth of a second at the end of the session. Andrea Kimi Antonelli, who will start the race from the back of the grid due to a power unit change penalty, was fourth-fastest.

Russell was fortunate to emerge from the session without incurring the wrath of the stewards. He clearly held Oscar Piastri up in Lesmo One yet they opted not to investigate. He also had to slam on his brake to avoid crossing the pit exit line when the light turned red at the end of the session.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Piastri went quickest of all through the first sector but ended up only eighth. His team mate Lando Norris was a tenth of a second quicker and the pair were separated by Charles Leclerc’s Ferrari and Arvid Lindblad’s rapid Racing Bulls. His usual team mate Liam Lawson was only 12th in his Red Bull.

The two Alpine drivers completed the top 10. The Williams drivers were much lower down and both are under investigation for potential yellow flag infringements.

As the cars’ lack of energy means they are losing significant amounts of speed on the straight, drivers used practice to work out how to best improve their lap times by getting a tow from another driver. Lambiase advised Verstappen “I would not recommend starting the lap closer than five seconds to Stroll” as the Red Bull was gaining around three seconds per lap on the Aston Martin.

Temperatures remained high at the Monza circuit, with the track surface hitting 53C during the session.

Prior to the session Cadillac were fined €30,000, all but €5,000 of which was suspended, but Colton Herta’s Clutch Deactivation System did not operate when his car stopped in first practice.

Sports.title: Court of Appeal issues defence to Briatore’s allegations of bias over Gasly decision | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The International Court of Appeal has issued a statement in reaction to the allegations of bias made by Alpine executive director Flavio Briatore yesterday.

The ICA, which is independent of the FIA, ruled against Alpine and the governing body in a case brought by Red Bull and McLaren over a decision made in the Monaco Grand Prix three months ago. The court reinstated two penalties issued to Alpine driver Pierre Gasly which the Monaco stewards previously struck out. Gasly fell from third place to seventh in the classification as a result.

Briatore suggested one of the four ICA judges involved in the decision, Filippo Marchino, favoured McLaren. In response the ICA defended the integrity of its selection process.

“The FIA Courts are aware of public comments questioning the independence and impartiality of the judges of the panel that decided Case ICA-2026-06-07-08-0,” it said in a statement issued by ICA president Laurent Anselmi, ICA vice-president Waltraud Wunsch, International Tribunal president Rui Botica Santos and vice-president Gerard Martin.

“The FIA Courts wish to make clear that the appointment and participation of the judges in that case, like for any other case, were conducted in accordance with the applicable FIA judicial procedures and usual practice, which are inspired by the highest standards like the IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest in International Arbitration.

“All judges are elected by the FIA General Assemblies, some of them upon proposition of a group of at least five F1 teams in accordance with the FIA Statutes. They are all subject to the independence and confidentiality requirements contained in the FIA Judicial and Disciplinary Rules, make annual disclosures of interests to the FIA Compliance Officer, and sign a specific declaration of independence for each particular case in consideration of the issue at stake and the parties involved, which is served to the parties.”

The ICA pointed out all parties involved in the case, including Alpine, had the opportunity to raise any concerns they had over the selection of judges.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“At both the beginning and conclusion of the hearing, the parties were invited to raise any issue concerning the proceedings or the composition of the Court,” they said. “None did so.

“No objection was raised during the hearing concerning the manner in which the Court questioned the witness or conducted the proceedings.”

Marchino, a US-based lawyer, was one of four judges involved in the decision. Michael Grech presided over the hearing and Tomas Borec and Luigi Fumagalli were also appointed.

“The ICA emphasises the importance of constituting panels with judges from different cultural and geographical backgrounds,” the statement continued, “This helps ensure that the deliberations and discussions reflect a diversity of legal traditions, perspectives and approaches, further strengthening the fairness, independence, credibility of the process and access to a fair trial.

“A Court’s decision can leave room for various interpretations and comments as for its legal merits; that is fair and accepted by all the judges. The Court is confident in the soundness of the proceedings and the integrity of the judges. The FIA Courts remain committed to the independence and impartiality of their judges and to the integrity of the judicial process.”

Sports.title: Russell leads Leclerc, Stroll faces investigation for “dangerous” incident with Norris | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell prevented Charles Leclerc from topping both practice sessions at Monza as Mercedes showed their potential on Friday afternoon.

Despite not setting the quickest time in any of the three sectors, Russell headed the table with a best lap of 1’22.559 – over two-and-a-half seconds off last year’s pace. However he reported a “weird vibration under braking” from his front suspension at the end of the session.

His team mate Andrea Kimi Antonelli was third fastest. The championship leader is expected to serve a penalty tomorrow for a power unit change.

Lando Norris put his McLaren fourth-fastest, almost four tenths of a second off the pace, following a near-miss with Lance Stroll. The Aston Martin driver drifted onto the race line as Norris approached him at the fastest point on the track, forcing the McLaren driver to avoid a collision by taking to the run-off area.

Norris branded his rival’s move “dangerous” on his radio. The stewards will investigate the incident after the session.

Lewis Hamilton and Oscar Piastri ensured the the three quickest teams filled the top six places. Max Verstappen was only ninth for Red Bull, behind Arvid Lindblad of sister team Racing Bulls and Oliver Bearman, enjoying improved performance in an upgraded Haas. Yuki Tsunoda put the other Racing Bulls in 10th.

Franco Colapinto had a scare at the exit of Ascari late in the session as he caught a huge snap of oversteer at high speed. His team mate Pierre Gasly was only 14th despite being quickest of all through the first sector.

The opening part of the lap appears especially sensitive to slipstreams as the cars run out of electrical energy so early. Several car topped out at around 330kph long before the end of the straight, then dipped to 320kph before hitting the brakes for the Rettifilo chicane.

While 1.3 seconds covered the top 17 cars, Esteban Ocon lagged further behind in his Haas, not yet having all the same upgrades as his team mate. The Aston Martins and Cadillacs filled the bottom for places.

Update: Stroll and Aston Martin were given formal warnings for impeding Norris

Sports.title: Alpine’s Briatore accuses Appeal Court judge of bias after losing Gasly case | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Alpine executive consultant Flavio Briatore has accused a member of the Court of Appeal of bias after the team lost its third place in the Monaco Grand Prix.

Red Bull and McLaren successfully petitioned the appeal court to reinstate the two pit lane speeding penalties issued to Gasly during the race. This relegated him to seventh in the final classification, promoting Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar to third place and McLaren’s Oscar Piastri to fourth.

In the FIA press conference following the publication of the decision, Briatore accused one of the court members of bias in favour of McLaren. He claimed an organisation linked to the member received cars through McLaren Special Operations, part of the McLaren Group’s road car division.

“We accept the decision,” said Briatore. “But what is very strange was four judge in the panel, and one of the judge act like a prosecutor. For this, not big problem.

“The problem is he’s very linked with the McLaren company because we have a nice picture of this guy at the speech for McLaren in 2018 in MSO Beverly Hills. Him have a foundation, it’s called One Drop Foundation, and McLaren gave two or three McLaren cars. And it was quite unfair one of the judges was linked with a team protesting us.”

Briatore confirmed he was referring to Filippo Marchino, one of the four ICA members, who serves on the board of the One Drop Foundation which promotes access to clean water. The foundation reportedly began winding down its operation last month.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella called Briatore’s claims in today’s FIA press conference “insulting” and defended the governing body’s handling of the hearing.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“I find that this conference is going in this direction quite insulting for McLaren, for the reputation of a team that deserves a lot of respect,” he said. “If anybody makes these kind of allegations which seem quite serious, they are going to have to take the responsibility for what they are saying in a public forum.

“The hearing, the whole International Court of Appeal was conducted to the highest standards and we should not question this phase like it’s been done.”

Marchino, who has been an FIA judge since 2024, is a US-based lawyer who specialises in cases involving serious personal injury, wrongful death and large class action lawsuits. He has also competed in rounds of the World Rally Championship.

Briatore continued his criticism of Marchino during the FIA press conference, calling his appointment “unfair.”

“The judge normally needs to be independent, completely,” he said. “And this judge, the name is kind of an Italian name, but he’s American, Filippo Marchino.

“Filippo Marchino is a judge, he was very nasty during the hearing, was acting as a prosecutor. And after, we found out what is the reason why so nasty, this guy. He is very linked with McLaren. This I notice.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“So whatever Stella said, for the sport, for this, first I think someone, where you have the judgement, the judge needs to be independent. Not somebody doing the speech for McLaren and somebody using the McLaren car in the charity. This is the point.

“After that, the points one, one, three, two, four, five, I don’t care. I’m very surprised this guy have the link with McLaren.”

The judging panel for the ICA is appointed by its president, currently Laurent Anselmi. Marchino was one of four judges appointed alongside Michael Grech, who presided over the hearing, Tomas Borec and Luigi Fumagalli.

In ICA decisions involving F1 matters, the panel must include at least one judge elected on proposal of at least five competitors in the championship. All nominees are subject to a due diligence process performed by the FIA’s compliance officer. The nominated judges are then reviewed by a further panel which makes recommendations to the FIA’s Eligibility Assessment Committee.

Briatore has clashed with the FIA before. In 2009 the governing body attempted to ban him from motorsport for life over his involvement in the ‘Crashgate’ conspiracy while he was team principal of Renault. He later successfully challenged the decision in the French courts and returned to the team, now operating as Alpine.

Other F1 team bosses have previously been sanctioned by the FIA for criticising their officials. In 2021 former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner was given an official warning for describing a marshal as “rogue” for waving a yellow flag which led to Max Verstappen being penalised. Guenther Steiner, previously Haas’s team principal, was twice penalised for similar transgressions, including when he was fined for calling a steward “stupid” and “idiotic”.

Sports.title: Leclerc leads Ferrari one-two as top speeds drop at hot Monza | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc led the opening practice session for the Italian Grand Prix in hot conditions at Monza.

The track temperatures soared to 53C during the opening hour. The FIA has issued a heat hazard warning for this weekend’s event.

Leclerc produced a fastest lap of 1’23.008 which was almost three seconds slower than the best time in the same session last year, set by his team mate Lewis Hamilton.

George Russell was second behind the two Ferraris and separated from team mate Andrea Kimi Antonelli by the Red Bull of Liam Lawson. Lando Norris was the fastest McLaren driver, in sixth place.

As was widely predicted the 2026 generation of Formula 1 cars were significantly slower through the quickest points on the track. The front-running cars approached the first corner around 30 to 40kph slower than they did last year, though it remains to be seen how much quicker they might be in their qualifying simulation runs this afternoon.

The session was interrupted when Colton Herta’s Cadillac came to a stop after just five laps. The MAC-26 experienced a hydraulic fault and the session had to be stopped while it was recovered.

Herta, who was in Sergio Perez’s car, was one of four junior drivers who took part in the session as teams fulfilled their obligation to run them. Ayumu Iwasa drove Max Verstappen’s Red Bull, Luke Browning returned for Williams in Alexander Albon’s car and Paul Aron made his fourth appearance this year, this time in Pierre Gasly’s Alpine.

Sports.title: Terence Crawford Tests Jaron Ennis’ Easy Work Claim
Sports.content:
“For sure. Anybody that y’all ask me, if somebody gives y’all a list and y’all ask me who I think is easy work, I’m going to say easy work every single time because I believe in myself,” Ennis said to TNT Sports. “Can’t nobody in this game do what I do. I feel like I’m the best.”

That answer was predictable. He could hardly stand beside Crawford and concede that the former undisputed champion would beat him. Crawford was more interested in testing the confidence behind the words.

Crawford Wants More Than Josh Kelly

Questioning the punishment Ennis has taken, Crawford suggested he would have attacked rather than allowing Boots to recover. Ennis responded that he would have done the same to Crawford.

The discussion then turned to Vergil Ortiz Jr. and Sebastian Fundora. In Crawford’s view, beating Josh Kelly would not earn Ennis the same credit as defeating either of those two junior middleweights.

“We would have seen it if you would have fought Vergil,” Crawford told him.

In response, Ennis insisted that he has always stepped forward when opponents hurt him. Crawford gave him credit but wants to see that aggression against a dangerous pressure fighter or a 6’5″ champion who can overwhelm opponents with volume.

“If you step on Fundora, I give you props,” Crawford said. “If you step on somebody like Vergil, I give you props.”

The criticism will lead some fans to accuse Ennis of choosing Kelly over the strongest opposition at 154. That conclusion would be premature without knowing which fights were financially and politically available. Ortiz fights under Golden Boy, Fundora has been associated with PBC cards, and Ennis has his own promotional obligations.

Those divisions between promoters can prevent an obvious fight without either boxer refusing it. Still, Crawford’s point carries weight. Ennis cannot build his claim as boxing’s next dominant star by repeatedly destroying opponents one level below the elite.

Vergil Would Test Boots’ Defensive Habits

To Boots, Ortiz is made for him. His speed, combinations, switch hitting, and counterpunching would give him obvious opportunities against an opponent who continually advances.

There was some agreement from Crawford that Ortiz’s style may suit Boots, but he also reminded him that seeing openings is different from surviving the pressure long enough to exploit them.

Rather than merely walking forward looking for one punch, Ortiz attacks the body, stays close after throwing, and forces opponents to work when they would prefer to rest. Ennis has occasionally backed away in straight lines while depending on his reflexes to escape. Against Ortiz, those retreats would give up ground and leave Boots near the ropes, where the incoming body shots would become harder to avoid.

The move deeper into junior middleweight adds another concern. Ennis absorbed clean shots from Karen Chukhadzhian and Avanesyan at welterweight without losing control, but natural 154-pound fighters bring greater strength into exchanges. Boots may still possess the better skills, but Crawford wants to see how those skills hold up after a physically stronger opponent forces him through several hard rounds.

Crawford’s Avanesyan Argument Cuts Both Ways

The Avanesyan comparison was also used to reduce the value of Kelly as an opponent. Avanesyan stopped Kelly in six rounds in 2021 before Crawford knocked him out in the sixth round the following year. Ennis then forced Avanesyan’s corner to end their fight after five rounds in 2024.

“Kelly already got knocked out by a person that you knocked out,” Crawford said after briefly struggling to remember Avanesyan’s name.

That is classic boxing mathematics, and it rarely provides a reliable forecast. Kelly losing to Avanesyan does not automatically mean he would lose to every fighter who later beat Avanesyan. Styles, preparation, timing, and a fighter’s development can change the result.

The comparison also gives Boots an answer. Crawford cannot use Avanesyan to separate himself from Ennis when both men stopped him. Ennis technically did it one round sooner, although Crawford produced the cleaner individual knockout.

His broader criticism is more persuasive than the triangle theory. Kelly has rebuilt since his loss, but beating him would not answer the same questions as defeating Ortiz or Fundora. Kelly can box, move, and counter. He would not bring the sustained physical pressure that makes the other two opponents more revealing tests.

Questioning the punishment Ennis has taken, Crawford told him, “You know what I would’ve done to you if you would’ve got hurt in that last fight?” His point was that he would have attacked rather than allowing Boots to recover. Ennis responded that he would have done the same to Crawford.

By the end, Crawford had softened his tone, saying he wants Ennis to succeed at 154, 160, and even 168 pounds. There was respect in the exchange, but Crawford was also guarding his position.

Long discussed as Crawford’s successor, Ennis invites comparisons with what the former welterweight champion accomplished every time he produces a dominant performance. Questioning Boots’ opposition allows Crawford to encourage him while reminding everyone that talent and accomplishments are not the same thing.

Sports.title: What Does Hearn Do With Andy Ruiz Jr. Now?
Sports.content:
Knyba was supposed to provide a credible bridge to something lucrative. If Ruiz Jr. handled the tall Polish heavyweight, Hearn could begin selling another fight with Joshua or offer him to Moses Itauma, Filip Hrgovic, Daniel Dubois, or Fabio Wardley. Instead, Ruiz Jr. lost a unanimous decision and was dropped heavily in the seventh round.

The official scores also disguised how poorly he performed. One judge had Knyba winning 117-110, while Glenn Feldman and Kevin Morgan returned narrow 114-113 cards. Those two tallies flattered Ruiz Jr., who spent most of the fight struggling to cross the distance behind Knyba’s jab.

Without the knockdown, Feldman and Morgan would each have scored the fight 114-114, producing a majority draw. Ruiz Jr. came surprisingly close to escaping without another defeat, but the 117-110 card gave a more accurate picture of Knyba’s control.

Scraping out a draw would not have repaired the damage to his value, either. Matchroom needed Ruiz Jr. to beat Knyba convincingly enough to support talk of something bigger.

Matchroom Had to Take the Risk

Plenty will second-guess the decision to put Ruiz Jr. in with Knyba after such a long absence. The matchmaking was not the mistake.

Ruiz Jr. was a fringe contender when he replaced Jarrell Miller against Joshua in June 2019. His stunning knockout victory changed boxing history, but everything that followed suggested the performance was an extraordinary night rather than the beginning of a dominant championship run.

Poorly prepared for the Joshua rematch, he then fought sporadically against Chris Arreola, Luis Ortiz, and Miller. Weight changes, injuries, trainer switches, and long absences became the story of his career.

If he required two or three soft opponents before facing somebody at Knyba’s level, Matchroom had no reason to sign him. Hearn needed immediate proof that the old-hand speed, combination punching, and hunger were still there. He did not receive it.

The lower weight created another false signal. Ruiz Jr. came in at 254.3 pounds, his lightest weight in eight years, allowing the comeback to be presented as evidence of renewed discipline. The scale showed that he had lost weight. It did not show that he had recovered the timing, hand speed, or mobility that once made him dangerous.

Faced with a 6’7″ opponent possessing an 86-inch reach, Ruiz Jr. struggled to cut off the ring and rarely got into punching range in position to release combinations. He followed Knyba, reached with punches, and repeatedly allowed the taller man to jab before tying him up.

Weight can be managed during a training camp. The physical decline caused by age, injuries, and years of inactivity is harder to reverse. Matchroom signed Ruiz Jr. because his fast combinations once made him unusually dangerous for a heavyweight. Against Knyba, that version was nowhere to be found.

What Does Queensberry Gain?

The defeat also leaves Hearn dependent on other promoters if he wants to recover value from Ruiz Jr.’s name.

Itauma needs rebuilding after his loss to Hrgovic, but Frank Warren gains little from helping Matchroom rescue a failed signing. A victory over Ruiz Jr. carries far less weight now that Knyba has exposed him. If Itauma struggles or loses, Queensberry damages one of its most important young heavyweights.

The same issue applies to Hrgovic, Dubois, and Wardley. Ruiz Jr. remains experienced and can still punch, yet beating him no longer proves that one of Warren’s heavyweights belongs near a championship. Queensberry would accept the risk while Matchroom received most of the benefit.

Money might persuade Warren, but he has plenty of available opponents without taking responsibility for Matchroom’s problem.

David Adeleye may be the only recognizable heavyweight Hearn can match with Ruiz Jr. without seeking help from another promoter.

Such a fight would amount to combining two damaged investments. Adeleye was comprehensively beaten by Hrgovic, while Ruiz Jr. has now lost to a lower-level heavyweight. It may produce entertaining action, but it would not restore either man to serious contention.

At 36, Ruiz Jr. would also be facing a younger, larger puncher after Knyba dropped him and left him badly marked around the left eye. Another loss might erase the remaining value of his name.

Saudi-funded heavyweight cards offered Hearn the easiest way to turn Ruiz Jr.’s reputation into money. A convincing comeback win would have allowed Matchroom to offer him for Itauma, Hrgovic, Dubois, Wardley, or another boxer being positioned for a lucrative event.

Losing to Knyba removes much of that appeal. Ruiz Jr. can still be advertised as a former unified champion, but he no longer resembles a credible opponent for a championship fight. The familiar name remains while the sporting justification has disappeared.

Hearn is left without the cash-out opportunity that made the original gamble worthwhile. Ruiz Jr. is too diminished to sell as a contender and still dangerous enough that a rival promoter receives little benefit from using him.

Can Hearn Escape the Contract?

Matchroom announced Ruiz Jr.’s agreement as a multi-fight promotional deal. Other reports described it as a three-fight arrangement, although the full terms and any release clauses have not been made public.

An escape clause after a first fight loss would give Hearn an easy answer. Without one, Matchroom remains tied to a former champion who was signed to reach lucrative bouts quickly but failed at the first stage.

A long rebuilding program makes no sense for Ruiz Jr. His age, inactivity, and history of poor discipline make further investment difficult to justify. Another Joshua fight now looks like nostalgia; Queensberry has little incentive to lend Hearn one of its heavyweights, and easier opposition only delays the same question.

Ruiz Jr. was supposed to provide a shortcut to a profitable heavyweight event. Following the loss to Knyba, Hearn is on his own with an albatross.

Sports.title: Knyba Upsets Andy Ruiz Jr. in Newark
Sports.content:
The Polish heavyweight dropped Ruiz heavily in the seventh round after hurting him with a right hook and following with a barrage. Referee David Franciosi administered the count and allowed Ruiz to continue, with the bell arriving before Knyba could launch another sustained attack.

Ruiz fought with greater urgency in the eighth and ninth, finding some success with body punches and right hands. Knyba regained command over the final three rounds by returning to his jab and maintaining distance.

The judges scored the fight 117-110 and 114-113 twice for Knyba. The two narrow cards did not reflect his overall control or the seventh-round knockdown.

Mielnicki Outboxes Williams

Vito “White Magic” Mielnicki Jr. (24-1, 13 KOs) retained his WBO Global and WBC Continental Americas middleweight titles with a clear unanimous decision over Austin “Ammo” Williams (20-3, 13 KOs). All three judges scored the 10-round fight 98-91.

Mielnicki dropped Williams with a hard right hand during the opening round. Williams rose quickly and survived Mielnicki’s attempt to finish him before the bell.

The New Jersey fighter continued landing the cleaner punches, rocking Williams late in the third and fourth rounds. A right hand from Mielnicki bloodied Williams’ mouth in the fifth.

Williams produced his best sequence in the eighth, landing a counter left that bloodied Mielnicki’s nose and briefly hurt him. Mielnicki recovered, returned to his jab and movement, and finished the fight with the sharper work. David Fields served as the referee.

Garcia Drops Chaves Four Times

Eridson Garcia (24-2, 14 KOs) captured the WBO Latino lightweight title by defeating Alan “Veneno” Chaves (22-1, 19 KOs) over 10 rounds. The scores were 99-87, 99-88, and 98-88.

Garcia scored the first knockdown with a combination during the opening minute of round two. He floored Chaves twice more with body shots in the fifth, leaving the heavily favored Argentinian far behind on the cards.

Garcia slipped while avoiding a punch in the sixth. The referee initially ruled it a knockdown for Chaves, but the commission corrected the call.

A right hook sent Chaves down for the fourth time midway through the ninth. Chaves pursued a stoppage in the final round but never came close to overcoming Garcia’s lead. Earl Brown served as the referee.

Moses Stops Contreras After Five

Newark lightweight Zaquin Moses (8-0, 4 KOs) stopped Angel “Cachorro” Contreras (18-11-2, 12 KOs) after five rounds of their scheduled eight-round fight.

Moses controlled the action with his jab, hand speed, and southpaw pressure. Contreras remained on his stool after the fifth, giving Moses the stoppage victory at the official time of 3:00. Harvey Dock served as the referee.

Sports.title: Damian Knyba Destroys Eddie Hearn’s Andy Ruiz Plans
Sports.content:
Ruiz had a little success attacking the body in the sixth, but the fight nearly ended one round later. Knyba hurt him with a right hook, poured on punches, and dropped him hard near the bell. Ruiz rose with his legs gone and was fortunate that the referee allowed the fight to continue.

The official gave Ruiz a long look and considerable time before restarting the action. Without that delay, Knyba likely would have finished him. The bell then provided another escape before Ruiz had to survive any meaningful follow-up attack.

Hearn’s Ruiz Plans Collapse

Ruiz showed some urgency in the eighth and ninth while Knyba recovered from his attempt to secure the knockout. That brief rally did not make the contest close. Knyba returned to his jab during the later rounds and resumed landing the cleaner punches from distance.

The result leaves Eddie Hearn in a difficult position after recently signing Ruiz to Matchroom. Hearn had discussed moving him quickly toward an IBF title fight with Filip Hrgovic or matching him against Moses Itauma. He can forget about either option after this performance.

Hrgovic is larger, stronger, busier, and far more dangerous than Knyba. Itauma possesses the speed and power to punish the slow feet and defensive openings Ruiz displayed in Newark. Sending Ruiz into either fight next would look less like title planning and more like cashing him out.

Knyba deserves credit for refusing to serve as the opponent in somebody else’s comeback story. Ruiz, however, looked fortunate to hear the final bell. The former unified champion did not resemble a heavyweight one fight away from another title opportunity.

Sports.title: Andy Ruiz Jr vs Damian Knyba Live Results and Fight Updates
Sports.content:
Undercard results

Vito “White Magic” Mielnicki Jr. (24-1, 13 KOs) defeated Austin “Ammo” Williams (20-3, 13 KOs) by unanimous scores of 98-91, 98-91, and 98-91. Mielnicki dropped Williams with a hard right hand in the opening round, then controlled most of the fight with his jab, movement, and counters. Williams bloodied Mielnicki’s nose and briefly stiffened his legs with a counter left during his strong eighth round. The hometown fighter recovered, regained command through cleaner punching, and retained his WBO Global and WBC Continental Americas middleweight titles in his Matchroom debut.

Eridson Garcia (24-2, 14 KOs) scored a massive upset over Alan “Veneno” Chaves (22-1, 19 KOs), winning the WBO Latino lightweight title by unanimous decision. The judges scored the 10-round fight 99-87, 99-88, and 98-88. Garcia dropped the heavily favored Argentine four times: once in the second, twice in the fifth, and once in the ninth. The Dominican controlled the fight with pressure, counters, and superior activity as Chaves never produced the rally he needed.

Super featherweight Zaquin Moses (8-0, 4 KOs) stopped Angel Antonio Contreras (18-11-2, 12 KOs) when Contreras remained on his stool after the fifth round. Moses controlled the fight with his jab, hand speed, and southpaw pressure. Contreras absorbed steady punishment before his corner ended the fight. The official time was 3:00 of round five in Moses’ first professional appearance at Newark’s Prudential Center.

Start time: 8:00 p.m. ET

TV: TNT

Streaming: DAZN

Location: Prudential Center, Newark, New Jersey

Running Order

Andy Ruiz Jr vs Damian Knyba, 12 rounds, heavyweight

Vito Mielnicki Jr vs Austin Williams, 12 rounds, middleweight

Alan Chaves vs Eridson Garcia, 10 rounds, lightweight

Zaquin Moses vs Angel Antonio Contreras, 8 rounds, super featherweight

Live Results

Sports.title: Vito Mielnicki Uses Size to Defeat Ammo Williams
Sports.content:
Williams continued pressing, but his defense remained too porous. He frequently followed Mielnicki without moving his head, allowing the New Jersey fighter to land jabs and counters before sliding away. When they exchanged at closer range, Mielnicki’s uppercuts and body shots were sharper. He couldn’t miss with his uppercuts on Ammo all night.

How Much Did Ammo Have Left?

This was the best name on Mielnicki’s record, although Williams may no longer be the same dangerous contender he was several years ago. Ammo had already been softened up in a one-sided loss to WBC middleweight champion Carlos Adames last March. That beating, combined with Friday’s knockdown and wide scores, raises questions about how much punishment Williams can continue absorbing at this level. Ammo looked half-stunned from the get-go, legs looking wobbly with every hard shot that Mielnicki threw. The heavy pounding that Ammo took in the Adames fight couldn’t have helped him.

He still produced one threatening moment in the eighth, landing a counter left that bloodied Mielnicki’s nose and briefly stiffened his legs. Mielnicki responded intelligently rather than getting dragged into a reckless exchange, returning to lateral movement and cleaner combinations over the final two rounds.

The performance was an important step for Mielnicki, but the size advantage and Williams’ recent damage should be considered before treating it as proof that he is ready for the leading middleweights. He handled the opponent Matchroom placed in front of him and showed more discipline than in earlier fights. The next test needs to come against a physically comparable middleweight who has not already been through a punishing loss.

Sports.title: Eridson Garcia Exposes Alan Chaves in Newark
Sports.content:
Garcia floored Chaves in the second round and nearly put him down again in round four. Things grew worse in the fifth, when Chaves took a knee before hitting the canvas again moments later. In the ninth, Chaves went down again after eating a left from Garcia.

The referee Albert Earn Brown looked like he was ready to stop the contest after Chaves was dropped in round nine. By that stage, the fight had become less about who would win and more about whether Chaves would survive the full 10 rounds. You got to give Chaves credit for being a warrior to toughen it out, but there are no words to describe how one-sided this fight was. Chaves looked like he didn’t belong in the same ring with Eridson. The size advantage Eridson had was noticeable. He looked like he’d rehydrated to a welterweight, and appeared considerably bigger than Chavez.

Matchroom’s Lightweight Plans Take a Hit

Chaves was completely out of his league against a 32-year-old opponent brought in to test him. Garcia was quicker, smarter, and far more comfortable during every phase of the fight. Hearn recently signed Chaves to Matchroom and regarded him as a future lightweight star, but this performance exposed how far he is from competing with the division’s better fighters.

The result makes retaining Andy Cruz even more important for Hearn. Matchroom has spent time and money developing Cruz, yet the Cuban is unhappy with the promotion and has discussed becoming a free agent. Watching Chaves fall apart against Garcia should erase any thought that Matchroom can afford to lose its best lightweight.

Cruz would likely have cleaned Eridson out tonight. His timing, footwork, defensive awareness, and ability to read a southpaw would have made this a completely different fight. Chaves had none of those answers, and Eridson made him pay for it from the first bell to the last.

Sports.title: Canelo Alvarez Takes Spain Route Before Christian Mbilli Fight
Sports.content:
The change follows Canelo’s uncomfortable experience against William Scull in May 2025. That bout began around 6 a.m. in Riyadh so it could air during prime viewing hours in North America. He arrived three weeks early, but preparing to fight near sunrise still forced his body through an unnatural schedule.

Reports describing an eight-week stay in Spain followed by another week in Riyadh do not fit the calendar. September 5 to October 31 is exactly eight weeks. The more logical interpretation is that Canelo will spend close to seven weeks in Gandía before completing the final week in Saudi Arabia.

Spain changes its clocks on October 25, creating a two-hour difference from Riyadh during fight week. For most of camp, that difference will be only one hour.

Oleksandr Usyk reportedly invited Canelo to use his training base in Gandía. That does not necessarily mean the two will spar or follow the same program, but Usyk’s camp offers the controlled setting Canelo wants for a fight carrying substantial physical risk.

“He’s a strong rival. He throws a lot of punches. He’s a very strong person. That’s what I like, being in there. He throws a lot of punches, and I really like that,” Canelo told Box Azteca.

Canelo Returns As The Challenger

His position has also changed. The unanimous decision loss to Terence Crawford in September 2025 cost Canelo the undisputed super middleweight championship and led to elbow surgery. He now returns as the challenger, trying to take the WBC belt from Mbilli.

That role may give him more urgency than he showed during the later years of his championship reign. Canelo controlled opponent selection, pace, and most of the commercial terms for more than a decade. This time, his reputation will not be enough if a younger champion is throwing twice as often and taking rounds through work rate.

Mbilli’s pressure should give Canelo more countering opportunities than Scull provided, but it will also test the 36-year-old’s conditioning. With age, Canelo has become increasingly economical, often conserving energy while waiting for isolated power shots. The champion keeps punching after the first exchange and is willing to absorb clean shots to maintain his attack.

Mbilli’s Pressure Creates Openings

That aggression carries defensive costs. While throwing hooks, Mbilli sometimes leans forward, lowers his head, and squares his shoulders. Canelo’s right uppercut is built to punish an opponent entering in that posture. The problem is finding enough room to generate force before the champion crowds him against the ropes.

A similar risk accompanies the body attack. Mbilli will remain close enough for Canelo to target the ribs instead of chasing a mobile opponent across the ring. Every committed shot downstairs, however, leaves him exposed to hooks and overhand punches coming back.

Trust in the repaired elbow will also be essential. Canelo’s right hand does not need to stop Mbilli immediately, but it must carry enough force to interrupt his entries. Any reluctance to release it at full speed would encourage the champion to attack without respecting the return fire.

“I really feel very good. I feel very good in the gym. I was thinking yesterday that in two or three weeks I’d be ready. We still have eight or nine weeks left, and I feel very good,” Canelo said during the same Box Azteca interview.

The scoring may depend on the contrast between Mbilli’s quantity and Canelo’s accuracy. Many of the champion’s punches strike gloves, arms, and shoulders, but sustained output can control how a round looks from ringside. Canelo favors clean, visible power punches separated by long periods of inactivity.

If Mbilli throws two or three punches for every one coming back, a handful of sharp counters may not automatically carry each round for Canelo. Judges may favor the fighter forcing the action, especially if the challenger spends extended stretches covering up against the ropes.

The Spanish camp removes the body clock problem that complicated Canelo’s first Saudi appearance. It cannot restore his younger reflexes or erase the effects of surgery and inactivity. He still owns the cleaner counters, but must land them often enough to prevent Mbilli from turning the fight into a twelve-round argument over quality against quantity.

Ghana News.title: ‘My Police, Your Police, Our Police’: the Aboso fire and a lesson in Policing together
Ghana News.content:
Boldly written on the fence wall of the Joint Operation Centre (JOC) within the premises of the Ghana Police Service Headquarters is a simple but profound inscription: “My Police, Your Police, Our Police, let’s make it better.”

For anyone passing by, it may appear to be an ordinary inscription on a wall.

But beneath those few words lies a powerful truth about policing — the Police belong to the people, serve the people and, ultimately, cannot protect the people without their support.

The Police cannot protect the public without the public. And the public cannot enjoy lasting peace, security and stability without the Police.

Aboso fire incident

That truth came alive in Aboso in the Western Region on August 26, 2026.

As flames engulfed some shops at the Aboso Main Lorry Station, destroying property and threatening lives, Inspector Hance Atubra of the Tarkwa Divisional Headquarters was the first Police officer to arrive at the scene.

He did not stand by and watch. He immediately moved into action, helping people trapped in the affected area and evacuating victims to safety.

In doing so, he demonstrated what the Police uniform should represent — courage, sacrifice and an unwavering commitment to protecting life and property.

The people saw it. And they responded.

Public appreciation

In an extraordinary display of appreciation, members of the public carried Inspector Atubra shoulder-high and sang his praises, celebrating the officer who had risked his own safety to save theirs.

That spontaneous act by the public should not be dismissed as a mere emotional reaction.

It was a powerful statement: when Police officers protect us, we must stand with them.

And the Police Administration responded swiftly.

In less than 24 hours, the Inspector-General of Police (IGP), Mr Christian Tetteh Yohuno, promoted Inspector Atubra to the rank of Chief Inspector in recognition of his courage, quick response and efforts to save life and property.

It was later followed with a decoration at the National Police Headquarters in Accra.

That was more than a promotion. It was a message to the Ghana Police Service that good work will be recognised and rewarded.

But it should also be a message to the public. If we want a Police Service that is courageous, responsive and committed, then we must give officers the support and cooperation they need to do their work.

Citizens must stop treating the Police as an institution to be remembered only when trouble comes.

When criminals strike, we call the Police.

When our property is threatened, we call the Police.

When our lives are in danger, we expect the Police to come running.

But when Police officers are performing their duties, some members of the public turn against them, obstruct their work or, even worse, attack them. This must stop.

There is no justification for attacking a Police officer who is lawfully performing his or her duty.

If an officer acts improperly, there are lawful avenues for redress. Complaints can be made. Conduct can be challenged.

Accountability can and must be demanded.

But violence against Police officers cannot be the answer.

Ghanaians must understand that every attack on a Police officer is an attack on public safety itself.

When officers are assaulted, their authority is undermined. When they are prevented from performing their duties, criminals are emboldened. When attacks become normalised, respect for law and order begins to collapse.

And when law and order collapses, everybody suffers.

The businessman, the farmer, the student, the trader, the driver, the professional and the ordinary family at home — all depend on a functioning security system.

We, therefore, cannot demand security from the Police with one hand and undermine their authority with the other.

We cannot ask the Police to run into danger for us and then turn around and attack them for doing their job.

The public must become active partners in policing.

Give the Police credible information. Cooperate with investigations. Help officers when they need assistance. Respect lawful instructions.

Report suspicious activity. Stand up for officers who are doing the right thing. And when there are genuine concerns about police conduct, use the appropriate channels to demand accountability.

That is what responsible citizenship requires.

Our elders say, “As you advise the cat, you must advise the salted fish as well.”

The Police must also earn and preserve the public's trust.

Officers must remain professional, disciplined, respectful and faithful to the law.

IGP Yohuno's approach

That is why the approach of IGP Yohuno deserves commendation.

His leadership is showing that the Police Administration can both reward exceptional service and punish misconduct.

Officers who distinguish themselves through courage and dedication are being recognised, including through special promotions, while those who violate the law or breach professional standards are being disciplined.

That balance is essential. It tells the good officer: your sacrifice matters.

It tells the erring officer: your uniform is not a licence to break the law.

And it tells the public: this is your Police Service, and it must be supported while being held accountable.

Inspector Atubra's experience is therefore bigger than one fire incident.

The residents of Aboso showed what public appreciation can look like when citizens recognise a Police officer who has served them well.

The IGP showed what institutional appreciation can look like by rewarding that officer within hours.

Now the rest of the country must show what public support for policing can look like.

Let us stop attacking those who protect us.

Let us stop treating Police officers as enemies.

Let us stop cheering when officers are humiliated or assaulted.

Instead, let us support officers who are doing their work diligently, cooperate with them and demand accountability through lawful means when necessary.

The Police have a duty to protect Ghana.

We, the public, have a duty to help them do it.

The inscription on the JOC wall should therefore be more than words.

Perhaps the real question is not whether we have a Police Service. We do.

The question is whether all of us — Police and public alike — are prepared to make it better.

The answer must be emphatic yes.

Because after all, it is my Police, Your Police and everyone's Police.
