World.title: A month after migrants surged into Ceuta, thousands of kids are still stranded on the streets
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

"I'm back on the street," 17-year-old Ikram wrote in a text message to CBC on Monday.

For a brief period, Ikram had felt relief in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. After spending almost a month sleeping in a forest, an abandoned bathhouse and on the street, the young Moroccan had finally found somewhere to stay. For three days, a family had hosted her as she helped look after their young children.

Then the work ran out.

Ikram left the Moroccan coastal town of Fnideq at the end of July, when an estimated 80,000 Moroccans and migrants from countries further south travelled to the north, hoping to cross into Ceuta. For many, the Spanish territory represents a possible route toward legal residency in Europe.

"In Morocco we are living, but not living the life we want," she said. Her father works as a tailor but earns little.

Most of the migrants who arrived during the July surge returned to Morocco within hours. But Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said 5,000 remain in Ceuta. Local authorities estimate 9,000 remain in and around the small enclave, whose population is roughly 80,000.

Among those who remain are hundreds of unaccompanied minors, including Ikram, living in extremely vulnerable conditions.

Ikram looks out toward the sea as she stands on a bridge in Ceuta near the border checkpoint through which migrants enter the city. (Marouane Beslem/CBC)

Many minors under 13, Spain says

According to Jennifer Zuppiroli, a migration specialist at Save the Children Spain, the Spanish Ministry of the Interior has registered 2,500 "children and adolescents" in Ceuta so far.

The actual number could be considerably higher.

"Various social and neighborhood organizations estimate that there could still be thousands of minors awaiting identification and referral to protection services," Zuppiroli told CBC News. Spain's Minister for Youth and Children, Sira Rego, said many of the minors are under the age of 13 and that around 700 of the migrant minors were girls.

WATCH | The humanitarian challenge in Ceuta: Ceuta faces humanitarian challenge after surge of migrants | Duration 2:06 Roughly 2,000 migrants are left in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after 70,000 surged into the autonomous city last week, leaving humanitarian organizations stretched to their limits.

Most of the children and adolescents in Ceuta are from Morocco, Zuppiroli says, although minors from other countries are also there, particularly from sub-Saharan Africa, including Sudan.

(CBC is not using the last names of the migrants in this story because they fear deportation and reprisals from locals. For this reason, CBC is also not showing the faces of some of the migrants.)

Rego has reiterated that family reunification is the priority while acknowledging that "in most cases, there is no possibility of return." Under international law, the removal of unaccompanied minors is subject to strict safeguards, including the requirement to consider the child's best interests.

Ikram had tried to reach Ceuta alone during a previous mass crossing attempt in 2024. This time, however, she hadn't actually planned to go.

"My mom told me in the morning that people were crossing. Then, on my way to work, I met a friend who told me to go. I told her, 'No, I have a job.' She said, 'Let's just go and see.' And then I said, 'OK, let's go,' and we went."

At the border, they were confronted with a scene of chaos, with hundreds of people trying to swim around the border fence.

"We saw so many dead people," Ikram said. "Still I said, let me try my luck, and I went in. I almost died, too. I kept crying, and then I couldn't go on anymore."

One boy helped keep her afloat. "He kept pushing me, pushing me until I reached the shore."

When Ikram eventually reached the beach, she fainted and was taken to hospital. She was released the following day.

Her 15-year-old brother, Marwan, had crossed the land border earlier that day but left shortly afterward.

"He couldn't handle it," Ikram said, referring to the dire situation for migrants in Ceuta.

A scene from a recent protest against migrants in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. (Marouane Beslem/CBC)

Ikram, however, insists she'll stay in Ceuta despite not having a place in any official accommodation or child-protection facility.

"I wish to build my future abroad, so I can help my mom and dad," she said. "Because right now, they're the ones counting on me."

For unaccompanied minors, Ceuta is 'a war zone'

Khadija Toufik, a French independent journalist who has reported for France Télévisions and TV5Monde, has seen how many minors are on the streets of Ceuta.

"They sleep alone outside," she said. "Every night is a night of terror, as soldiers come to wake them up, and very often, they are beaten with batons. Most of the minors I encountered in the streets were scarred and injured. For them, this is a war zone."

This vulnerability extends beyond unaccompanied minors. Some parents who have arrived in Ceuta with their children have also found themselves without stable shelter.

A man named Anouar crossed with his nine-year-old son, Wael, leaving his wife and three other children behind in Morocco. Since arriving, he and his son have moved between the streets and the homes of people who occasionally offer them a place to sleep, charge their phones or take a shower.

Anouar, left, came to Ceuta with his nine-year-old son, Wael. (Marouane Beslem/CBC)

Meanwhile, tensions on the streets of Ceuta have escalated in recent weeks.

"There has been a rise in demonstrations by fascists calling for attacks against migrants," Toufik said. Last week , dozens of residents blocked Red Cross workers from distributing food and water to migrants. Later, fires were set at migrant encampments on a beach.

The unrest came after the arrest of 12 migrants accused of throwing stones at a military vehicle, smashing its windows and injuring four people inside.

'The soldier hit me with a stick'

A 17-year-old named Abdo told CBC News that about three weeks ago, some 30 Spanish soldiers used violence to force him and other migrants out of an abandoned hospital where they had been sleeping.

"The soldier hit me with a stick. He broke my phone and my power bank," Abdo said in a video call with CBC News. He held up his hand, which was in a cast.

Medical volunteers with No Name Kitchen (NNK), a humanitarian organization established in Ceuta, treated Abdo's injured hand.

Ric Fernández, co-ordinator of NNK, says the group has collected more than 150 testimonies from migrants reporting violence by "uniformed agents, from the National Police, the military or civilians in disguise."

Seventeen-year-old Abdo, who did not want his face to be shown in this photo, told CBC News that about three weeks ago, Spanish soldiers used violence to force him and other migrants out of an abandoned hospital where they had been sleeping. His arm is now in a cast. (Marouane Beslem/CBC)

Abdo has been in Ceuta for more than a month. It was his ninth attempt to reach Europe.

In the previous two years, he had tried crossing the Mediterranean by boat, by hiding inside a truck on a ferry bound for Spain and by trying to enter through Melilla, Spain's other North African exclave.

"In Morocco, there aren't opportunities to work," he said. Youth unemployment in Morocco is around 36 per cent, according to the pan-African research institution Afrobarometer.

Abdo's father, a taxi driver, died in a car accident 10 years ago. His mother, who has five children and suffers from a uterine condition, is unable to work. His sister has a master's degree in law but has also been unable to find employment.

This year, Abdo completed Morocco's baccalaureate, a national qualification students can get at the end of high school, and says he was among the three top students at his school. He dreams of becoming a writer or journalist.

In the meantime, his main preoccupation is finding a safe place to sleep.

Abdo's friend l'Fassi looks out from a bridge in Ceuta at lights back in Morocco. Ceuta is one of two autonomous Spanish territories, along with Melilla, that has a land border between Africa and the EU. (Marouane Beslem/CBC)

For the past three days, Toufik, who helps minors wherever she can, has arranged temporary accommodation for Abdo and another migrant in a hotel room. But with hotel prices rising, they will soon have to leave.

As for Ikram, she has become friends with an 18-year-old named Hasna, also from Morocco.

Members of NNK informed Ikram and Hasna they had received notice that a local organization had set up a safe camp for girls. The two told CBC News they walked together through the night looking for the camp but eventually decided it was safer to wait in a park.

"Honestly, we are scared, but it's night. We'll go in early in the morning."

The next day, Ikram was accepted into the camp. Hasna, who is not a minor, was not — and is still living on the streets of Ceuta.

World.title: Toronto orders Live Nation Canada to repair Rogers Stadium after 'significant damage'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The City of Toronto has issued an 'unsafe building' order to Live Nation Canada about the state of Rogers Stadium after the concert venue was damaged by Wednesday's storm. As CBC's Christian D'avino explains, a sold-out concert by heavy metal band AC/DC is scheduled for Sept. 16. The show has not been cancelled or rescheduled.

Rogers Stadium was seriously damaged by GTA storm. What happens now?

The City of Toronto has issued an "order to remedy unsafe building" to Live Nation Canada about the state of Rogers Stadium after the concert venue was damaged by Wednesday's storm.

The order was issued Thursday after the city inspected the open-air venue in North York that seats 50,000 people.

A sold out concert by AC/DC is scheduled to take place at the stadium, located on the former Downsview Airport lands, on Sept. 16. The show has not been cancelled or rescheduled.

Live Nation Canada, which operates the venue, said late Wednesday that no one was injured by the extreme weather but Rogers Stadium sustained "significant damage."

"Our teams are continuing to assess the extent of the damage. We will provide more information as it becomes available," a spokesperson for Live Nation Canada said in an email on Friday.

'They may not be able to get AC/DC in': councillor

Coun. James Pasternak, who represents York Centre, said safety must be guaranteed before any crowds can return.

"This stadium collapsed in a major storm event, and the question is, can they reconstruct it and repair it so that it's satisfactory, so that it's safe," he said. "They may not be able to get AC/DC in this year."

Drone photos of the stadium show bright blue bleachers crumpled and strewn across grandstands that appear to have partially collapsed.

WATCH | Rogers Stadium seriously damaged by GTA storm: Rogers Stadium seriously damaged by GTA storm | Duration 0:39 The storm left some serious damage to Rogers Stadium, a 50,000-capacity music venue in the city's north end. Live Nation said no one was injured and they are assessing the extent of the damage.

According to the order, Live Nation Canada must take immediate steps to secure the site, hire an engineer and repair the damage.

The order describes the damage in detail, saying it included "collapsed sections of the north stadium structure, damaged seating areas, and distorted, displaced, or otherwise compromised structural framing associated with various temporary structures.

"In addition, other structures and equipment within the stadium grounds were impacted by high winds, including overturned viewing stations, tents, and shipping containers."

The order goes on to say the damage "may pose a risk to the health and safety of persons" due to structural elements that are displaced and the potential for the structure to be unstable.

The city has ordered Live Nation Canada to:

Prevent access to all damaged structures, temporary structures, and areas affected by the storm.

Hire a licensed professional engineer to assess all structures, including seating areas, affected by the storm, identify unsafe areas and determine the measures to be taken to address those areas.

Prepare a report by Sept. 8 identifying the damage, measures to be taken and a schedule for the work.

Carry out the necessary repairs identified by the engineer.

Submit another report by Sept. 11 confirming the status of the repairs to be taken and "whether the affected structures are safe and structurally adequate for their intended use and occupancy."

Australian rock band AC/DC perform on stage during their PowerUp Tour 2024 at the VELTINS-Arena in Gelsenkirchen, western Germany on May 17, 2024. (Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty Images)

For at least one fan, however, there is still hope that the show will go on.

Miguel Avila, 61, a Toronto resident, said his tickets for the Sept. 16 show are in the grandstands and he is following the situation closely.

'We all love AC/DC and we're willing to wait'

Avila said he hasn't tried to get a refund yet. If the stadium is deemed not ready for the concert, he said that will not be a problem for him.

"We all love AC/DC and we're willing to wait. If the organizers decide to rebuild it, reconstruct it, we're willing to wait."

But he said the damage does raise concerns.

"It open up questions about the way it was constructed," he said.

Avila said he started listening to AC/DC when he was a teenager and hopes to see the band perform.

"I was really excited but I'm patient," he said. "Let's see what happens."

World.title: Rescuers in Nepal pull 2 people alive from the debris 10 days after devastating floods
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Rescuers in Nepal pulled out a Chinese man and a woman in separate operations on Saturday, 10 days after devastating floods hit the country, as teams continued searching for thousands of missing people.

The man was rescued from a hydropower tunnel, according to a social media post by the country's prime minister's office, bringing the total to three workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project. Two Nepalese workers were rescued on Friday.

Nepal's army said a joint rescue team of Nepalese military personnel and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre tunnel and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Images showed him being evacuated by helicopter, with an army medic checking on him during the flight.

A photo released by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed two rescuers carrying the man out of the tunnel.

CCTV shared audio of the man talking to an officer, saying how he repeatedly shouted whenever he saw the rescue crews' lights, but they could not hear him.

"When they rescued me today, when they shone [the light] before my eyes, I couldn't believe it," he said.

The man was taken to hospital and was in stable condition, according to CCTV.

Rescue efforts have increasingly focused on 12 hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects, hoping to find survivors.

WATCH | 2 Nepalese workers rescued on Friday: 2 workers rescued from buried Nepal tunnel | Duration 1:54 Two workers were rescued from a hydroelectric tunnel nine days after devastating flash floods in Nepal. Nearly 5,000 are still missing, including 29 Canadians.

In flood-hit Nuwakot town, a woman was rescued alive from a house, Nepal's army spokesperson said Saturday. Officials said she was airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment.

Images released by Nepal's army showed rescuers finding the woman covered in mud inside the damaged house. They gave her bottled water before pulling her to safety, wrapped in a grey blanket.

At least 1,300 people were killed in the Aug. 26 floods, which were likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.

World.title: After 12 years of fried chicken and flirting, hit YouTube series Chicken Shop Date to end
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After more than a decade of interviewing and flirting with movie stars, musicians and athletes while sharing some fried chicken, Amelia Dimoldenberg, the host of the popular YouTube talk show Chicken Shop Date, announced this week she's closing up shop.

"To me the show is my very own romcom and I have loved creating so many stories for you to watch. I am so grateful to everyone who has followed me on this journey and found some joy in these episodes," Dimoldenberg wrote in an Instagram post on Thursday.

"I never thought I'd stop Chicken Shop Date, I thought maybe it would be a part of me forever, and in some way it always will, but I feel like it's now time to move on from this adventure and onto a new one."

Dimoldenberg started the show 12 years ago, interviewing musicians in Britain's underground rap scene. Since then, she's gone on to chat with celebs, including Keke Palmer, Conan O'Brien, Paul McCartney and Jack Harlow and garnered close to 3.5 million subscribers to her YouTube channel.

WATCH | Her interview with Jack Harlow:

Chicken Shop Date follows a simple format: Dimoldenberg goes on a date of sorts with a celebrity at a fried chicken shop in London and asks them a blend of questions that are flirty, funny and sometimes awkward.

It produces the type of banter you'd more likely expect on a first date than a typical sit-down, talk show style interview. In some cases, like her 2024 sit-down with Andrew Garfield, it's led to what seemed to be some actual flirting.

"This is called flirting, Amelia, this is called flirting," Garfield says at one point.

WATCH | Her Andrew Garfield interview:

Dimoldenberg also has some Canadians among her dozens of interviews. That includes Ryan Reynolds, whom Dimoldenberg corrects when he gives the wrong name for the character his wife Blake Lively played on Gossip Girl.

"That is right, Brooke from Gossip Girl loves you," Reynolds tells Dimoldberg, hinting at Lively's fandom of her show. At that point, Dimoldenberg points out Lively's character was named Serena.

"I don't think there is a Brooke," Dimoldenberg says.

WATCH | Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman on the show:

Shania Twain also sat down for a date with Dimoldenberg in 2023, where Twain revealed that she'd never actually met Brad Pitt (despite mentioning him in her hit song That Don't Impress Me Much).

WATCH | Shania Twain on the show:

The massive success of her YouTube channel has led to opportunities for Dimoldenberg outside the chicken shop, including working the red carpet at the Oscars this year, where she interviewed another Canadian, Hudson Williams.

WATCH | Dimoldenberg interviews Hudson Williams at 2026 Academy Awards:

It's unclear what Dimoldenberg's next move is after Chicken Shop Date, but it appears she has some irons in the fire. She's currently signed on to develop a young adult drama series for the BBC, according to Deadline.

But in her goodbye post on Instagram, Dimoldenberg also promised "a few final dates" before ending the show for good.

Article content

If the prime minister is not successfully contradicted, as I wrote here last week, it will be a challenging time but a great opportunity to strengthen the Canadian nationality. If we really have been provoked into a commercial war, it will be time for Canada to shed the somewhat hackneyed image of the upright, red-coated Mountie portrayed by Nelson Eddy in the famous 1954 film Rosemarie, (where someone purporting to be Québec Premier Maurice Duplessis makes a cameo appearance), and resort to further unsportsmanlike measures. We should make cooperative arrangements with some of the Commonwealth Caribbean countries and actively entice winter migrants from Florida and other temperate U.S. states. More piquant and an undoubted public service to the United States would be to provide heavy funding for authentic American legal aid charities and clog American courts and reduce the obscene 98 per cent conviction rates in American criminal courts, 95 per cent of those without a trial. The United States today has four percent of the world’s population and about 25 per cent of its incarcerated people; many Americans would thank us for helping to relieve “the sweet land of liberty” of this shame and hypocrisy. These are areas where it would be hard for the United States to retaliate-both sides can keep raising tariffs if they want but it is unlikely to achieve very much, although we could eventually manufacture much more for ourselves and take over the U.S. part of our automobile industry.
