World.title: Baja California Sur, Nuevo León and Querétaro lead new foreign investment in first half of 2026
World.content:
Baja California Sur, Nuevo León, and Querétaro emerged as the top destinations for new foreign investment in Mexico during the first half of 2026, even as new foreign investment in the country slowed overall.

According to new data from the Economy Ministry (SE), Mexico received US $2.7 billion in new investments from January to June — one of the three components of foreign direct investment (FDI) — down 13.4% compared to the same period in 2025. At the same time, total FDI grew as established ventures reinvested profits.

However, three entities maintained investor confidence.

Baja California Sur topped the list with US $524 million of new FDI, followed by Nuevo León with $473 million, and Querétaro with $410 million. Together, these three states accounted for nearly half of the funds allocated to new projects.

Baja California Sur’s tourism industry pushed it to the top of the list. In the first half of 2026, over 95% of the state’s total FDI was new investment. Of that new investment, over 97% ($511.9 million) went toward lodging services including guesthouses, boarding houses and furnished apartments with hotel services.

Meanwhile, Nuevo León registered a 190.1% annual growth in new FDI. The capital was concentrated in wholesale trade of trucks and auto parts, vehicle manufacturing and the iron and steel industries.

The result reflects the state’s importance as a manufacturing, logistics and automotive hub, favored for its proximity to the U.S. market and the integration of its suppliers into global supply chains.

Finally, Querétaro saw a 158.6% increase in new capital investment after receiving a boost of US $410 million. The main sectors receiving this investment include electricity generation and supply, confectionery, auto parts, and electronic components — sectors that confirm the state’s industrial diversification and its importance within the Bajío economic corridor.

These three states were followed by Jalisco, Quintana Roo, Nayarit, Chihuahua, Baja California, Puebla and Guanajuato, which received between US $100 million to $300 million in new capital investment apiece.

In contrast, Tlaxcala — the smallest state in Mexico — was the only state that saw no foreign investment.

Meanwhile, México state, Zacatecas, Sonora, Aguascalientes and Mexico City registered capital outflows.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: Marie, now a Category 2 hurricane, brings rain and flooding to Baja California Sur and the Pacific coast
World.content:
Rapidly intensifying Hurricane Marie reached Category 2 status off the coast of Baja California Sur on Friday, closing ports and suspending classes across the state.

A 10 a.m. social media post from the National Meteorological Service (SMN) said Marie was located 885 kilometers west-southwest of Cabo San Lucas, at the southern tip of the Baja Peninsula.

“It has maximum sustained winds of 155 km/h, gusts of 195 km/h and is moving west-northwest at 15 km/h,” the National Water Commission (Conagua) reported.

A Tropical Cyclone Advisory was issued by the SMN which forecast intense localized rains for the northwestern coast of Mexico, including the states of Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima and Michoacán to the south of BCS.

Civil protection authorities urged the public to take extreme precautions and heed the recommendations issued by the authorities of the National Civil Protection System.

Navigation is also severely restricted due to the extreme weather conditions. Maritime authorities have closed ports to small vessels in San José del Cabo and Magdalena Bay.

High waves are another risk factor along the western coastline, with waves of 1.5 to 2.5 meters (5-8 feet) in height forecast for the peninsula.

Conagua said Marie’s main threat is the extensive cloud bands which increase the likelihood of heavy rainfall and could cause more flooding in vulnerable coastal areas. This prompted BCS Governor Víctor Manuel Castro to suspend all school activities in the municipality of Los Cabos.

Cabo San Lucas was battered by high winds and heavy rain on Wednesday while Marie was still a tropical storm.

Legendary rock musician Sammy Hagar — owner of the resort city’s famous Cabo Wabo Cantina — said in an Instagram post that the storm caused a great deal of damage, asking his fans to pray for his club and the city.

In a Thursday Instagram post, Hagar praised the authorities for their quick reaction to the flooding.

“Cabo to the rescue,” he wrote. “Congratulations to the community for pulling the cleanup crew together so quickly.”

Hurricane Marie — along with the Mexican monsoon, low-pressure troughs, cyclonic circulations at high levels of the atmosphere and Tropical Wave Number 36 in southern and western Mexico — was also forecast to generate intense rains in Veracruz, Oaxaca, Chiapas and Tabasco on Friday.

Conagua said Marie is expected to weaken to a Category 1 storm on Saturday as it moves further out to sea.

Though it could soon thereafter be downgraded to a tropical storm, atmospheric instability is likely to continue interacting with low-pressure troughs in the interior of the country into next week.

With reports from Informador, El Universal and N+

World.title: Defense minister responds to US anti-drone border operations: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📉 Zacatecas homicides down 85%: National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported an average of 0.17 homicides per day in Zacatecas in August, an 85% reduction compared to September 2024, the final month of the López Obrador administration. The 2026 daily average is down 96% versus 2021.

The 2026 daily average is down 96% versus 2021. 🚔 Thousands arrested since Sheinbaum took office: Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 3,824 people were arrested in Zacatecas between October 2024 and August 2026 for high-impact crimes. He said that 1,240 firearms and 7.3 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period, while six meth labs were dismantled.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 3,824 people were arrested in Zacatecas between October 2024 and August 2026 for high-impact crimes. He said that 1,240 firearms and 7.3 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period, while six meth labs were dismantled. 💰 Atizapán killings tied to money demand: García Harfuch said one of two men arrested over the multiple homicide in México state had a “commercial relationship” with victim Jonathan Meléndez and had been demanding money from him before the killings.

García Harfuch said one of two men arrested over the multiple homicide in México state had a “commercial relationship” with victim Jonathan Meléndez and had been demanding money from him before the killings. 🇲🇽🇺🇸 Defense minister addresses cartel drone reports: Responding to a Fox News report on U.S. operations against cartel drones at the border, Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said the drones are mostly used by migrant smugglers to scout routes free of authorities. He didn’t confirm or deny Mexican military involvement in the U.S. takedown operations.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Guadalupe, a municipality that is part of the metropolitan area of Zacatecas city.

She was accompanied by Zacatecas Governor David Monreal and various members of her cabinet, including Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez and Security Minister Omar García Harfuch.

Among Mexico’s 32 federal entities, Zacatecas has recorded one of the largest reductions in homicides this year.

At today’s mañanera, officials presented the latest security data for the state — statistics that allowed them to portray Zacatecas as an example of the success of the federal government’s national security strategy.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was García Harfuch’s remarks about the motive for a multiple homicide in México state.

Government reports 85% decline in homicides in Zacatecas

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported that there was an average of 0.17 homicides per day in Zacatecas in August, a reduction of 85% compared to September 2024, the final month of Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s presidency.

She said that the daily homicide rate so far this year is 0.2, a reduction of 50% compared to 2025.

Figueroa highlighted that the daily homicide rate in 2026 is down 96% compared to 2021, when an average of 4.5 murders per day were committed in Zacatecas.

In the first seven months of 2026, there were 51 homicides in Zacatecas, the eighth lowest total among Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

More than 3,800 arrests in Zacatecas since October 2024

According to data presented by García Harfuch, 3,824 people were arrested in Zacatecas between Oct. 1, 2024 — the date Sheinbaum was sworn in as president — and Aug. 31, 2026, for allegedly committing high-impact crimes such as homicide, kidnapping, extortion and violent robbery.

He also reported that 1,240 firearms and 7.3 tonnes of drugs were seized in the state in the same period. In addition, authorities dismantled six clandestine methamphetamine labs in Zacatecas, García Harfuch said.

photo-harfuch

He acknowledged that “there is still a lot to be done” to improve security in Zacatecas, noting that rival criminal groups continue to fight turf wars in the state. García Harfuch said that federal authorities are “maintaining and strengthening” intelligence and investigation “actions” in the state as well as “territorial presence” and “coordination” with state and municipal authorities. The aim, he said, is to detain “generators of violence” in Zacatecas.

García Harfuch subsequently noted that three people were arrested in connection with a car bomb explosion outside a municipal police station in Ojocaliente, Zacatecas, last Sunday night.

García Harfuch: Multiple homicide in México state related to a demand for money

García Harfuch said that one of two men arrested in connection with a multiple homicide in México state this week had a “commercial relationship” with one of the victims, namely Jonathan Meléndez, keyboard player with the well-known band Camilo Séptimo. The security minister was referring to Diego Sebastián Rosen Ferlini, an Argentine national who was detained in connection with the murders of Mélendez, his pregnant wife, their three-year-old daughter and a domestic worker. The victims were found dead in an apartment in the municipality of Atizapán de Zaragoza late Tuesday.

Asked how much money the alleged murderer was demanding from Mélendez, García Harfuch responded:

“I don’t know but I’ll ask the [México state] Attorney General’s Office. What is a fact is that he was demanding money. There was a demand, there were certain threats and this terrible multiple homicide was committed.”

Defense minister: People smugglers use drones to locate routes that are ‘free’ of US authorities

A reporter asked the president whether she could confirm the “participation” of Mexican authorities in U.S. operations to take down suspected cartel drones at the Mexico-U.S. border.

His question was related to a Fox News report that was published on Thursday.

Citing a senior U.S. War Department official, Fox reported that the U.S. military “took down ‘approximately 100′ suspected cartel drones in August alone” at the United States’ southern border.

Citing the same official, Fox wrote that “each operation was planned and closely coordinated with the Mexican military and border authorities to prevent interference or unintended conflicts between forces operating on either side of the border.”

Operation Ardent Vanguard Update 11 cartel drones defeated by the Army’s Multipurpose High Energy Laser as of Sep. 4. More than 300 defeats using kinetic and non-kinetic systems this year, with more than 100 occurring in August. “JTF Southern Border’s combined arms approach… pic.twitter.com/KexEOvgM9D — U.S. Northern Command (@USNorthernCmd) September 4, 2026

Sheinbaum referred the reporter’s question to her defense minister.

“Firstly I want to highlight that the relationship with the armed forces of the United States has been very good, very positive,” Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said.

He said that U.S. authorities have informed the Mexican government that drones are mainly used in the border region by people who smuggle migrants into the United States.

“They are commercial drones. They only capture images … and what they’re seeking to find are routes that are free, where there is no presence of [U.S.] authorities,” Trevilla said.

The defense minister didn’t confirm or deny Fox’s reporting that the Mexican military was involved in the planning of U.S. operations to take down drones.

World.title: ‘Sexy and hot, like Mexico’: How Mexican beauty brand AORA is taking on the global market
World.content:
Pyramid-inspired palettes, bilingual packaging and vivid shades drawn from Mexico’s streets are just some of the hallmarks of AORA, a Mexican beauty brand that’s challenging the beauty industry with its plastic-free packaging and strong Mexican identity.

“We wanted to bottle the feeling of Mexico,” co-founder Rodrigo Peñafiel told Mexico News Daily. “We wanted to bottle that feeling you get when you visit a beach in Oaxaca; that feeling you experience when you visit Mexico City for the first time.”

Since the opening of its flagship store in Mexico City in 2022, the brand has expanded into major retail chains, landed collaborations with international celebrities including Sofía Vergara, and most recently, served as one of the makeup brands used during Bad Bunny’s 2026 Super Bowl halftime show.

International expansion, however, didn’t come as a surprise. For Peñafiel and his co-founder Nour Tayara, going global was always part of the plan.

“Why would we build a small local brand when we have the opportunity to bring something big into the world?” Peñafiel said.

Combining Tayara’s experience in marketing and innovation roles within L’Oréal with Peñafiel’s background in public relations, the pair set out to create a brand that offered more than just clean, high-quality products. They wanted to create a luxury product with a strong focus on identity.

“We do luxury makeup by working with the best factories in the world. Because if we want to compete, let’s compete with spectacular quality. But what we’re bringing — we’re bringing culture,” Tayara said.

The brand’s DNA: Mexico

Rather than downplaying AORA’s Mexican identity to appeal to international consumers, the founders have made it central to the brand, drawing inspiration from the country’s creativity, colors, architecture and connection to nature.

From the brand’s signature Mírame Eyeshadow Palette to their lipsticks, pencils and accessories, AORA’s products evoke Mexico’s cultural icons, historic landmarks and scenes from everyday life.

“In our palette, you can see a hint of Frida Kahlo, of Matías Goeritz, of Chichén Itzá,” Peñafiel said. “The shades inside our palette could evoke any street in Mexico with a yellow house and a green Volkswagen parked outside,” he added with a chuckle.

Launching the brand from Mexico also meant producing its marketing campaigns in the country. From their photoshoots to their male and female models, everything is done in Mexico with Mexican talent.

“Every detail about the brand reflects Mexico. We could not have created this brand if we hadn’t launched it here,” Tayara remarked.

A retail presence at Sephora

AORA’s authentic vision has propelled the company into a new growth stage after entering Sephora in the United States, making history as the first 100% plastic-free beauty brand sold at the retailer, and the first brand to use both Spanish and English on its packaging.

“Sephora is betting on a brand that’s very colorful from Mexico and is betting on its first plastic-free brand in its portfolio,” Tayara pointed out.

In a competitive market dominated by European and U.S. brands, AORA is disrupting the beauty industry and aims to demonstrate that luxury also stems from cultural heritage.

“We started something that didn’t exist before, which is creating luxury beauty in Mexico,” Tayara said. “We come to challenge the industry in the language, in the visuals, in the products and in sustainability,” he said.

For the co-founders, AORA’s debut in Sephora goes beyond having its products on the shelves of one of the world’s leading beauty retailers. It also signals support for a Mexican brand and recognition for the Latino consumer market in the U.S.

“I think there’s a recognition of the amount of people in the U.S. that are of Latino descent and speak Spanish. It is an amazing message and signal Sephora is sending to the industry,” Tayara acknowledged.

A growing curiosity in Mexican identity and design

AORA isn’t the first brand to place Mexican identity as the center of its appeal. In recent years, global brands have increasingly sought partnerships that draw on Mexico’s visual identity, cultural heritage and creative talent.

In 2025, cosmetic brand Rare Beauty, founded by U.S. actress and singer of Mexican descent Selena Gomez, launched an exclusive, limited-edition makeup kit in collaboration with the Mexican seasoning Tajín.

Back then, Gomez described the collaboration as a “celebration of what makes us unique — our culture, our energy and the moments that bring us together.”

Last year also saw H&M launch a collection in collaboration with fashion designer Lorena Saravia, marking the first time the Swedish brand collaborated with a Mexican designer.

Joining the trend is Mestiz, a design studio founded by Daniel Valero in San Miguel de Allende, which recently collaborated with French design house Hermès to design their shop windows in Mexico.

Mexico’s appeal to consumers

“Mexico is trendy,” Peñafiel said with a smile. “I think there’s a celebration of Mexican culture that hasn’t been seen before. The challenge was to pass the front page of the news that we see every day about the dangers of Mexico, because the reality is that when people come here, they are amazed and fall in love with the food, with the culture, with the colors, the beaches, the brands,” he said.

As AORA seeks to reshape perceptions of Mexican luxury abroad and share a positive image of the country, its founders say the brand’s ultimate purpose is more personal — to make consumers feel attractive.

“We buy beauty because we want to feel good about ourselves. Because we want to feel sexy,” Tayara said.

“Yes, we want our clients to feel sexy and hot, like Mexico,” Peñafiel said.

Gabriela Solis is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: Brazil Cruise Season Opens in Recife With a Quarter More Berths
World.content:
BRAZIL · TRAVEL

Key Facts — What happens Brazil’s 2026 to 2027 cruise season opens on 31 October when a ship docks at Recife in Pernambuco.

— How big it is Operators have scheduled 831,254 berths for the season, about 24 percent more than the last one.

— The real story Eight ships will make 675 scheduled calls along the Brazilian coast over the season.

— The catch Berths are capacity offered, not passengers carried, so the final count depends on how many sell.

— Who it affects Port cities from Recife to Rio de Janeiro that earn from day visitors, taxis, guides and restaurants.

— What comes next The season runs through the southern summer and into the first months of 2027.

Brazil’s cruise year begins on the last day of October, and it begins in Recife. The capacity on offer is up by almost a quarter.

The entrance to the port of Recife in Pernambuco, where Brazil’s cruise season begins on 31 October. (Photo: “Entrada do Porto do Recife (470448066)” by Henrique Pinto from Recife, Brazil, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

Brazil’s cruise year is about to start, and it starts in the northeast. The Brazil cruise season opens on 31 October 2026 when a ship docks at Recife.

The vessel scheduled to open it is the Corazul Buenavista. Recife is the capital of Pernambuco state.

The season is bigger than the last one by a clear margin. Operators have scheduled 831,254 berths, an increase of about 24 percent.

Estado de Minas reported the figures on 4 September 2026. They are attributed to CLIA Brasil, the cruise industry association.

What the Numbers Mean

A berth is a bed offered for sale, not a passenger who bought one. The distinction matters when reading a capacity figure.

So 831,254 berths describes what the industry has put on the market. The number of people who actually sail will be lower.

Eight ships are scheduled to operate on the Brazilian coast. Between them they will make 675 port calls.

That call figure is the one port cities care about. Each call is a day of visitors arriving with money to spend.

Why Recife Goes First

Recife sits on the northeastern shoulder of Brazil, closest to Europe and to the Atlantic crossing. Ships repositioning from the northern hemisphere arrive there first.

That geography makes it the natural opening port. It also makes it a common first and last call on longer itineraries.

The city has a working commercial port alongside the passenger terminal. Cruise calls sit inside a larger cargo operation.

For Pernambuco, the season is a seasonal employment event. Guides, drivers, restaurants and craft sellers plan around the calendar.

A large modern cruise ship at sea. Eight vessels are scheduled to work the Brazilian coast this season. (Photo: “Allure of the Seas (ship, 2009) 001 (cropped)” by Jorge in Brazil, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

One Thing to Get Right

Some summaries have described the season as already open. It is not.

The opening date is 31 October 2026, which is still weeks away. What was published this week is the schedule, not the start.

The 24 percent increase also refers to berths rather than to bookings or revenue. Those are different measures and they do not move together.

Reading a capacity plan as a performance result is the most common error with cruise numbers. It is worth avoiding before the season begins.

What a Cruise Call Is Worth

The economics are concentrated into a few hours. A ship arrives in the morning and leaves in the evening, and everything is spent in between.

Passengers buy tours, meals, taxis and souvenirs. Crew members shop for themselves, which is a smaller but steadier flow.

Ports also earn directly through fees. In some markets, a share of a per-passenger charge goes to the terminal operator.

None of that is guaranteed by a schedule. Weather, itinerary changes and health rules have all cut Brazilian seasons short before.

The Wider Travel Picture

Brazil’s tourism sector has had a strong run on the back of a competitive currency. A weaker real makes the country cheaper for visitors paying in dollars or euros.

Cruise capacity responds to that with a lag. Ships are deployed a year or more in advance, so this season reflects decisions taken well before now.

A 24 percent capacity increase is therefore a statement of confidence from the operators. It is also a bet that has to be filled.

For travellers, more capacity usually means better prices. The Brazil cruise season starting at the end of October is the first chance to test that.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does Brazil’s cruise season start?

On 31 October 2026, when the Corazul Buenavista docks at Recife in Pernambuco. The season runs through the southern summer into early 2027.

How big is the season?

Operators have scheduled 831,254 berths, about 24 percent more than the 2025 to 2026 season, with eight ships making 675 port calls.

Is a berth the same as a passenger?

No. A berth is a bed offered for sale. The number of passengers who actually sail depends on how many of those berths are booked.

Why does the season open in Recife?

Recife is the closest major Brazilian port to the Atlantic crossing, so ships repositioning from the northern hemisphere arrive there first.

Where do the figures come from?

From CLIA Brasil, the cruise industry association, reported by Estado de Minas on 4 September 2026 and by Catraca Livre earlier in the year.

Sources: Estado de Minas, Catraca Livre, CLIA Brasil, Rio Times.

World.title: Argentina Reserves Climb Back Above Fifty Billion Dollars
World.content:
ARGENTINA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Gross international reserves recovered past US$50 billion in the first days of September after a sharp August drop.

— How big the move was Reserves rose US$1,948 million on 1 September to close at US$50,205 million.

— The real story A further gain on 3 September came mainly from higher gold prices and a friendlier external market.

— The catch The central bank’s own dollar buying in September has averaged just US$19 million a day.

— Who it affects Importers, savers and bondholders, for whom the reserve level is the headline measure of stability.

— What comes next The buying streak has run 26 consecutive sessions, but at a much smaller daily size than before.

Argentina’s central bank is back above a round number it lost at the end of August. Very little of the recovery came from buying dollars.

The Central Bank of Argentina in Buenos Aires, which publishes the daily reserve figures. (Photo: “Banco Central de la República Argentina – Buenos Aires” by Banfield, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

Argentina’s central bank has recovered a number it lost in late August. Argentina reserves closed back above US$50 billion in the first days of September.

On 1 September gross international reserves rose by US$1,948 million. They closed at US$50,205 million.

Ámbito Financiero reported the figures. They come from the central bank’s daily publication.

The recovery followed a sharp fall at the end of August. That drop is what pushed the total below the threshold in the first place.

What Actually Drove the Argentina Reserves Recovery

This is where the story gets more interesting than the headline. Very little of the gain came from the central bank buying dollars.

On Thursday 3 September, reserves rose a further US$315 million to close at US$50,800 million. The explanation given was the rising value of gold.

A more favourable external environment for asset valuation was the second factor. Both are revaluation effects rather than inflows.

Central banks hold gold as part of their reserves. When the gold price rises, the reported total rises without a single ounce being bought.

The same applies to bonds and other assets held in the portfolio. A better market marks them up.

The Buying That Did Happen

The bank has been buying, and the streak is long. It extended to 26 consecutive trading sessions.

The size is the problem rather than the consistency. September’s average daily purchase was US$19 million.

The net foreign-exchange purchase balance for September reached US$58 million by 3 September. That is a small contribution against a total above fifty billion.

So the picture is a bank that keeps showing up in the market and buys very little each time. That is a deliberate pace, not an accident.

Plaza de Mayo in Buenos Aires. The central bank sits a few blocks away in the city’s financial district. (Photo: “Buenos Aires-Plaza de Mayo-Overview” by Barcex, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5.)

Why Gross Reserves Are a Rough Measure

The figure quoted in headlines is gross reserves. It counts everything the bank holds, including money that is owed to others.

Swap lines, bank deposits held in dollars and other liabilities sit inside that number. Net reserves, which strip those out, are considerably smaller.

This is why analysts and the International Monetary Fund track net figures. A gross total can rise while the usable cushion does not.

None of that makes the gross figure meaningless. It is the number markets react to, which gives it a life of its own.

What It Means in Practice

For importers, the Argentina reserves level is a proxy for access to foreign currency. A comfortable number reduces the pressure for administrative rationing.

For savers, it is a proxy for how long the exchange-rate regime can hold. Argentines read reserve figures the way others read inflation prints.

For bondholders, it feeds directly into the risk premium. Argentina’s country risk has been falling through this period.

And for the government, a round number recovered is a political asset. That is why the fifty billion threshold gets the attention it does.

What to Watch

The first thing is whether the gold effect reverses. Revaluation gains disappear as quickly as they arrive.

The second is the daily purchase size. Nineteen million dollars a day is a very slow way to build a cushion.

The third is the net figure rather than the gross one. That is the number that determines what the bank can actually spend.

The fourth is the calendar. Argentina reserves face known payment dates, and each one tests the level again.

Frequently Asked Questions

How high are Argentina’s reserves?

Gross international reserves closed at US$50,800 million on 3 September 2026, after rising US$1,948 million on 1 September to US$50,205 million.

What caused the increase?

Mainly the rising value of gold held in the portfolio and a more favourable external environment for asset valuation, rather than large purchases of dollars.

Is the central bank buying dollars?

Yes, but in small amounts. It has bought on 26 consecutive trading sessions, averaging US$19 million a day in September, with a net September balance of US$58 million by the 3rd.

What is the difference between gross and net reserves?

Gross reserves count everything the bank holds, including borrowed funds and liabilities. Net reserves strip those out and are considerably smaller.

Why does the fifty billion level matter?

It is a psychological threshold that markets and the government both watch. Reserve levels feed into the country risk premium and into expectations about the exchange rate.

Sources: Ámbito Financiero, Banco Central de la República Argentina, Rio Times.

World.title: Brazil Amazonas Poll Flips the Governor’s Race in Round Two
World.content:
BRAZIL · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened AtlasIntel published an Amazonas state poll showing Omar Aziz ahead in round one and behind in round two.

— The numbers Aziz takes 31 percent to Maria do Carmo’s 27.4 percent first, then loses the runoff 46.7 to 53.3.

— The real story A first-round lead means little when the rest of the field’s voters break heavily one way.

— The catch The presidential figures circulating for Amazonas this week are from a different poll taken in May.

— How it was done AtlasIntel interviewed 1,185 voters in the state between 29 August and 3 September.

— What comes next Brazil votes in October, with a runoff where no candidate passes fifty percent.

A new state poll in Amazonas shows the leading candidate losing. That is not a contradiction, and it is the most useful thing in the survey.

The Amazon Theatre in Manaus, capital of Amazonas. The state votes for governor in October. (Photo: “Amazon Theatre, Teatro Amazonas. Manaus, Brazil. 01” by Ridiculopathy, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

A new state survey has produced the kind of result that confuses headlines. The Brazil Amazonas poll shows one candidate leading the first round and losing the second.

The pollster is AtlasIntel. Poder360 published the figures on 4 September 2026.

In the first round, Omar Aziz of the PSD takes 31 percent. Maria do Carmo of the PL takes 27.4 percent.

In a runoff between the two, the order reverses. Maria do Carmo takes 53.3 percent against Aziz on 46.7 percent.

Why a Leader Can Lose

This pattern is common and it is not a polling error. It happens when the voters supporting everyone else prefer the second-placed candidate.

In a first round, support is spread across many names. In a runoff, those voters have to choose between two.

If most of them move the same way, a four-point first-round lead disappears. That is what these numbers describe.

The practical reading is that Aziz has the largest single bloc and Maria do Carmo has the wider acceptance. Those are different political assets.

How the Poll Was Conducted

AtlasIntel interviewed 1,185 voters in Amazonas. Fieldwork ran from 29 August to 3 September 2026.

The margin of error is three percentage points at a 95 percent confidence level. That matters for the runoff figure.

A 53.3 to 46.7 split is a gap of 6.6 points. That is outside the margin, so the lead is real rather than statistical noise.

The first-round gap of 3.6 points is inside it. In other words, first place in round one is genuinely uncertain.

Rainforest near Manaus. Amazonas is Brazil’s largest state by area and among its smallest by electorate. (Photo: “AMAZON RAINFOREST IN BRAZIL IN MANAUS – Amazonia fotos aérea região de Manaus 2005 AM Brasil – panoramio” by James Martins, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.)

A Correction About the Presidential Numbers

A second set of figures has been circulating alongside this poll. It puts Flávio Bolsonaro at 48 percent against Lula on 41.3 percent in Amazonas.

Those numbers are not from this survey. The closest verified figures are 47.8 percent to 41.7 percent.

They come from an AtlasIntel poll in the same state published on 15 May 2026. That is nearly four months earlier.

The direction of travel is similar, and the date is not. Attaching May figures to a September poll makes a trend look like news.

Why Amazonas Is Worth Watching

Amazonas is Brazil’s largest state by area. Its electorate is small relative to that size, and most of it is concentrated in Manaus.

That concentration makes state races unusually volatile. A shift in the capital moves the whole result.

The state also matters economically beyond its population. The Manaus Free Trade Zone is a large industrial employer with its own tax regime.

Any governor there deals directly with federal decisions about that regime. It is one reason national parties invest in the race.

How This Fits the National Picture

Brazil votes in October with two rounds. Governorships and the presidency are decided on the same calendar.

National polling has tightened sharply. Recent surveys have shown Flávio Bolsonaro level with or ahead of Lula, depending on the pollster.

State races do not simply follow the national one. A governor’s contest can turn on local records and local alliances.

What the Brazil Amazonas poll adds is a warning about reading first-round numbers. In a two-round system, the leader is not the favourite by definition.

What to Watch Next

The first thing is whether the first-round order settles. A 3.6-point gap inside the margin can reverse without anything real changing.

The second is transfer behaviour. Runoff projections rest on assumptions about where eliminated candidates’ voters go.

The third is the next wave of state polling. One survey is a snapshot, and Brazilian races have moved fast this year.

The fourth is turnout in Manaus. In a state this size, the capital effectively decides it.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the new Amazonas poll show?

Omar Aziz of the PSD leads the first round with 31 percent against Maria do Carmo of the PL on 27.4 percent, but loses a runoff 46.7 to 53.3 percent.

Who conducted it?

AtlasIntel, with 1,185 voters interviewed in Amazonas between 29 August and 3 September 2026, at a margin of error of three points and 95 percent confidence.

How can the leader lose the second round?

Because voters supporting other candidates in round one break heavily towards the second-placed candidate. A narrow first-round lead does not survive that.

Are the presidential figures from this poll?

No. Figures of 48 to 41.3 percent circulating for Amazonas are not from this survey. The closest verified numbers are 47.8 to 41.7 percent, published on 15 May 2026.

When does Brazil vote?

In October 2026, with a second round where no candidate reaches fifty percent. Governorships and the presidency are decided on the same calendar.

Sources: AtlasIntel, Poder360, Exame, Rio Times.

World.title: Mexico Border Drones Were Smugglers’, Defence Chief Says
World.content:
MEXICO · DEFENSE & SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened Mexico’s defence secretary said drones shot down by the United States on the northern border were flown by smuggling groups.

— Who said it General Ricardo Trevilla Trejo, speaking at the president’s daily press conference in Zacatecas on Friday.

— The real story He described ordinary commercial drones used to check whether smuggling routes are clear of authorities.

— The catch He attributed the identification to United States authorities rather than to Mexican intelligence.

— Who it affects Communities and businesses along the border, where drone activity is now a routine security concern.

— What comes next No figures on detections, downings or countermeasures were released alongside the statement.

Mexico’s defence secretary was asked who was flying the drones the Americans have been shooting down. His answer was unusually specific, and it came with a caveat.

The border fence near Anapra, New Mexico, on the frontier with Ciudad Juárez. (Photo: “Anapra New Mexico partial border fence” by Jidanni, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Mexico has given an account of who is flying the aircraft being shot down at its northern frontier. The Mexico border drones belong to smuggling groups, the defence secretary said.

The speaker was General Ricardo Trevilla Trejo. He is Mexico’s secretary of national defence.

He spoke on Friday 4 September 2026 at the president’s daily morning press conference. That day’s conference was held in Zacatecas.

El Financiero and El Economista both reported his remarks. The wording is worth reading closely, because of where he sourced it.

What He Actually Said

Trevilla described what American commanders had told their Mexican counterparts. The information came from joint border commanders’ meetings.

Those authorities, he said, mention that criminal groups use the drones. The aircraft are commercial models that capture images.

The purpose he described is straightforward reconnaissance. The operators want to see whether routes are clear and free of any official presence.

El Financiero reported him identifying the users more narrowly. He referred to groups that traffic undocumented migrants.

The Attribution Matters

This is the detail most likely to be lost in summary. Trevilla did not present the identification as a Mexican intelligence finding.

He relayed what United States authorities had said in bilateral meetings. That is a meaningful difference in a subject where both governments guard their sources.

It also explains the careful phrasing. A minister repeating a partner’s assessment is not making his own accusation.

Reporting it any other way overstates what Mexico has claimed. The distinction is small on the page and large in practice.

A small quadcopter being launched at night. Commercial drones of this type are cheap, quiet and hard to trace. (Photo: “332 ESFS sUAS division launches first quadcopter in AFCENT history (9384785)” by U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Karalyn Degraffenreed, via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.)

Why Cheap Drones Are a Security Problem

The aircraft described are not military hardware. They are commercial quadcopters of the kind sold to photographers and surveyors.

That is precisely what makes them useful to smuggling networks. They are inexpensive, widely available and produce no paper trail.

Flown ahead of a crossing, one can show whether a patrol is parked on a road. That converts a guess into knowledge for the people organising the crossing.

The same technology has civilian uses across the border region. Any countermeasure therefore has to distinguish between a survey flight and a scouting run.

What Was Not Said

No numbers were released. There is no published figure for how many drones have been detected or brought down.

No named group was identified. Trevilla spoke of criminal groups and of migrant-smuggling networks in general terms.

No Mexican countermeasure programme was announced alongside the remarks. Nor was any joint operation described.

And no cartel was named. Reports summarising this as a cartel surveillance programme go further than the minister did.

The Context on the Border

Security cooperation between the two countries has been under strain and under renegotiation for two years. Border commanders’ meetings are one of the working channels that continued through it.

Drone activity has become a standing item in those meetings. The United States has been shooting some of them down, which is why the question arose at all.

Mexico has separately been pressed on cartel extraditions and on drug flows. A federal judge suspended one senior cartel figure’s extradition this week.

So the Mexico border drones statement lands in a busy file. It is a small technical answer inside a much larger argument about who does what along that line.

For residents and businesses in the border states, the practical effect is limited for now. Nothing announced on Friday changes how anyone flies, farms or ships across it.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who said the drones belong to smugglers?

General Ricardo Trevilla Trejo, Mexico’s secretary of national defence, at the president’s daily press conference in Zacatecas on Friday 4 September 2026.

What kind of drones are they?

Commercial models that capture images. According to the account he relayed, operators use them to check whether smuggling routes are clear of official presence.

Did Mexico identify the groups itself?

No. Trevilla attributed the identification to United States authorities speaking at joint border commanders’ meetings, rather than to Mexican intelligence findings.

Were any cartels named?

No. He referred to criminal groups and, in one account, to networks trafficking undocumented migrants. No specific organisation was identified.

How many drones have been shot down?

No figures were released. Neither detection numbers nor countermeasure programmes were announced alongside the statement.

Sources: El Financiero, El Economista, Rio Times.

World.title: Venezuela Oil Is Not the Government’s to Sell, Machado Says
World.content:
VENEZUELA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened María Corina Machado publicly questioned the oil arrangement between Washington and Venezuela’s interim government.

— What she said She said the wealth of the subsoil belongs to the Venezuelan people, not to what she called an illegitimate regime.

— The real story Her objection is about legal authority to sign, not about whether foreign investment is desirable.

— The catch She has no power to block any contract, and none of the parties has responded to her publicly.

— Who she was talking about She described the current occupants of the presidential palace as enemies of the United States.

— What comes next Contracts keep being signed, including a 25-year oilfield deal formalised the day after her remarks.

The opposition leader has put a direct objection on the record against the deals Washington is signing in Caracas. Her argument is about who has the right to sign them.

María Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader, at a public appearance. (Photo: “Maria Corina Machado” by Carlos Díaz, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

Venezuela’s opposition leader has objected in public to the deals being signed in Caracas. Venezuela oil wealth, María Corina Machado said, does not belong to the government negotiating it away.

The Guardian published her remarks on 3 September 2026. WION carried them the following day.

Her wording was precise and repeated. The wealth of the subsoil, she said, does not belong to an illegitimate regime.

It belongs to the Venezuelan people. That is the whole of her argument, compressed into one sentence.

What the Venezuela Oil Objection Is About

The United States has spent the past month signing agreements with Venezuela’s interim government. That government is led by Delcy Rodríguez.

The deals cover oil production, the electricity grid and a restructuring of the country’s defaulted debt. American officials have described a timeline for all three.

Machado is not arguing that foreign investment is wrong. She is arguing that this particular government has no standing to grant it.

In her words, the current occupants of the presidential palace lack the right or the democratic mandate to negotiate Venezuela’s natural resources. That is a legal claim as much as a political one.

The Sharpest Line

She went further than describing the government as illegitimate. She described its members as enemies of the United States.

That is aimed at Washington rather than at Caracas. It asks the American administration why it is dealing with people it spent years sanctioning.

The framing is uncomfortable for both governments. It puts the question of legitimacy back into a conversation that had moved on to contracts and timelines.

No response from the American administration or from the Venezuelan government has been reported. Neither has engaged with her publicly on this.

A Venezuelan opposition banner from the 2014 protests listing the movement’s core grievances. (Photo: “Opposition sign Venezuela 2014” by NoonIcarus, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

What Happened the Day After

Events did not pause for the objection. On 4 September, a 25-year contract for the Bare oilfield was signed in a ceremony broadcast on state television.

The parties were Colombia’s Grupo Gilinski, the oil company GeoPark and the state producer PDVSA. It is one of several agreements concluded in the past fortnight.

American companies have also signed. The energy secretary was in Caracas on 3 September discussing the electricity grid.

So the practical answer to Machado’s objection has been to keep signing. That is the position as it stands.

Why Her Objection Is Not Only Rhetoric

Venezuela oil contracts signed by a government whose legitimacy is contested carry a specific risk. A later government can seek to annul them.

Venezuela has done this before. Contracts from earlier periods have been renegotiated, nationalised or challenged in arbitration.

That history is why investors ask about legal certainty before they ask about geology. It is also why Machado’s words are read carefully by people who are not Venezuelan.

Nothing she said creates a legal obstacle today. It records an objection that could be cited later, which is a different kind of leverage.

Where the Opposition Stands

Machado remains the most prominent figure in the Venezuelan opposition. Her public role has continued through a period in which the political landscape changed sharply.

The interim government under Delcy Rodríguez is the counterpart Washington has chosen to deal with. That choice is the thing Machado is contesting.

She has not called for sanctions to be reimposed in the reported remarks. Her objection is narrower and is about consent rather than punishment.

For readers following Venezuela oil, the useful summary is short. The deals are being signed, the objection is on the record, and nobody in a position to decide has answered it.

More: Venezuela news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Machado say?

That the wealth of Venezuela’s subsoil does not belong to what she called an illegitimate regime but to the Venezuelan people, and that the government has no mandate to negotiate the country’s natural resources.

When and where did she say it?

Her remarks were published by The Guardian on 3 September 2026 and carried by WION on 4 September, in coverage of the US oil arrangement with Venezuela’s interim government.

Who is she objecting to?

The interim government led by Delcy Rodríguez, whose members she described as enemies of the United States, and by implication the American officials negotiating with it.

Can she block the deals?

No. She holds no office and no legal instrument to stop a contract. Her objection is a public record that could be cited by a future government or in arbitration.

Has anyone responded?

No response from the American administration or the Venezuelan government has been reported. A 25-year oilfield contract was signed the day after her remarks.

Sources: The Guardian, WION, Rio Times.

World.title: Cuba Health Alert: US Embassy Warns Over Water and Medicine
World.content:
CUBA · TRAVEL

Key Facts — What happened The US embassy in Havana issued a health alert on Friday about a sharp rise in diarrhoeal illness across Cuba.

— What it blames The alert links the increase to the deterioration of the island’s water and electricity infrastructure.

— The real story It advises visitors to bring their own basic medicines because pharmacies and hospitals are short of them.

— The catch This is a travel advisory, not an outbreak declaration, and no case numbers have been published.

— Who it affects Anyone travelling to Cuba, and residents who depend on the same water and pharmacy networks.

— What comes next The embassy tells travellers to avoid tap water and to be careful with perishable food.

The American embassy in Havana has told visitors to treat the tap water as unsafe and to pack their own painkillers and antibiotics. The reason it gives is infrastructure, not weather.

A street in Old Havana. The embassy alert ties rising illness to failing water and power infrastructure. (Photo: “AJM 065 Habana Vieja street” by Arnoud Joris Maaswinkel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)
